p: Part 1: Intensity in Cardio
x: Cardio Regulations 1 ended with workload: the amount of work done, which in cardio is determined by speed, distance and time. This lecture starts with intensity, this time in terms of cardio. (The earlier intensity lecture was entirely about weight training.) Class question: What is intensity, if workload is the amount of work done? One answer ("the amount of work done with respect to time, distance and speed") was in fact the definition of workload. The correct idea: Intensity is the level of effort applied while doing that work, or the difficulty level of the work, within a time frame. Analogy: an exam. Thirty students sit an exam with 30 multiple-choice questions. Solving 30 questions is the workload and it is the same for everyone. But the questions are not equally easy for everyone: Students who have prepared well put in a low level of effort, so the intensity is low for them. Students who have not prepared well put in a high level of effort, so the intensity is high for them. Workload is equal for all, but intensity may vary. Intensity is nothing but the level of effort applied.

t: 1.2 How intensity was decided in weight training
p: Part 1: Intensity in Cardio
x: In weight training, intensity was determined with the RM method (and the RIR method). The logic: RM is the number of repetitions a person can do at most before failure. When comparing two people, or the same person in two different sets, the set in which fewer reps could be done before failure was the more intense one. So the RM number was the key deciding value: Lower the RM, higher the intensity. Cardio also needs a number that decides whether intensity is low or high. | Weight training | Cardio | Deciding value | RM (reps before failure) | HR during the cardio activity | Relationship | Lower RM means higher intensity | Higher HR means higher intensity |

t: 1.3 Heart rate: the deciding factor in cardio
p: Part 1: Intensity in Cardio
x: Two statements were written on the board: Intensity in cardio is determined by the HR during the cardio activity. (In brackets: HR as a percentage of MHR.) The higher the HR during cardio, the greater the intensity. Note that it is not any random heart rate: it is the heart rate during cardio activity, and it must be turned into a percentage of the person's own MHR.

p: Part 1: Intensity in Cardio
x: To understand the topics, one hypothetical client is carried from topic to topic. Sumit is a new client. He is 20 years old. That is all that is known at first, and more details are added as the lecture goes on. A vertical intensity scale (also called the heart rate scale) is drawn for Sumit: At the bottom is the RHR: the heart rate from which his day starts, when he wakes up in the morning, with no physical effort and only involuntary metabolic functions taking place. This end is written 0% efforts (the "no effort" zone). At the top is the MHR: the maximum number of times his heart can beat in a minute. This end is 100% efforts. MHR for Sumit: 220 minus age = 220 minus 20 = 200 bpm. Analogy: a bottle filled to the brim. A one litre bottle filled to the brim overflows if more water is added. In the same way a person's heart rate cannot go beyond the MHR (200 for Sumit): it is the maximum, the 100% effort level. (The bottle is then used a second time to practise percentages: if 500 ml is drunk from the full bottle, 500 ml remains, so the bottle is at 50% of its capacity.)

t: 1.5 Turning a heart rate into an intensity percentage
p: Part 1: Intensity in Cardio
x: Sumit is given an activity on a treadmill and his heart rate is checked after some time. The first statement says intensity is found from the HR during cardio. HR = 100 bpm. This is 100 out of 200, so he is working at 50%. That is Sumit's intensity. After 5 minutes HR = 180 bpm. 180 out of 200 is 90%. Later he slows down and HR = 160 bpm. 160 out of 200 is 80%. The method is: Intensity (%) = (HR during cardio ÷ MHR) × 100 Intensity scale for the case study client Observations from the scale: As the HR goes up, the intensity (in percent) goes up. The lower on the scale, the lower the intensity (statement 2). The key learning: the HR during cardio is the main input, and the only thing done with it is to see what percentage it is of that person's MHR. Do not copy these numbers. A client with a heart rate of 100 is not automatically at 50% intensity. The 50% came from using Sumit's MHR of 200. For any client, first find that client's own MHR and take the percentage of that, not of 200. The value 200 is only used for the case study so that the calculation is easy to follow (a 20 year old is chosen for an easy MHR).

p: Part 2: Classification of Cardio Intensity
x: In weight training, after the RM method came a chart that gave predefined RM ranges for low, moderate and high intensity and linked each to a training level. For example, beginners (low intensity, so a high RM number) worked in roughly the 15 to 20 RM range, and as intensity rose the range narrowed, to about 2 to 6 RM for super advanced, and 1 RM was the heaviest and most intense. (This is recalled from the earlier lecture.) The same idea is applied to cardio, but with percentages of MHR instead of RM. The same scale is used. Intensity | % of MHR | Trainee level | Low | 50 to 60% | Beginner | Moderate | 60 to 70% | Intermediate | High | 70 to 85% (pay attention: not 80 to 85) | Advanced | Very high | Above 85% | Super advanced | Classification of cardio intensity

p: Part 2: Classification of Cardio Intensity
x: Clients with less than about 2 to 3 months of cardio training experience are beginners. They start their cardio journey from this level. Restarting clients are also beginners. Someone who did cardio before but took a gap (personal reasons, an underlying health condition, rehab) cannot be started directly at moderate or high just because of old experience. They go step by step again from the beginning.

t: 2.3 Promotion is about performance, not the calendar
p: Part 2: Classification of Cardio Intensity
x: Consider a person who followed the prescribed intensity and every instruction for the 2 to 3 month beginner phase. This applies to weight training as well as cardio: A person is not promoted from beginner to intermediate just because three months have passed on the calendar. What if the person showed up only about three times in three months, was not consistent or regular, only checked social media during the session, and did not follow the instructions, neither in the one hour with the trainer nor in the remaining 23 hours (nutrition, rest, recovery)? Such a person has not earned the next level. This is the reason for the next two lectures, Fitness Testing 1 and 2. A fitness test is done on the first day and again after the beginner phase (about 3 months), for all five components of fitness. The numbers show whether there is a significant improvement. That is progress tracking, and that is how a client is promoted. It is not "you joined on 1 January, now it is 1 April, here is your intermediate certificate". When the improvement is seen, the level of effort (the difficulty, in short the intensity) is increased to 60 to 70%, moderate, and the client is called an intermediate. Using time as a rough guide only (performance matters as well): Level | Rough experience | Beginner | Less than 3 months | Intermediate | More than 3 months and less than 1 year | Advanced | After a year of consistent performance and progress, when the client is ready for promotion, 70 to 85% | Super advanced | Can go above 85% easily, smoothly and safely, and come back without fatigue and without risk (athletes and sports people) |

t: 2.4 Super advanced, and an unofficial "elite" level
p: Part 2: Classification of Cardio Intensity
x: Super advanced means those who can take their intensity above 85% safely and consistently and come back from it. The examples mentioned: top footballers and cricketers (such as Kohli, Messi, Ronaldo). There is no official category above super advanced, but if there were one it would be "elite": people like Usain Bolt and Michael Phelps, who can go not just above 85% but very close to their MHR and come back safely. Their blood circulation system (heart anatomy, blood vessels, stroke volume, cardiac output, VO2 max) works extraordinarily well. The point of mentioning it: it is not everybody's cup of tea to reach there safely and return. Safety rule. Some clients, taking it on their ego, insist "I can go near 100%, even to 200 and come back". Even beginners say this. Never take that risk, at least under your guidance. They might reach 200 but then go "somewhere else" and not return from the treadmill. Things have to go step by step, and the client must understand that the whole cardiorespiratory system has to be made ready to go to a level and return efficiently, smoothly and safely. That is why there are steps to pass before going to the next level.

t: 2.5 Student question: can intensity change from day to day?
p: Part 2: Classification of Cardio Intensity
x: Q: Sumit's day-to-day condition may change (for example if he is not healthy). Does his intensity change daily? A: It is not changed daily. An intensity level is set for the client based on the client's current training level, through several factors (covered in Part 3). Once set, the client works at that level. From time to time a fitness test is conducted to see how the client performs at the allocated intensity. A task is given at that intensity and the client has to show consistent performance. Judging from one day to the next cannot tell whether the level works. The numbers from consistent performance show whether the decided intensity worked.

t: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: The word prescribing fits: just as a doctor prescribes a medicine, a trainer prescribes (assigns) an intensity level to a client. Meeting Sumit for the very first time, his name and age are not enough to decide at which level to start his cardio. More inputs are needed, which is why there is an initial client interview with small forms to fill in. The course's training program delivery module includes a client interview form with questions of this kind (lifestyle, training experience and others). With these answers, one key decision is the cardio intensity to start with. The class was asked to suggest factors one by one. The six factors are shown below with Sumit's values (the values were added to the board later, see 3.9). Six factors with the case study values

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: This tells at a broad level whether the person has ever done cardio. If not, that is a separate case. If yes, a lot can be learned: The type of aerobic activity done (weight-bearing impact-based, weight-bearing non-impact-based, or non-weight-bearing non-impact-based). The frequency: how many sessions per week and how much time per session. Preferences: morning or evening, outdoor or indoor.

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: Lifestyle is a big umbrella. It includes: Food habits and daily nutrition: someone may follow strict, well balanced nutrition while someone else eats pizzas and burgers daily. Daily routine and nature of the job, and how much physical activity it involves: a corporate employee on a laptop all day versus an architect moving from site to site and climbing stairs (no lifts installed yet), a salesman or anyone on a field job. Habits: staying away from smoking and drinking versus daily drinking at a fixed time. Sleep, which has both quality and quantity: good quality sleep of 7 to 8 hours versus 3 to 4 hours at random, inconsistent times. Stress also comes under this heading.

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: The client may have a heart related, joint related or neurological condition. If the trainer is not aware and straight away gives advanced, high intensity, the client could suffer a severe condition during cardio. Being aware of the medical background is crucial.

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: Age is sometimes forgotten while looking for something fancy. Why is it needed? Student answer: different intensities are given to children and older people. The lecture pointed out that this reasoning can go wrong, because of stereotyping: Stereotyping means that when a fact is very popular or widely believed, people start assuming it must be true. The stereotype here: a 60 year old must be a beginner, while a 20 year old can be given more than beginner, just because of age. A hypothetical case (not a generalisation). Consider only the first three factors. The 20 year old has nil training experience, a sedentary lifestyle (junk food, parties, smoking, drinking, wrecked sleep, hardly moving) and the 60 year old has never missed a session in 30 or 40 years, a very active lifestyle, clean nutrition, no poor habits, perfect sleep, and a clear medical background (no heart or joint issue). Going by age alone would be unfair to the 60 year old, who stands at a much better place. This is not saying all 20 year olds or all 60 year olds are like that. The real, basic reason age is needed: without age the MHR cannot be calculated (MHR = 220 minus age), and without MHR the intensity cannot be determined.

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: RHR is a quantifiable number and an indicator of a person's cardiorespiratory fitness, so it shows the person's current fitness level on the day of meeting the trainer. Normal range: 60 to 80 bpm. The lower the better (promised: why, in Part 4). One chronic adaptation of cardio is that it helps in reducing the RHR.

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: What does the client want to achieve and why are they doing cardio? Two types of goals: A specific goal: for example taking part in HYROX, a marathon, or climbing Mount Everest. A basic goal: just a basic level of fitness so that day-to-day tasks are done efficiently and any emergency can be handled with efficiency. This is the definition of GPP (general physical preparedness).

p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: The list is not a rank: it does not mean training experience is most important and goal is least important. All six are equally important and have to be seen collectively while taking the decision. "Not one but all six." The slides list the same factors with slightly different names: age, medical background, past training history (FITT), current fitness level, lifestyle and goal. Training experience corresponds to past training history, and the RHR corresponds to current fitness level.

t: 3.9 Applying the six factors to Sumit
p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: More assumptions are made about Sumit for the case study (written in red on the board): Factor | Sumit | 1. Training experience | Nil. He has never seen a treadmill and does not even know where the park near his home is. | 2. Lifestyle | Average for a 20 year old student: gets up late, goes to college, eats mostly outside in cafes with friends, junk food, an occasional party, entertainment is Xbox, PlayStation and Netflix, no outdoor activity, no physical activity or workout. | 3. Medical background | Clear. No condition yet. | 4. Age | 20 years (for MHR), so MHR = 200. | 5. RHR | 80 bpm. With these data his RHR is certainly not in the good zone near 60. It is at the borderline but on the higher, poor side. | 6. Goal | GPP. No special goal, he only wants general physical preparedness. | Decision (made together in class): Sumit starts as a beginner. (If it were up to the lecture, there would be one more category, "pre-beginner", but the course works with what exists.) One topic paves the platform for the next: from here the intensity is 50 to 60%.

t: 3.10 From a percentage to a number the client can use
p: Part 3: Factors to Consider While Prescribing Cardio Intensity
x: Imagine Sumit's very first cardio session. The trainer gives a gym tour, familiarises him with the weight training and cardio machines and sections, and then does mobility drills. (Before a workout, the stretching to do is dynamic, not static.) On the treadmill the trainer shows how it starts and stops, speed up, incline up and down, and the emergency stop. Then a task is set: do this for a given number of minutes at a given speed, at an intensity between 50 and 60%. (A beginner is not told "because you are a beginner".) Sumit will naturally ask: do I have to take a calculator and run on the treadmill and calculate? No. The percentages are the background science for the trainer. The client needs a number that is easy to notice during cardio: a heart rate. So the percentage is converted into a target heart rate (THR): "T" stands for target, a target that is achievable for the client. The client can then follow a number on a device (a wrist heart rate monitor such as a smartwatch, a chest strap, or others covered later in this lecture) instead of a percentage. The next part shows how to calculate the THR.

t: Part 4: Calculating the Target Heart Rate (THR)
4.1 A single value or a range?
p: Part 4: Calculating the Target Heart Rate (THR)
x: A THR can be given in two formats: a single number (for example 155 bpm) or a range (for example 150 to 160 bpm). Which makes more sense? It should be a range. Heart rate is not fixed all the time. It fluctuates, like room temperature, by plus or minus 1, 2, 3, 4. For a 20 minute activity, reaching 155 is possible, but maintaining exactly that number is impossible. A range tells the client: do not go below 150 and do not exceed 160, stay in that range. Analogy: buying a shirt. Walking into a high-end store and asking for a shirt of exactly 4,832 rupees will get a person shown the door. A range works: "between 4,500 and 5,000" or "between 4,000 and 5,000". (The student reason "beginners do not want to look at a particular number" was not correct, and the answer "an approximate value, not a particular heartbeat for every person" was close to the point.) So the THR has a lower limit (L) and an upper limit (U), and in both methods the formula is calculated twice: once for the lower limit and once for the upper limit. (The board shows 155 bpm on one side and 150 to 160 bpm with L and U marked on the other.)

p: Part 4: Calculating the Target Heart Rate (THR)
x: Formula: THR = MHR × intensity, which is THR = (220 minus age) × intensity. Nickname: because the formula uses MHR, this is also called the MHR method. It is the same method, so do not get confused if an exam, viva, MCQ or interview uses either name. Make the formula ready to use by opening up MHR (breaking a complex formula into its simplest form), then put in values. For Sumit: age 20, beginner (50 to 60%), RHR 80 bpm. The lower limit uses the lower intensity, 50%, written as 50/100. The upper limit uses the upper intensity, 60%, written as 60/100. | Calculation | Result | THR (L) | (220 minus 20) × 50/100 = 200 × 50/100 | 100 bpm | THR (U) | (220 minus 20) × 60/100 = 200 × 60/100 | 120 bpm | THR range | | 100 to 120 bpm | The RHR of 80 is not used in this method.

t: 4.3 Does this range make sense? The loophole
p: Part 4: Calculating the Target Heart Rate (THR)
x: The lecture then validates the range. There is "something fishy" here, which is why a second method was needed. Draw Sumit's scale again: RHR 80 at the bottom, MHR 200 at the top, and the THR zone 100 to 120 according to this method. A story shows the problem: Moment | Heart rate | Wakes up in the morning, resting | 80 | Morning routine, then a 10 minute walk to the gym, then three floors by stairs (no lift) to the gym door | about 90 | Meets the trainer, gym tour, mobility drills, waiting at the treadmill | about 95 | So the cardio starts at 95. If Sumit simply continues to walk casually for a couple of minutes, chatting to a friend on the next treadmill, his heart rate will be in the 100 to 120 THR zone within a couple of minutes. Does he look like someone working at 50% intensity? No. That is the catch. THR zones of the two methods for the same client The loophole: this method gives a very generalised, age-predicted THR. It considers only one variable, age. It never considers Sumit's current fitness level, which is exactly what the RHR of 80 indicates. Following the formula, all 20 year old beginners would get the same THR, but not all 20 year olds have the same RHR: one may be near 60, one at 70, one at 80. It is not fair for all three to get the same THR. Analogy: buying jeans. Three friends, all 30 years old, ask for a pair of jeans and the salesman says "30 year old, 36 waist" for all three. The body composition is not the same for all 30 year olds. Sizes vary for shoes, shirts and everything, and so do fitness levels. A customised THR is needed that considers the person's current fitness level, not a generalised one. This is why Karvonen (an exercise physiologist) came up with a more valid and reliable method.

t: 4.4 Method 2: The heart rate reserve (HRR) method (Karvonen's formula)
p: Part 4: Calculating the Target Heart Rate (THR)
x: This is the HRR method, also known by its inventor's name as Karvonen's formula. (This is the point where HRR, promised in the previous lecture, is explained in detail.) Formula: THR = HRR × intensity + RHR. Like before, MHR was multiplied with intensity. Here HRR is multiplied with intensity and then the resting heart rate is added. Make it ready to use, step by step: Step | Form | 1 | THR = HRR × intensity + RHR | 2 | Open HRR: THR = (MHR minus RHR) × intensity + RHR | 3 | Open MHR: THR = (220 minus age minus RHR) × intensity + RHR | Heart rate reserve method on the board Using the same case data (the previous data was intentionally not erased, so the same client gets a drastically different THR): | Calculation | Result | THR (L) | (220 minus 20 minus 80) × 50/100 + 80 = 120 × 50/100 + 80 = 60 + 80 | 140 bpm | THR (U) | (220 minus 20 minus 80) × 60/100 + 80 = 120 × 60/100 + 80 = 72 + 80 | 152 bpm | THR range | | 140 to 152 bpm | Order of calculation (BODMAS). Solve the brackets first: 220 minus 20 = 200 (the MHR), and 200 minus 80 = 120 (so both brackets are 120). Then multiplication before addition: 120 × 50% is half of 120 = 60, and then 60 + 80 = 140. Do not jump to 120 + 80 first, or the answer changes entirely. Likewise 120 × 60% = 72, and 72 + 80 = 152. (The board shows the letters B, O, D, M, A, S written down the side as a reminder.) Comparison. The earlier range was 100 to 120. Now the lower limit (140) is higher than the previous upper limit (120). | Age-predicted (MHR) method | HRR (Karvonen) method | Formula | THR = (220 minus age) × intensity | THR = (220 minus age minus RHR) × intensity + RHR | Variables used | Age only | Age and RHR (current fitness level) | Sumit (20 years, RHR 80, 50 to 60%) | 100 to 120 bpm | 140 to 152 bpm | Result | Generalised | Customised | Age-predicted method on the board

t: 4.5 Heart rate reserve: why a lower RHR is better
p: Part 4: Calculating the Target Heart Rate (THR)
x: HRR is more than the number 120. Look at it as a range, a reserve for the heart to go up: it starts from the RHR (80 for Sumit) and can go up to the MHR (200). It is like a reserve meter or a reserve tank: the heart always fluctuates in this meter, it can go up but not beyond 200. Analogy 1: the reserve fuel tank of a vehicle. Cars and bikes have a reserve tank so that when fuel runs low a petrol pump can be found and the rider is not stuck in the middle of nowhere. Is it positive to have one? Yes. The bigger the reserve, the better: if 3 litres are not enough to reach a pump, an additional 2 litres (5 litres in total) helps. Analogy 2: extra cash. Someone who travels by metro keeps extra cash in the backpack as well as the wallet, in case the wallet is stolen. If it is only a 100 rupee note, they can only take a cab home. With 500 rupees they could also enjoy a meal and a coffee and then take the cab home. Bigger reserve, better. Applying it to the heart. If a person's heart rate reaches very close to the maximum while doing some amount of work, the person starts to feel exhausted because they are near their all-out level. If Sumit had a bigger reserve (RHR 70 instead of 80), the same type and amount of work leaves him still far from exhaustion, because he has a bigger tank, thanks to a lower RHR. This answers why a lower RHR is better: As the RHR goes lower, the tank expands. Mathematically: HRR = MHR minus RHR, so reducing the RHR widens the reserve (the RHR has a minus sign next to it). MHR cannot be played with: it is based on age and changes by just one digit every year. But RHR can be worked on by doing cardio, because cardio reduces the RHR. When the RHR drops, the capacity of the heart to go up widens. The guitar class story (hypothetical). Sumit finishes college at 4:00 pm and has guitar class at 4:15 nearby, in a building where the class is on a floor reached only by stairs. Stage | Story | RHR 80 (current) | Walks to the class but reaches the building at 4:25, exhausted. After climbing one floor he sits on the stairs gasping for breath. Reaches the class at 4:35, recovers by 4:40, and one track has already been taught. | After 3 months of cardio, RHR 70 | Reaches the building around 4:20, climbs the floors without a break, waits a short time at the third floor at 4:25 (the recovery time has reduced) and reaches the class at 4:28. | After 3 more months, RHR 60 | His fittest version, with an even bigger reserve. Reaches the building at 4:10, needs no break, and is seated with his friends at 4:15 sharp. | Guitar class story The client sees an actual performance improvement in day-to-day life as well. That is how crucial a bigger reserve is.

t: 4.6 Why the HRR method is customised
p: Part 4: Calculating the Target Heart Rate (THR)
x: The HRR method is customised for Sumit because it considers his current fitness level as well as his age: 140 to 152 (on the board: THR 140 to 152, marked on the scale between 140 and 152 with HRR as the bracket from RHR to MHR). The age-predicted method would have given 100 to 120 whether Sumit was at his unfit side or at his fittest, because his age and therefore his MHR stay the same (20, 200). Now think of three different clients, with RHR 80, 70 and 60 (drawn on the board as three scales with the same MHR of 200; called Client A, B and C here). If all three also got 140 to 152, that would be unfair. Each one's calculation should keep in mind their current fitness level, so the formula uses their own RHR (70 and 60 instead of 80). This gives a foolproof, valid, accurate and customised value, and this is the method accepted worldwide. Reserve tank for three clients The THR values for Clients B and C in the figure were computed for these notes with the same formula, to show the effect (they were not worked out in the lecture): Client | RHR | HRR (200 minus RHR) | THR (L) | THR (U) | Range | Client A (same RHR as Sumit) | 80 | 120 | 120 × 0.5 + 80 = 140 | 120 × 0.6 + 80 = 152 | 140 to 152 | Client B | 70 | 130 | 130 × 0.5 + 70 = 135 | 130 × 0.6 + 70 = 148 | 135 to 148 | Client C | 60 | 140 | 140 × 0.5 + 60 = 130 | 140 × 0.6 + 60 = 144 | 130 to 144 |

t: Part 5: Monitoring Heart Rate with Electronic Devices
x: Once a THR has been calculated for a client (Sumit: 20 years, RHR 80, beginner, 140 to 152), the client needs a way to check whether the heart rate is within the prescribed range. This section covers the case where electronic devices are used to monitor the calculated THR. There are three types. Electronic devices compared

p: Part 5: Monitoring Heart Rate with Electronic Devices
x: Known for high accuracy: the readings are considered the most accurate. Why it is accurate: the main device sits just above the sternum, closest to the heart. Behind it are electrodes. When the heart beats and sends electric signals, the electrodes on the rear side of the unit receive those signals, and the heart rate is displayed on whichever device is connected to the strap by Bluetooth (a phone or a watch). Who needs this almost real time, highly accurate heart rate? Athletes. Popular brands: Wahoo, Garmin, Polar.

p: Part 5: Monitoring Heart Rate with Electronic Devices
x: Known for convenience and ease of use. Rings are also popular now and use the same technology. There is no hassle of wearing a strap across the chest. Entry level and high-end models: accuracy varies. The more spent, the more accurate the sensors and the more features. A basic one gives calories burned, steps and heart rate. A more expensive one adds things like VO2 max, sleep quality (it can show when the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems were active, and when you woke in the night), modes that detect whether you are outdoors in the sun or walking in an air conditioned mall, and a GPS tracker. Mostly used by gym goers. Popular brands: Apple, Samsung, Fitbit, Garmin, and cheaper Chinese brands such as Xiaomi. How a smartwatch measures heart rate: PPG (photoplethysmography). On the rear of the watch there are circles: some are LEDs (light emitting devices) and some are light sensors. When the watch is asked to monitor heart rate, the LEDs blink (the circles that glow are the LEDs, the ones that do not are sensors). The LEDs send light into the body. When the heart beats, blood flow in the vessels is higher, and the absorption of light increases. In the small gap between two beats the blood flow goes lower, so less light is absorbed and more light is reflected back by the body. The reflected light is captured by the light sensors. The watch analyses how much was absorbed and how much came back, and the screen displays the heart rate. Any device with such green or red lights uses this technology. PPG principle

t: 5.3 Grip sensors: not recommended due to inaccuracy
p: Part 5: Monitoring Heart Rate with Electronic Devices
x: Grip sensors are the built-in heart rate monitors in gym machines (elliptical cross trainer, upright bike, treadmill). On the handles there are holes in which the fingers are placed. When the fingers cover those holes, the heart rate light starts blinking on the screen. The sensors are inside the holes, on the handles one grips, hence the name. Many people rely on this because they have paid for a gym membership and ask why they should spend on a smartwatch or chest strap. But it is not recommended because it is not reliable, for these reasons: Reason | Explanation | Weak signals | Each heartbeat creates weak electric signals on the skin surface (like the slight current felt on suddenly touching a surface or a person). The sensors detect these. They are very weak, unlike the chest strap that receives directly from the heart. | Motion interference | Walking gives a consistent contact with the holes, but when jogging or running the contact cannot be maintained. With weak signals and continuous motion, the sensors cannot analyse consistently. | Salt accumulation | Everyone using the machine sweats. The salt from sweat gradually accumulates on the sensor as a thin, invisible layer that works as a barrier. Housekeeping sanitiser spray also leaves a chemical that piles up on the sensor. | With weak signals, motion interference and an invisible barrier on top, such a number cannot be relied on. Communicating with clients. The trainer has to convince the client that investing in even a very basic smartwatch is not an overhead expense but an investment in themselves, which is crucial. Student question: Will the course cover how these devices measure calories? A: No, that is not part of this curriculum. What was taught about calories in the body composition lecture can be explored further. If a workshop on it takes place later, there will be a notification. Devices, RPE and talk test on the board

t: Part 6: Estimating Intensity Without Electronic Devices

p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity Without Electronic Devices
x: Here the intensity is estimated, not calculated. No THR is involved, so electronic devices are out of the picture. The target group: Patients (any health condition: heart related, joint related, neurological). Pregnant women. People on special medication such as beta blockers. The slides add cardiac and diabetic patients and clients who do not have access to heart rate monitors. For these clients, the trainer does not want to take any risk. Imagine giving a heart patient a THR such as "160 is your target for the day": that person may end up "somewhere else". Instead of relying on a THR, such clients are given a flexibility, a luxury: they self-regulate their intensity. No doctor, trainer or teacher can judge their condition better than they can while doing the activity. Only they can say "this is still where we can go, after this it is risky". So these clients use one of two methods without electronic devices. Methods without electronic devices

t: 6.2 Method I: RPE (Rating of Perceived Exertion), an experience-based method
p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity Without Electronic Devices
x: Discovered by the exercise physiologist Gunnar Borg (mentioned long ago in the intensity lecture, now shown on its cardio scale). R = Rating (a score), P = Perceived (the client's experience), E = Exertion (the difficulty or intensity). Instead of a THR number, the client is given a rating, a score indicating the difficulty level being experienced. Analogy: the restaurant feedback form. At a fine dining restaurant a feedback form comes with the bill, asking for a rating from 0 to 5 on food, staff service, ambience and overall experience: 0 is poor and 5 is excellent, and a higher rating is better. The RPE scale (Gunnar Borg) is similar but runs from 0 to 10, and on the higher side of the scale the difficulty level is maximum. RPE | Name (as on the slide) | Board grouping | 0 | Rest | Rest | 1 | Really easy | Easy (1 to 2) | 2 | Easy | Easy (1 to 2) | 3 | Moderate | Moderate | 4 | Sort of hard | (not grouped) | 5 | Hard | Hard (5 to 6) | 6 | Hard | Hard (5 to 6) | 7 | Really hard | Very hard (7 to 8) | 8 | Really hard | Very hard (7 to 8) | 9 | Really really hard | Maximal efforts (9 to 10) | 10 | Maximal | Maximal efforts (9 to 10) | RPE scale and where each training method sits How it is used. Instead of a THR the trainer says: do this activity at a rating of 3 (moderate). When the activity is over, or during it, the client gives themselves a rating. In an ideal situation the client gives the same number the trainer suggested (3 out of 10, so the client does not cross that treadmill speed). If at a higher speed the client feels more than 3 out of 10, the speed is not correct. Shortcoming: rating mismatch. The trainer suggests 3 but the client ends up giving 5 during or after the activity: they found it hard at a speed that should have been a 3. A mismatch can come from two factors: State of mind. Analogy: a birthday dinner at a new fine dining restaurant on a busy weekend. The reserved table is not available, the staff are rude, and the guest plans to give zero and write something nasty. But then the food is out of this world, a live band plays, everybody enjoys the evening, and the birthday person is lost for words of thanks. By the time the bill comes there is a positive shift in state of mind (plus some pity for the staff member) and the rating is 2 or 3. In cardio: the client gets a message from the boss ("what kind of report did you submit yesterday, full of errors, come and meet me first thing tomorrow") and is upset. It is not the activity, machine or speed making it seem harder, it is the state of mind. Environment. The activity may really be moderate, but if the air conditioning is not working, there is heat and the ventilation is poor, the client gives a 5. The environment, not the activity itself, made it feel hard. Why a rating is subjective, and why that is the point (class question). Like rating a movie from 0 to 5, a rating differs from person to person. At 6 km per hour one person may say "moderate, anything beyond is sort of hard", another may say 2 or 3 because it was really easy, and a person with a medical condition may say 8 out of 10. That is why this is called estimation. The client is given the authority to self-regulate: if the client says that is the speed at which they are at moderate, they stay at that speed. What is a beta blocker? A medication given by cardiologists to heart patients whose heart rate usually stays on the higher end because of their condition. It artificially brings the heart rate down to a certain level and never lets it go beyond that. If someone is on a beta blocker that does not let the heart rate cross 100 and is given a THR of 140, their heart rate will never go above 100 on the treadmill, whatever they do. So an experience-based method helps in such cases.

t: 6.3 Method II: The talk test, an observation-based method
p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity Without Electronic Devices
x: Intensity is classified into three levels (low, moderate, high). The trainer observes two things in the person doing cardio: the pattern of breathing and the pattern of talking. Intensity | Breathing | Talking | Low | Normally | Yes | Moderate | Deep and often (deep breaths, not once or twice but quite often) | Yes (still able to talk) | High | Deep and quick (deep breaths coming very fast) | Briefly: words do not come out properly, "half air, half word" | Where it helps: avoiding risky situations. Imagine two clients being trained at the same time, one on cardio and one on weight training. The cardio client is a heart patient. The trainer has to spend more time with the weight training client (form, technique, guidance) and cannot stand beside the cardio client all the time. So the trainer goes to the general trainer on duty in the cardio section and asks them to keep an eye on the client on, say, treadmill number three, who has been told to stay at low intensity. The general trainer strikes up a random conversation (for example about yesterday's cricket match) and observes whether the client can reply normally with a normal breathing pattern and whether the words come out clearly. If anything looks suspicious, the general trainer informs the personal trainer, who takes the necessary action.

t: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: The last segment answers the question: should I do a cardio activity non-stop at the same activity for a duration, or should I do one activity at a pace for some duration and then switch to something else for another duration? There are two broad categories. Types of training methods

p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: Continuous: something happening non-stop. Also called steady state. Interval: something happening in phases. Analogy: driving. Driving in a city has traffic jams, signals and speed breakers, so it happens in phases. A highway is non-stop (leaving aside present-day construction jams). Interval has subtypes: LIIT/MIIT, HIIT, and Fartlek (the board draws Fartlek as an arrow out of interval; the first mention in the recording was misheard as "smart").

t: 7.2 A common framework for the graphs
p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: The slides have graphs for these, but to avoid overwhelming a first-timer simpler graphs are drawn, one each for continuous, LIIT/MIIT and HIIT. The vertical axis is the intensity scale (heart rate). The horizontal axis is the time of the cardio activity. Every graph is divided into three phases, drawn with red dotted lines between them: Phase | Name | Shape | Short form | 1 | Re-warm-up | Incline (rise) | RWU | 2 | Main phase or work phase | Different in each method | M/W | 3 | Cool down | Decline (fall) | CD | Only the main phase is different in each method. Why "re-warm-up"? Before getting onto the treadmill, the client has already done mobility drills (dynamic stretching), which is the general warm-up. The warm-up on the treadmill is a cardio-specific warm-up done to reach the heart rate zone, so it is called a re-warm-up. Example used for all graphs: re-warm-up about 5 minutes, main phase 20 minutes, cool down about 5 minutes. The 20 minutes is the main phase only: the incline and decline are not included, so the total is 30 minutes. (The 20 is only an example; it does not always have to be 20.) Phases of a cardio session (continuous training example) Why a re-warm-up is needed. Sumit starts at 95 and cannot straight away enter the THR zone. He has to progress step by step: for example speed 2, 4, 6, 8. When the speed became 8 he noticed on his smartwatch that he had entered his THR. It took about 5 minutes to gradually reach the THR zone. This is the reason for the incline phase, and the reason for the warm-up and cool-down is the same in all three graphs. Why a cool down is needed: syncope. At the end of the main phase the heart rate is still in the THR zone, so Sumit cannot just go home. The heart rate has to come back down to normal step by step, as it went up step by step. He should not press the emergency stop at speed 7 or 8: the speed is reduced gradually. This is done to avoid a medical condition known as syncope: dizziness or a blackout that some people experience when the activity or machine is stopped abruptly. Why it happens. There is a saying, "calves are the second heart of the body". During cardio the heart pumps blood from the upper body to the lower body, and the calves pump the blood back up: deoxygenated blood has to go back via venules, veins and the vena cava to the heart. When the activity stops abruptly, the calf "engine" is switched off and, for a fraction of a second, the pumping of blood back from the lower body to the upper body halts. When the heart and brain do not receive that blood, the dizziness and blackout occur. So: bring it down slowly and gradually. Why the cool down matters

p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: The main phase is a flat line. What is continuous? The THR is maintained in the THR zone throughout the main phase (Sumit's zone: 140 to 152). On Sumit's scale: RHR 80, the day's rise 80, 90, 95, MHR 200 at the top, and the THR zone 140 to 152. From the moment the main phase starts to the moment it ends he cannot go lower than 140 or higher than 152. That is what the flat line shows. Key points about the main phase (written on the board): Speed and intensity remain fixed. If speed 8 got him into the THR zone, he cannot reduce the speed (the heart rate would drop below the THR) or increase it (it could go above the THR). So the speed and intensity are fixed so that he never leaves the zone, for 20 or 30, 40, 50 minutes. Aerobic pathway of energy. Something done non-stop for more than 3 minutes uses the aerobic energy pathway. (The class exchange here was muddled, but the answer is aerobic: the 3 minute rule from earlier.) Slow twitch (type 1) muscle fibres. RPE for this type: about 3 to 4, since the intensity is controlled and maintained (see 7.8). Types of training methods on the board

p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: L = low, M = moderate, I = intensity, I = interval, T = training. (Do not confuse "LIT" with the slang word.) MIIT, the moderate version, is the more popular one that people do. In the main phase, instead of a flat line the graph looks like buildings: the top of a building is a moderate intensity zone and the gap between two buildings (the base) is the low intensity zone. Work happens in phases: moderate, low, moderate, low, moderate, low, moderate. Example for a beginner. For a beginner, jogging is moderate and walking is low. The task: jog for 2 to 3 minutes, then walk, jog, walk, jog, walk, jog. That is four bouts of jog and three bouts of walk in between, about 2 to 3 minutes each, making the 20 minutes. (The board marks J for jog, W for walk, and "2 to 3" minutes under the walk bouts.) For an intermediate. The person does not stay a beginner. When they become an intermediate, running is moderate and jogging is low: the four bouts of jogging become four bouts of running, and the three bouts of walking become three bouts of jogging. The graph changes but the pattern and training method are the same. LIIT / MIIT graph Key points of the main phase: Speed and intensity will vary (low, moderate, low, moderate...). In continuous training they were fixed. Aerobic pathway: walk, jog or run can all be done for more than 3 minutes (even more than 30), so this is still the aerobic pathway. Slow twitch fibres: the central nervous system can manage with slow twitch fibres. RPE 5 to 7 (hard). In continuous training the rating was about 3 to 4 because the intensity was maintained. Here it goes between 5 and 7.

p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: The main phase (20 minutes in the example) looks like four mountains, each with a peak: S1, S2, S3, S4 are the peaks: S = sprint. The narrow gap between two mountains is an AR (AR1, AR2, AR3): active rest. In the example: four sprint bouts and three bouts of active rest. A HIIT main phase is made of a sprint phase and an AR phase. HIIT graph The sprint phase The intensity is taken above 85% (very high intensity in the classification). The body switches to the anaerobic zone: it cannot be done for more than 3 minutes. A sprint is usually 10 to 30 seconds. It is not purely the ATP-PC system (which covers only about 10 to 12 seconds) and it is not aerobic, but because a sprint can go up to 30 seconds it falls in the middle: anaerobic. The body uses fast twitch (type 2) fibres, because type 1 are not sufficient. There is an adrenaline rush: adrenaline is a temporary state in which the heart rate is higher, focus is higher, and the sympathetic (fight or flight) nervous system is active. RPE is 9 to 10 (maximal efforts). The active rest (AR) phase Active rest means do not rest completely: do something between two sprints, and that "something" must be set carefully, at moderate intensity. You cannot come down to walking: the heart rate would drop to a very low level and it would take ages to bring it back above 85% for the next sprint. You also cannot continue running: the intensity only comes down to the 70 to 80% range, which compromises the number of sprints that can be done. So bring it down to something like jogging, neither too low nor too high. The ratio of sprint to active rest depends on how challenging it should be: 1:2 or 1:3. For a 30 second sprint, 1 minute of active rest is 1:2, and 1.5 minutes is 1:3. In active rest the body switches back to the aerobic pathway and uses slow twitch fibres only. So the body goes aerobic, anaerobic, aerobic, anaerobic, and so on. Guidelines for HIIT Not for beginners. A beginner may insist, but they cannot be taken above 85%: beginners have the 50 to 60% range and start there. Even when an intermediate or advanced client does HIIT, not more than twice a week, so that there is no cardiorespiratory fatigue, no musculoskeletal fatigue, and recovery is kept in mind.

p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: Fartlek comes from Sweden. In the Swedish language fartlek means "speed play", and the graph shows that the speed is literally played with. It is also an interval type (otherwise the line would be flat), but in HIIT and LIIT/MIIT the phases were consistent, with the same durations, whereas here the graph goes up and down randomly like a mountain range. Speed and intensity can vary, as per need, and so can the direction (the slide states "variation in direction as per need"). Why: some sports require it. Athletes and sports people are trained so that speed can go up or be slowed down randomly. Think of someone fielding on a cricket field: you do not know from which direction or at which speed the ball will come. The slide graphs: an effort chart that rises and falls irregularly, and a track route that "looks like an F1 race track", with green for jogging pace, blue for running pace, red for sprints. How it is run: the trainer and athlete are connected by a walkie-talkie device. The athlete wears a chest strap, the heart rate data comes into the trainer's phone in real time, and on that basis the trainer instructs "now jog, run, jog, sprint, jog, run", changing the pace as needed. It is covered so that students are aware of it.

p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: Training methods compared | Continuous | LIIT / MIIT | HIIT | Main phase shape | Flat line | Buildings | Mountains | Speed / intensity | Fixed (THR maintained) | Varies (moderate and low) | Varies (sprint and active rest) | Energy pathway | Aerobic | Aerobic | Sprint anaerobic, active rest aerobic | Muscle fibres | Slow twitch | Slow twitch | Fast twitch in sprints, slow twitch in active rest | RPE | 3 to 4 (moderate to sort of hard) | 5 to 7 | 9 to 10 | Notes | THR zone held for the whole main phase | Beginner: jog and walk. Intermediate: run and jog | Not for beginners, not more than twice a week |

p: Part 7: Types of Training Methods in Cardio
x: There are six ways to progress. The first three are the factors of workload (from the previous lecture): # | Way | Example | 1 | Increase speed | Treadmill 6.0 to 8.0 (slide) | 2 | Increase distance | Longer distance | 3 | Increase duration (time) | 15 to 20 minutes | 4 | Increase the angle | Change from flat to incline (treadmill) | 5 | Increase the resistance level | Turn the knob (bike, cross trainer) | 6 | Increase the gradient | Run uphill outdoors instead of flat | These are "good to know". Six ways to progress

Q: How long should cardio be? (For example, how long should the main phase be?) A: This depends on the client's goal, and it is something to learn by applying these concepts in real life. The Scheduling lecture also will not give a fixed number of minutes for cardio. It teaches the factors to consider. If the goal is not bodybuilding or weightlifting but training the cardiorespiratory fitness, for example taking part in long marathons, then cardio sessions are kept longer, mimicking what the client wants to achieve. If the goal is strength or hypertrophy, cardio for hours is not needed: it is fitted in only as needed, the focus is weight training, and cardio is added on the non-weight-training days. (As in the previous lecture, the question whether to do cardio or weights first is also a Scheduling question.) Q: Can an example of giving an RPE rating to a client be given? A: Covered in 6.2: the rating is subjective, like rating a movie out of 5. The client does the activity and says how it feels. At 6 km per hour, one person finds it moderate, another finds it really easy, and a person with a medical condition may find it 8 out of 10. That is how the client self-regulates, and it is the reason this is an estimation method. Q: A lower resting heart rate comes with aerobic cardio. Is that because stroke volume increases? A: Stroke volume and resting heart rate are two different things. Stroke volume is the blood pumped per beat (about 70 ml on average), and it improves with cardio. Cardiac output Q = SV × HR, and the resting value was calculated earlier with a resting HR of 72 and SV of 70. An athlete's Q can be much higher than an average person's because both their per-beat output (SV) is higher and their heart rate goes up near the MHR. The "Q rest" formula was only for calculating the rest value. If someone's RHR goes down (for example from 72 to 60), that improves too, and the SV does not stay at 70 always (70 is an average). So doing cardio has two benefits: it reduces the RHR and it increases the stroke volume, and that is how the overall Q gets better. Comment from a student on HIIT group classes. Many gyms conduct group classes called HIIT. Ideally these are not actually HIIT: HIIT is not for beginners, but everybody joins a group class, so the intervals are shorter and the intensity is not at its highest. They are named HIIT as branding, because HIIT became popular, and some of the people in the group are really doing MIIT. What comes next. The next lecture starts the second main topic of the last module: fitness testing (two lectures).

Course: Personal Training Certification Topic: Cardio Regulations, part 2 of 2 About these notes: Short revision version of the Cardio Regulations 2 lecture. For the full explanation of every concept, example and class question, see the Detailed Notes. Sources: the lecture recording, the course slides ("Cardio Regulations"), the board photos and the E-book chapter on cardiovascular training techniques. Big idea: In cardio, intensity is the heart rate during the activity, expressed as a percentage of the person's own MHR. The level (50 to 60%, 60 to 70%, 70 to 85%, above 85%) is chosen from six factors and is converted into a target heart rate range with the age-predicted method or, better, the HRR (Karvonen) method. The client follows the range with a device, or by RPE and the talk test when numbers are risky. The main phase of a session can be continuous, LIIT/MIIT, HIIT or Fartlek.

Workload = the amount of work done (speed, distance, time). Intensity = the level of effort or difficulty of that work. Same workload, different intensity for different people (exam analogy). Weight training: lower RM = higher intensity. Cardio: higher HR = higher intensity. The HR is turned into a percentage of that person's MHR: Intensity (%) = (HR during cardio ÷ MHR) × 100 Intensity scale for the case study client Sumit (20 years, MHR = 220 minus 20 = 200) | Intensity | HR 100 | 100 ÷ 200 = 50% | HR 160 | 160 ÷ 200 = 80% | HR 180 | 180 ÷ 200 = 90% | The bottom of the scale is the RHR (the "no effort" end) and the top is the MHR (100% effort). The numbers are only for the case study. For any client, use that client's own MHR.

Intensity | % of MHR | Trainee level | Low | 50 to 60% | Beginner | Moderate | 60 to 70% | Intermediate | High | 70 to 85% | Advanced | Very high | Above 85% | Super advanced | Classification of cardio intensity Beginner: less than about 2 to 3 months of experience. Restarting clients are beginners too. Rough guide: intermediate is more than 3 months and less than 1 year, advanced is after a year of consistent progress. Promotion is by performance, not the calendar. A fitness test on day one and after the beginner phase (Fitness Testing 1 and 2) shows whether improvement is significant. Super advanced = can go above 85% easily and come back safely (athletes). There is no official level above it, but "elite" (Bolt, Phelps) would be very close to MHR. Safety rule: never let a client take the ego risk of going near 100%. Step by step. The intensity is not changed daily. It is set from the client's current level and judged by consistent performance and fitness tests.

Six factors with the case study values # | Factor | What it tells | Sumit | 1 | Training experience | Type, frequency, preferences of past cardio | Nil | 2 | Lifestyle | Food, job, habits, sleep (quality and quantity), stress | Average, mostly inactive | 3 | Medical background | Heart, joint or neurological conditions | Clear | 4 | Age | Needed to calculate MHR (not for stereotyping) | 20 (MHR 200) | 5 | RHR | Current fitness level (normal 60 to 80, lower is better) | 80 | 6 | Goal | Specific goal, or GPP (general physical preparedness) | GPP | All six are equally important and are seen together. Decision for Sumit: beginner, 50 to 60%. The client is given a THR number, not a percentage, because a number is easy to follow on a device.

The THR is a range (lower limit L and upper limit U), because heart rate fluctuates and an exact number cannot be maintained. Calculate the formula twice. | Age-predicted (MHR) method | HRR (Karvonen) method | Formula | THR = (220 minus age) × intensity | THR = (220 minus age minus RHR) × intensity + RHR | Uses | Age only | Age and RHR | Sumit, 50% | 200 × 0.5 = 100 | 120 × 0.5 + 80 = 140 | Sumit, 60% | 200 × 0.6 = 120 | 120 × 0.6 + 80 = 152 | Range | 100 to 120 bpm | 140 to 152 bpm | Nature | Generalised | Customised (accepted worldwide) | THR zones of the two methods for the same client BODMAS: brackets first, then multiplication, then addition. Do 120 × 50% = 60 first, then add 80. The loophole: Sumit's cardio starts at about 95 bpm (walk, stairs, drills), so 100 to 120 is reached by casual walking. All 20 year olds would get the same THR even with RHR 60, 70 or 80. Reserve tank for three clients HRR = MHR minus RHR is a reserve tank for the heart to go up. A bigger reserve is better, so a lower RHR is better. MHR cannot be changed (age), but cardio lowers the RHR and widens the reserve. Guitar class story: RHR 80 means arriving exhausted and late, RHR 70 means a short wait, RHR 60 means arriving on time and fresh. Computed for the notes (not in the lecture): RHR 70 gives 135 to 148, RHR 60 gives 130 to 144 (age 20, 50 to 60%).

Methods without electronic devices For patients, pregnant women and people on beta blockers. Intensity is estimated, not calculated, and the client self-regulates. Beta blocker: a medicine that artificially holds the heart rate down, so a THR cannot be reached. RPE (Gunnar Borg, 0 to 10): Rating, Perceived, Exertion. The trainer gives a rating (for example 3, moderate) and the client checks the same feeling. RPE scale and where each training method sits Rating mismatch comes from state of mind (stress, mood) and environment (heat, poor ventilation). It is subjective, and that is why it is called estimation. Talk test: the trainer observes breathing and talking. Intensity | Breathing | Talking | Low | Normally | Yes | Moderate | Deep and often | Yes | High | Deep and quick | Briefly (half air, half word) | It also lets a general trainer supervise a risk client from a distance.

Types of training methods Continuous (steady state) = non-stop. Interval = in phases (LIIT/MIIT, HIIT, Fartlek). Every session has three phases: re-warm-up (rise, cardio specific, about 5 minutes in the example), main phase (20 minutes in the example), cool down (fall, about 5 minutes). Phases of a cardio session (continuous training example) Cool down avoids syncope: dizziness or a blackout when stopping abruptly. "Calves are the second heart": they pump blood back up, and an abrupt stop pauses that return. Intermediate: run (moderate) and jog (low). HIIT: sprints (S1 to S4, above 85%, 10 to 30 seconds, adrenaline) with active rest (AR1 to AR3) at moderate intensity, such as jogging (not walking, not running). Sprint to rest ratio 1:2 or 1:3. Not for beginners, not more than twice a week. Fartlek ("speed play", Sweden): random changes in speed and direction, used for sports. The trainer calls the pace using a chest strap reading. Beginner band and the HRR method: 50 to 60% is applied to HRR, giving 140 to 152 bpm for Sumit, which is 70 to 76% of MHR (the high band of the classification). The lecture does not reconcile this. The 85% boundary: the lecture says high is 70 to 85% and very high is above 85%. The slide writes "greater than or equal to 85%" for very high. HIIT versus classification: sprints go above 85% (super advanced band), yet the lecture allows intermediate and advanced clients to do HIIT (twice a week at most). Time guide for levels: the lecture gives months. The slides give none. The E-book gives weeks for its phases. Graph timing: the HIIT graph is schematic (four sprints and three rests would not fill 20 minutes). LIIT/MIIT bouts of 2 to 3 minutes do not exactly add up to 20. Fartlek is under interval in the lecture, but the E-book lists it as a separate modality. RPE labels differ slightly between the lecture grouping and the slide wording. The THR values for the clients with RHR 70 and 60 were computed for the notes, not taken from the lecture. See the Detailed Notes, Points to Confirm, for the full list.

What is the difference between workload and intensity in cardio? Give the exam analogy. What deciding value is used for intensity in cardio, and how does it compare with weight training? A client has an MHR of 200. Find the intensity at HR 100, 160 and 180. State the four cardio intensity levels, their percentage ranges and the matching trainee levels. Why is a client not promoted just because three months have passed? What is used instead? List the six factors used to prescribe cardio intensity. Why is age needed as a factor? What stereotype should be avoided? Why is the THR given as a range and not as a single number? Write the age-predicted (MHR) method formula and calculate the THR for a 20 year old beginner. What is the loophole in the age-predicted method? Write the HRR (Karvonen) formula and calculate the THR for a 20 year old beginner with an RHR of 80. Why must the brackets and multiplication be done before the addition in the Karvonen formula? Why is a lower RHR better? Which part of HRR can be changed, and how? A client is 30 years old with an RHR of 70 and is an intermediate (60 to 70%). Find the THR with both methods. Compare the chest strap, smartwatch and grip sensor on accuracy, who uses them and how they sense the heart rate. Give three reasons grip sensors are not reliable. Who uses estimation methods instead of a THR, and why? What is RPE, and what two factors can cause a mismatch between the trainer's rating and the client's? Describe the talk test for low, moderate and high intensity. Compare continuous, LIIT/MIIT and HIIT (main phase shape, energy pathway, fibres, RPE), and state the HIIT rules. Name the six ways to progress.

Workload is the amount of work done (speed, distance, time). Intensity is the level of effort or difficulty. In the exam analogy, 30 students solve the same 30 questions (same workload), but a well-prepared student puts in low effort (low intensity) and an unprepared one puts in high effort (high intensity). The heart rate during the cardio activity, as a percentage of MHR. In weight training a lower RM means higher intensity. In cardio a higher HR means higher intensity. Intensity = HR ÷ MHR × 100: 100 ÷ 200 = 50%, 160 ÷ 200 = 80%, 180 ÷ 200 = 90%. Low 50 to 60% (beginner), moderate 60 to 70% (intermediate), high 70 to 85% (advanced), very high above 85% (super advanced). Time alone does not show progress. A client may be irregular, inattentive or not following the plan in the other 23 hours. A fitness test on day one and after the beginner phase (Fitness Testing 1 and 2) shows significant improvement, and that is when the client is promoted. Training experience, lifestyle, medical background, age, resting heart rate, goal. All six are equally important. Age is needed to calculate MHR (220 minus age), and without MHR intensity cannot be found. It should not be used to stereotype (for example assuming every 60 year old is a beginner and every 20 year old is fit). Heart rate fluctuates by a few beats, so an exact number cannot be maintained. A range (lower and upper limit) tells the client to stay within it. (Shirt price analogy.) THR = (220 minus age) × intensity. MHR = 200. Lower: 200 × 50/100 = 100. Upper: 200 × 60/100 = 120. Range 100 to 120 bpm. It uses only age, ignoring the client's current fitness level (RHR). Sumit's heart rate is already about 95 before cardio, so 100 to 120 is reached by casual walking, and every 20 year old gets the same THR whatever the RHR (jeans analogy). THR = (220 minus age minus RHR) × intensity + RHR. HRR = 220 minus 20 minus 80 = 120. Lower: 120 × 0.5 + 80 = 60 + 80 = 140. Upper: 120 × 0.6 + 80 = 72 + 80 = 152. Range 140 to 152 bpm. BODMAS: brackets first, then multiplication, then addition. Adding 80 to 120 before multiplying would give a completely different (wrong) value. Right order: 120 × 0.5 = 60, then 60 + 80 = 140. HRR = MHR minus RHR is the heart's reserve tank, so a lower RHR means a bigger reserve and the same work feels easier and leaves the client further from exhaustion. MHR depends on age and cannot be changed, but cardio lowers the RHR, which widens the HRR. MHR = 220 minus 30 = 190. Age-predicted: 190 × 0.6 = 114 and 190 × 0.7 = 133, so 114 to 133 bpm. Karvonen: HRR = 190 minus 70 = 120. Lower: 120 × 0.6 + 70 = 72 + 70 = 142. Upper: 120 × 0.7 + 70 = 84 + 70 = 154. So 142 to 154 bpm. Chest strap: highest accuracy, electrodes just above the sternum read the heart's electric signals and send them by Bluetooth, used by athletes. Smartwatch: convenient, accuracy depends on price, uses PPG (LED light absorbed and reflected by blood, read by light sensors), used by gym goers. Grip sensor: built into machines, reads weak skin signals through handle holes, not recommended. Weak signals at the skin surface, motion interference when jogging or running, and salt from sweat and sanitiser residue forming a barrier on the sensor. Patients, pregnant women and people on beta blockers (the slides add cardiac and diabetic patients and those without monitors). A THR could push them into risk, or a beta blocker holds the heart rate down so the THR is never reached. They self-regulate using RPE or the talk test. RPE = Rating of Perceived Exertion (Gunnar Borg, 0 to 10): the client rates how hard the activity feels. A mismatch (for example trainer says 3, client says 5) comes from state of mind (such as upsetting news) and environment (such as heat or poor ventilation). Low: breathing normally, can talk. Moderate: deep and often, can still talk. High: deep and quick, can talk only briefly (half air, half word). Continuous: flat line, aerobic, slow twitch, RPE 3 to 4, THR held. LIIT/MIIT: buildings

p: Part 1: Cardio, Endurance and Cross Training
x: Hi everyone, and welcome to this study series on Cardio Regulations. I'm Maya. And I'm Dev. This is the series where we turn two lectures of cardio into something you can simply listen to. That's the idea. You should be able to close the slides, put your headphones on, and by the end understand every concept, not just memorise it. I explain, Dev asks the questions you're probably thinking, and every few minutes we stop and recap. So what's the plan? Six parts. The first three cover the first cardio lecture. Part one, today, is what cardio actually is, the two kinds of endurance, and aerobic cross training. Part two is the classification of aerobic activities by joint stress, plus a quick revision of blood circulation. Part three is the key terms and formulas, like heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output and VO₂ max, then workload, the long term benefits of cardio, and the class questions. And the second lecture? Parts four to six. Part four is intensity, the heart rate scale, the levels from beginner to super advanced, and the six factors a trainer uses to prescribe cardio. Part five is calculating the target heart rate with two methods, why a lower resting heart rate is better, and the devices that monitor heart rate. Part six is how to estimate intensity without devices, the rating of perceived exertion and the talk test, then the training methods, continuous, interval and Fartlek, and how to progress. Part six ends with a twelve question quiz on everything. That's a lot of numbers. It's very logical, and we'll build it step by step. Let's start at the beginning.

t: Cardio and the two kinds of endurance
p: Part 1: Cardio, Endurance and Cross Training
x: Dev, if I say cardio, what comes to your mind? Jogging, treadmill, walking, cycling. And honestly, losing weight. Those activities are right. And the weight loss answer is what most of the public thinks. But from the course point of view, fat loss is not the result of any one type of training by itself. Without a well balanced nutrition plan designed for fat loss, no training type produces it. Cardio and weight training can facilitate fat loss, but they're not the tools that remove fat. So what is cardio actually for? Stamina. And stamina is the same thing as endurance. The word cardio comes from the Greek word cardium, which means heart. Think of cardiology and cardiologist. So cardio training means training the heart for a purpose, and the purpose is building endurance. So if someone asks for the main benefit of cardio, the answer is building endurance. Exactly. And two of the five components of fitness are about endurance. Cardiorespiratory endurance, and muscular endurance. Let's take them apart. Forget the textbook definition for a moment. Just take the word apart. Endurance, also called stamina, is the ability of someone to do something for a long duration without getting fatigued. Someone, something. So for each type of endurance we ask three questions. Who is the someone? What is the something? And how can it be improved? Who, what, how. Okay, start with cardiorespiratory endurance. Who? The answer is hidden in the name. Cardio is heart, respiratory is lungs. So the heart and lungs. What? To deliver oxygenated blood to the working skeletal muscles. Supply, deliver and transport all mean the same thing here. And how? By doing any type of aerobic activity. Cycle, jog, walk, run, swim, anything aerobic. What does working skeletal muscles mean? Skeletal muscles are the ones attached to the bones. Working ones are the ones actually doing the activity. In jogging, that's mainly the leg muscles. The heart and lungs deliver oxygenated blood to them, and the heart and lungs themselves should not get tired. If they start tiring during the task, that person needs to work on cardiorespiratory endurance. And why is aerobic activity the right tool? Aerobic means in the presence of oxygen. In the aerobic energy system, the mitochondria, the powerhouse of the cell, use oxygen to make ATP, which is usable energy. Aerobic activities are the ones you can do for more than three minutes non stop. Doing them creates a continuous demand for more and more oxygen, and the heart and lungs get better at supplying it. Like supply and demand. If there's no demand, the supply has no reason to improve. Perfect. Now muscular endurance. Who? The working skeletal muscles. What? To contract sub maximally. Maximally means one hundred percent effort. The prefix sub means under, so sub maximally means contracting with less than one hundred percent effort. And how? By doing task specific aerobic activity. Why task specific? It's the same leg muscles in jogging and cycling. Same muscles, different movement pattern. If your muscles are trained all year to contract sub maximally in the jogging pattern, you can't expect them to perform equally well in a cycling tournament at the end of the year. To improve muscular endurance for jogging, jog. For cycling, cycle. For swimming, swim. Example? Usain Bolt and Michael Phelps. Bolt can't swim like Phelps, and Phelps can't run like Bolt. Both have very well trained hearts and lungs, so both have top notch cardiorespiratory endurance. But their muscular endurance is excellent only in their own field. Here's the analogy that makes the difference stick. Think of a car. The engine has one job, give the power to move the car from point A to point B, whatever the terrain. Desert, snow, hills, a normal road. The heart and lungs are the engine. They do the same job for any activity. And the tyres? The tyres can't be the same for all terrain. For snow you wrap chains around them, or you use an all terrain vehicle. The tyres ar

p: Part 1: Cardio, Endurance and Cross Training
x: Now, who needs task specific muscular endurance? People whose daily life uses the muscles in the same movement pattern again and again. A cricket batsman perfecting one shot, who practises that shot for hours in the nets. A tennis player practising a forehand. A carpenter cutting wood. A junior chef rolling out chapatis day after day. But most of our clients aren't like that. Right. Most future clients are general lifestyle people. A homemaker, a business owner, a student, a corporate employee. Their day is wake up, work or college, meetings, lunch, maybe a workout two or three times a week, then home. Their muscles don't move in one pattern for long durations. So what do they need? Muscular endurance that is complete and overall, not specific to one task. It's called comprehensive muscular endurance, a three hundred and sixty degree endurance. And the technique to build it is aerobic cross training. What does cross training mean? Doing multiple activities and not sticking to one. Athletes do it a lot to get better in their main sport. Add the word aerobic, and it means doing multiple aerobic activities, not just one. Cricketers who post videos of sprinting and weightlifting are cross training. Sprinting helps a veteran batsman run fast between the wickets, and lifting builds the power to hit the ball over the boundary. A student might ask whether cross training is the same as functional training. The lecture says no, not for this topic. Functional training and things like HYROX mix anaerobic and aerobic work, for example a sled push, and many parts can't be done for more than three minutes non stop. Here we stay in the purely aerobic zone, with no weights. There are two ways to apply aerobic cross training. Way one, do multiple aerobic activities, either within a week or within a session. Within a week, for example, cycling on Monday, a run on Wednesday, a swim on Friday. Within a session, split the time, for example a thirty minute session of ten minutes jogging, ten minutes on the cross trainer and ten minutes rowing. And way two? Do one activity that uses the upper and lower body together. That's why the elliptical machine is called the cross trainer. Two pedals connected to two handles, so hands and legs move together. And these numbers are only hypothetical examples to explain the idea, not a prescription. The slides use sixty minute sessions and twenty minute blocks, the E-book uses twenty minute blocks, so check your course material. Why does cross training actually help? What are the benefits? The lecture gives three. Benefit one, capillarization over a larger surface area. Capillaries are the tiniest blood vessels, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the cells. Cardio builds new capillaries, which is called neocapillarization. If you only do a lower body activity, capillaries improve only there. With upper, lower and combined activities, they spread across the body. Is there an analogy? Mobile network towers. A company doesn't get good coverage by putting more and more towers in one place. Coverage is best when towers are evenly distributed. Same with capillaries. Benefit two? Avoiding overuse injuries. Someone who only cycles puts all the work on the same joints, knee, ankle and hip, the same bones and the same tendons. Like a machine, it gets wear and tear. When the whole body is recruited, the responsibility is shared. And three? Boosting interest, which is about the client, not the trainer. Gym memberships peak on the first of January, and new members trust every word. But after about a month, if cardio means only the treadmill for thirty or forty minutes, monotony arrives. Excuses start showing up only on cardio days. With variety, there is a surprise element in the week, and within a session the client keeps looking forward to the next activity, so thirty minutes pass without noticing. The E-book gives four benefits, including recruiting more muscles, and no capillarization. Good catch, so check

p: Part 1: Cardio, Endurance and Cross Training
x: Time for the closing recap. Cardio means heart training, and its purpose is endurance. Cardiorespiratory endurance is heart and lungs, any aerobic activity. Muscular endurance is task specific. Most clients need comprehensive muscular endurance, built with aerobic cross training, in two ways, multiple activities, or an activity using upper and lower body together. And the three benefits are larger capillary coverage, fewer overuse injuries, and better interest. Here are the five things to remember. One, cardio builds endurance, and fat loss needs nutrition. Two, cardiorespiratory endurance is the engine, any aerobic activity. Three, muscular endurance is the tyres, task specific. Four, comprehensive endurance comes from aerobic cross training. Five, the three benefits, towers, wear and tear, and interest. Next time, we classify aerobic activities by how they stress your joints. See you in part two.

p: Part 2: Classifying Aerobic Activities and Blood Circulation
x: Welcome back to part two of Cardio Regulations. Last time we learned that cardio builds endurance, that cardiorespiratory endurance is the engine and muscular endurance is the tyres, and that aerobic cross training builds comprehensive endurance. And today? Two big topics. First, how to classify aerobic activities by the stress they put on joints, so you can always give a client the right activity. Second, a revision of blood circulation, because the next terms and formulas all depend on it.

t: Classifying aerobic activities by joint stress
p: Part 2: Classifying Aerobic Activities and Blood Circulation
x: The goal of this topic is right client, right activity. Whatever stress an activity involves, or whatever stress a client already has, there should never be a day when you can't assign a suitable aerobic activity. A client should not leave empty handed. And aerobic here still means more than three minutes non stop? Yes. Only aerobic activities are considered. There are three categories, each with rules. Category one is weight bearing, impact based, short form WBIB. It has three rules, and the activity must meet all three. Rule A, the body is upright. Rule B, body weight comes on the key load bearing joints, the hip, knee and ankle. Rule C, there is a foot strike. The foot touches the surface, leaves it, touches again. On, off, on, off. So A and B make it weight bearing, and C makes it impact based. Exactly, but you check all three together. Examples. Walking, jogging and running, the same family at different pace. Skipping. Stair climbing, or the stair master machine, because each step is a foot strike. Zumba and step aerobics. Combat fitness. And the treadmill. Hold on. The treadmill has a moving belt. Is that really a foot strike? This confuses many people. The platform doesn't matter. Road, beach, park or treadmill, foot strike is foot strike. The foot leaves the surface and lands again, the body is upright, and the weight is on hip, knee and ankle. So the treadmill is WBIB. What about jumping jacks, burpees and high knees? They're upright with a foot strike. They came up in class, but they're not purely aerobic. They contain an anaerobic element, and jumping jacks are counted in repetitions, not time. They fail the three minute rule. Skipping with a rope, though, is aerobic and qualifies. HYROX is not here either, because of the sled push and squats. And combat fitness? It was written with a question mark in the lecture and not formally settled, but it's in the WBIB list on the board and the slides, so keep it there. Does this classification help beyond joints? Yes, with personality. An introvert who dislikes group training can be given solo activities. An extrovert gets bored alone and would enjoy group activities like zumba, dance aerobics, step aerobics or combat fitness. Category two is weight bearing, non impact based, WBNIB. Rules A and B are copied from category one, upright and weight on hip, knee and ankle. Rule C changes. There is no foot strike. The feet stay fixed on a pedal or platform, and the pedal moves. What are the examples? All machines. The elliptical cross trainer. The arc trainer, whose pedals move in an arc, hence the name. The adaptive motion trainer, which adapts to different motion styles, so it can feel like elliptical, jogging, mountain climbing or running.
