And the stepper machine, where two pedals move up and down. Isn't the stepper the same as step aerobics? No, and this is a classic trap. In step aerobics you hop on and off a step board, so there are foot strikes, and it's WBIB. On the stepper machine the foot stays on the pedal, so no foot strike, so WBNIB. The skier machine, which mimics skiing on snow, is also WBNIB. Why is the cross trainer called elliptical? A revision link to joint types. A condyloid joint, like the wrist, is also called ellipsoid, meaning oval shaped. In a ball and socket joint the socket is round. In a condyloid joint it's oval. The pedals move in an oval path, so elliptical. Category three is non weight bearing, non impact based, NWBNIB. This is the low stress category, and all activities that didn't fit the first two end up here. The only rule is that the body is in water, or seated, or lying down. So swimming, rowing and cycling. Yes. Swimming, body in water. Rowing machine, seated. Cycling, which falls here by default because the body is seated. Ankle movement happens, but there's no foot strike and no body weight on the load bearing joints. There are different bikes, right? Five to know. The upright bike is the regular gym bike with a V shaped seat. The recumbent

p: Part 2: Classifying Aerobic Activities and Blood Circulation
x: Now the walk along revision of blood circulation. Draw three boxes in your mind. Lungs, with alveoli. The heart with four chambers, two upper atria and two lower ventricles. And the cells of the body. In the drawing, the heart is shown in the anatomical position, so the right chambers appear on the left of the page. Any rules to remember? Four. Atrium, left or right, is inflow. Ventricle, left or right, is outflow. Arteries go away from the heart. Veins come towards the heart. Red means oxygenated blood, blue means deoxygenated. Start walking. Oxygenated blood leaves the lungs through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium, which is inflow. It crosses the bicuspid valve, two flaps, into the left ventricle. From the left ventricle it goes out through the aortic valve into the aorta, the biggest artery, then to the arteries, medium sized, then the arterioles, the smallest. The sizes reduce along the way. And then? Capillaries. The end point of contact. They wrap around the cells, and this is where exchange happens. Capillaries deliver oxygen, and the cells give back carbon dioxide. The lecture called it the return gift. Then the same capillaries carry deoxygenated blood. And the way back? The sizes are the same, but the flow is reversed. Small to medium to big. Capillaries to venules, the smallest veins, then veins, then the vena cava, the biggest. The vena cava splits into the superior vena cava, carrying blood from above the heart, and the inferior vena cava, from below the heart. The inferior one is a little thicker because more of the body lies below the heart. Then into the right atrium. Yes, inflow again. Then across the tricuspid valve, three flaps, into the right ventricle. From there across the pulmonary valve, into the pulmonary arteries, to the lungs. In the lungs the alveoli, tiny air sacs, do gaseous exchange. Carbon dioxide leaves, oxygen is added, and the cycle continues. Tricuspid has three, bicuspid has two. Yes. The valves' job is to make sure there is no backflow. One way traffic. Is there a trick for the word pulmonary? Whenever the lungs are directly involved, the word pulmonary appears. Pulmonary valve, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins. And there are two exceptions to remember. The pulmonary arteries go away from the heart, so they are arteries, yet they carry blue blood. The only arteries with blue blood. The pulmonary veins come towards the heart, yet carry red blood. The only veins with red blood. So the rule about arteries and veins is about direction, not colour. Exactly. The slides split this into two circulations. Pulmonary circulation is between the heart and the lungs, for oxygenating the blood. P because the lungs are directly involved. Systemic circulation is between the heart and the cells, the bigger cycle. S from system, because cells make tissues, tissues make organs, organs make systems. Two names for the two loops of one big cycle. Quick recap of circulation. Atrium inflow, ventricle outflow, arteries away, veins towards, and two loops, pulmonary and systemic.

p: Part 2: Classifying Aerobic Activities and Blood Circulation
x: Here are the five things to remember. One, WBIB needs upright, weight on hip, knee and ankle, and a foot strike. Two, WBNIB has no foot strike, like the elliptical, arc trainer, adaptive motion trainer and stepper. Three, NWBNIB is water, seated or lying, like swimming, rowing and cycling. Four, atrium is inflow, ventricle is outflow, arteries away, veins towards. Five, pulmonary arteries carry blue blood and pulmonary veins carry red. Next, the key terms and formulas, and workload. See you in part three.

p: Part 3: Key Terms, VO₂, Workload and Long Term Benefits
x: Welcome to part three, the last part on the first cardio lecture. So far we have endurance, cross training, the three categories of aerobic activity, and blood circulation. And now the numbers. Yes. The key terms, the formulas, VO₂, workload with a worked case study, the long term benefits of cardio, and the questions from class. Take your time with the calculations, because we'll use them again in the second lecture.

p: Part 3: Key Terms, VO₂, Workload and Long Term Benefits
x: Start simple. Heart rate, HR, is the number of times the heart beats in a minute. Resting heart rate, RHR, is the same thing measured in a resting state. What counts as resting? Imagine waking up in the morning. You've made no physical effort. Only involuntary functions are going on. The heart beats, the brain works, the liver and kidneys work, body temperature and glucose are maintained, digestion carries on. The normal range of resting heart rate is sixty to eighty beats per minute, and the average is seventy two. So if someone says the average is sixty, they're wrong? That was a class answer, and the correction was that sixty to eighty is the range, and the average is a different number, seventy two. One thing to check, the E-book gives different values, sixty as good, forty as exceptionally good, and forty to a hundred as the general range, so check your course material. The lecture and slide use sixty to eighty and seventy two. Next, maximum heart rate. Maximum heart rate, MHR, is the maximum number of times the heart can beat in a minute. It's estimated as two hundred and twenty minus age. And heart rate reserve, HRR, is MHR minus RHR. We'll explain the logic behind that in lecture two. Okay, so reserve is the gap between resting and maximum. Exactly. Now stroke volume, SV. It's the amount of blood pumped by the left ventricle in one beat. Picture a spray bottle. One push of the pump, one stroke, sends out some liquid. That amount is the stroke volume. The bottle is the left ventricle. The average resting stroke volume is seventy millilitres per beat. And watch the unit, right? Yes. Exam options may say per beat, per second or per minute. Stroke volume is per beat. A small note, the lecture and slides say left ventricle, and the E-book says each ventricle, so check your course material. Then cardiac output. Cardiac output, Q, is the amount of blood pumped by the left ventricle in one minute. The formula is Q equals stroke volume times heart rate. It isn't a special formula, it's logic. Blood per beat, times beats per minute, gives blood per minute. Do the rest value. At rest, stroke volume is seventy, resting heart rate is seventy two. Seventy times seventy two is five thousand and forty millilitres, close to five thousand, so about five litres per minute. And during cardio? That's the acute response, the immediate effect of doing cardio. Heart rate increases, and cardiac output increases. One student said Q stays the same, but it can't, because there's physical effort now. The lecture says the resting five litres is speeded up five times, so five times five is twenty five litres per minute. The slide says a sportsman reaches thirty to thirty two litres during maximal exercise. Those are different cases, an average person versus a sportsman at maximal effort, so check which one your course wants. Quick recap? Heart rate, beats per minute. Resting rate, sixty to eighty, average seventy two. Maximum, two twenty minus age. Reserve, maximum minus resting. Stroke volume, about seventy millilitres per beat. Cardiac output, stroke volume times heart rate, about five litres at rest, about twenty five in the acute response.

p: Part 3: Key Terms, VO₂, Workload and Long Term Benefits
x: Now VO₂. The V stands for volume, the actual volume of oxygen, not the ventricle. O2 is oxygen. So VO₂ is the volume of oxygen the body consumes to produce energy, ATP. And VO₂ rest? The same thing at rest. Even sitting still, your involuntary functions need energy, so they need some oxygen. It depends on body weight. VO₂ rest is three point five millilitres of oxygen per kilogram of body weight per minute. This value is also called one MET. Do an example. A person weighing eighty kilograms. Three point five times eighty is two hundred and eighty millilitres of oxygen per minute, just to stay alive. Quick note, the board photo can look like thirty eight, but the slide and E-book say three point five. What does MET mean? Metabolic equivalent of task. Think of it as an energy currency, the amount you spend to buy oxygen. At rest it's one MET. As activity rises, the number rises. The lecture gave illustrations, three or four for jogging and running, and nine or ten for a sprint. These were only illustrations, not slide values. And VO₂ max? Imagine a graph, heart rate on the vertical axis, oxygen volume on the horizontal. A brisk walk sits low on both. A jog is higher. A run is higher still. A sprint takes someone close to their maximum heart rate, and the oxygen consumed at that maximum is VO₂ max. It's the person's aerobic capacity, their maximum aerobic capacity. How it's tested comes in the fitness testing lectures. Workload next. Workload is the amount of work done. In weight training four factors tell it, range of motion, poundage, speed and number of reps. In cardio, three factors, distance covered, speed and time taken. Changing just one is enough to raise the workload. Examples. Distance, a person who jogs two kilometres is told to do two and a half. Speed, treadmill from seven to seven and a half kilometres per hour. Time, a person used to ten minutes of cycling adds ten minutes of running and ten minutes of swimming. That raises time and also uses cross training. And the case study? Goal, don't change the distance. The client covers two kilometres. Old time was fifteen minutes. New time must be twelve minutes. The workload has gone up, because the same distance in less time is harder. So speed has to increase. Speed equals distance divided by time. Yes, and the unit is kilometres per hour, so minutes must become hours, by dividing by sixty. Old, fifteen minutes is a quarter of an hour, zero point two five. Two divided by zero point two five is eight kilometres per hour. New, twelve minutes divided by sixty is zero point two hours. Two divided by zero point two is ten kilometres per hour. So speed rose from eight to ten. All three factors together. Exactly.

t: Long term benefits and class questions
p: Part 3: Key Terms, VO₂, Workload and Long Term Benefits
x: Chronic means long term and adaptations means benefits. Cardiovascular adaptations first. Better contractility of the myocardium, the heart muscle, meaning better pumping. That leads to increased stroke volume and increased exercise cardiac output. Decreased resting heart rate. Increased red blood cell count, the transport agents carrying oxygen and nutrients. Neocapillarization, more new capillaries. Increased elasticity of blood vessels, so they regain their shape and blood flows smoothly. Increased mitochondrial density, more energy production per cell. Then increased resistance to fatigue, you tire later, and increased endurance. Is there a way to group them? Yes. More capillaries, more red blood cells and more mitochondria are about quantity. Tiring later and higher endurance are about quality. And respiratory? Respiratory muscles get stronger, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. Lung volume and capacity increase. Blood flow to the lobes of the lungs improves. The alveoli are used more efficiently. Gaseous exchange increases. And recovery from exercise improves, so you get back to normal faster. Now the class questions. First, some people say cardio isn't necessary, only strength training. The answer is that all components of fitness are interdependent. You don't leave your heart and lungs at home on a strength day. Oxygenated blood is needed, and that's partly why rest intervals between sets matter, for cardiorespiratory recovery. How much cardio depends on the goal, for a marathon more, for bodybuilding less. But in general cardio is important for everyone. And cardio first or weights first? That's a scheduling question, answered in the scheduling lectures.

p: Part 3: Key Terms, VO₂, Workload and Long Term Benefits
x: Pause and think. A person weighs sixty kilograms. How much oxygen per minute do they need at rest? Three point five times sixty. That's two hundred and ten millilitres per minute. Correct. And two kilometres in ten minutes, what's the speed? Ten minutes is one sixth of an hour, so two divided by one sixth is twelve kilometres per hour. Right. Here are the five things to remember. One, resting heart rate sixty to eighty, average seventy two, maximum is two twenty minus age. Two, stroke volume is about seventy millilitres per beat, and cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate, about five litres at rest. Three, VO₂ rest is three point five millilitres per kilogram per minute, one MET. Four, cardio workload is distance, speed and time, and speed is distance over time. Five, chronic adaptations improve both quantity and quality, in the heart, vessels and lungs. Next lecture, intensity. See you in part four.

p: Part 4: Intensity, Training Levels and the Six Factors
x: Welcome to part four. We've finished the first cardio lecture, and now we move to the second one. Part four covers intensity, the levels from beginner to super advanced, and the six factors a trainer considers before prescribing cardio. Last lecture ended with workload, right? Yes. Workload is the amount of work done, set by speed, distance and time. Today starts with intensity.

t: Intensity and the heart rate scale
p: Part 4: Intensity, Training Levels and the Six Factors
x: Dev, if workload is the amount of work done, what is intensity? The amount of work done with respect to time, distance and speed? That's actually the definition of workload. Intensity is the level of effort applied while doing that work, the difficulty level. Here's the exam analogy. Thirty students sit an exam with thirty multiple choice questions. Solving thirty questions is the workload, and it's the same for everyone. But a student who prepared well puts in low effort, so the intensity is low. A student who didn't prepare puts in high effort, so the intensity is high. Same workload, different intensity. So how did we measure intensity in weight training? With the RM method. RM is the most repetitions you can do before failure. The lower the RM, the higher the intensity. Cardio needs its own deciding number, and it's heart rate during the cardio activity. The higher the heart rate during cardio, the greater the intensity. Any heart rate? Or something specific? Specific. Intensity is the heart rate during cardio, expressed as a percentage of the person's own maximum heart rate. Now meet our case study client, Sumit. He's a new client, twenty years old. His intensity scale runs vertically. At the bottom is his resting heart rate, the heart rate from which his day starts, no effort. At the top is the maximum heart rate, one hundred percent effort. What's his maximum? Two hundred and twenty minus twenty. Two hundred beats per minute. And there's a bottle analogy. A one litre bottle filled to the brim overflows if you add more water. In the same way, heart rate can't go beyond maximum. And if you drink five hundred millilitres from the full bottle, the bottle is at fifty percent, which helps with percentages. Show me the calculation. Intensity percent is heart rate during cardio, divided by maximum heart rate, times one hundred. Sumit is on a treadmill. His heart rate is one hundred. One hundred out of two hundred is fifty percent. After five minutes it's one eighty, which is ninety percent. Later he slows down to one sixty, which is eighty percent. So a heart rate of one hundred is always fifty percent? No, and this is the key warning. Don't copy these numbers. The fifty percent came from Sumit's maximum of two hundred. For any client, first find that client's own maximum, then take the percentage of that. Two hundred was used only because a twenty year old gives easy maths. Quick note on the scale. The lecture writes resting heart rate as zero percent effort, but the percentages are of maximum, so eighty is really forty percent of two hundred. It's a schematic. Good point. The scale is a schematic, with resting as the no effort end. Recap? Intensity is the level of effort. In cardio it's heart rate during the activity as a percentage of maximum heart rate, and higher heart rate means higher intensity.

p: Part 4: Intensity, Training Levels and the Six Factors
x: In weight training there was a chart linking RM ranges to training levels. Cardio uses the same idea with percentages of maximum heart rate. Low intensity is fifty to sixty percent, for beginners. Moderate is sixty to seventy percent, intermediate. High is seventy to eighty five percent, advanced. And very high is above eighty five percent, super advanced. So the high band is seventy to eighty five, not eighty to eighty five. Exactly, a common slip. One small difference. The lecture says above eighty five for very high, but the slide writes greater than or equal to eighty five, so eighty five appears in both rows. Check your course material. Who counts as a beginner? Clients with less than about two to three months of cardio experience. And restarting clients are also beginners. Someone who did cardio before but took a gap, for personal reasons, a health condition or rehab, can't be started at moderate or high because of old experience. They go step by step again. And when does a beginner become an intermediate? After three months? Not because the calendar says so. Imagine a client who came about three times in three months, checked social media during sessions, ignored instructions on nutrition, rest and recovery. That client hasn't earned the next level. A fitness test is done on the first day and again after the beginner phase, for all five components of fitness. If the numbers show significant improvement, that's progress tracking, and that's how a client is promoted. Then intensity moves to sixty to seventy percent and the client is an intermediate. Are there rough time guides? Only as a rough guide. Beginner, under three months. Intermediate, more than three months and under a year. Advanced, after a year of consistent performance, seventy to eighty five percent. Super advanced, can go above eighty five percent easily, smoothly and safely, and come back without fatigue and without risk, like athletes and sports people. The slides give no durations, and the E-book has its own phases, so check your course material. Is there anything above super advanced? Not officially. If there were, it would be elite, people like Usain Bolt and Michael Phelps, who go very close to maximum and return safely, because their circulatory system works extraordinarily well. It's not everybody's cup of tea. What if a client says, I can go to two hundred and come back? Never take that risk, at least under your guidance. Some clients say it out of ego, even beginners. They might reach it and not come back from the treadmill. The cardiorespiratory system has to be made ready step by step. Does intensity change daily, if Sumit isn't feeling well? No. It's set from his current training level, and then a fitness test shows how he performs at that intensity. Consistent performance, not one day, tells whether the level works.

p: Part 4: Intensity, Training Levels and the Six Factors
x: Why do we say prescribing? Because like a doctor prescribes a medicine, a trainer prescribes an intensity. And name and age aren't enough, which is why there's an initial client interview. There are six factors. Think of them as a checklist. Go through them. Factor one, training experience. Has the person ever done cardio? If yes, which type, weight bearing impact based or the other categories, how many sessions a week, how long, and preferences like morning or evening, indoor or outdoor. Two? Lifestyle, a big umbrella. Food habits and nutrition. Daily routine and the nature of the job, a corporate employee on a laptop versus an architect climbing stairs on sites. Habits, like smoking and drinking. Sleep, both quality and quantity, seven to eight good hours versus three to four random hours. And stress. Three? Medical background. Heart, joint or neurological conditions. If the trainer is unaware and gives high intensity, the client could suffer a severe condition. Awareness is crucial. Four is age. Isn't that because kids and older people get different intensities? That's stereotyping, the assumption that something popular must be true, such as a sixty year old must be a beginner and a twenty year old can do more. Imagine a twenty year old with no experience, junk food, poor sleep, versus a sixty year old who hasn't missed a session in thirty or forty years, with clean nutrition and a clear medical history. Going by age alone would be unfair. The real reason age is needed is that without age you can't calculate maximum heart rate, and without it you can't determine intensity. Five? Resting heart rate. A quantifiable number and an indicator of cardiorespiratory fitness, so it shows current fitness level on the day you meet the client. Sixty to eighty is normal, lower is better. And six, goal. A specific goal, like HYROX, a marathon or climbing Everest, or a basic goal, general physical preparedness, GPP, meaning basic fitness for day to day tasks and emergencies. Is the list a ranking? No. All six are equally important and seen together. The slides use slightly different names, age, medical background, past training history, current fitness level, lifestyle and goal. Same six.

p: Part 4: Intensity, Training Levels and the Six Factors
x: Now Sumit. Training experience, nil. Lifestyle, average for a twenty year old student, junk food, no physical activity. Medical background, clear. Age, twenty, so maximum two hundred. Resting heart rate, eighty. Goal, GPP. The decision, he starts as a beginner, fifty to sixty percent. And what does he do with a percentage? He can't carry a calculator on the treadmill. Exactly. The percentages are background science for the trainer. The client needs a number that's easy to notice during cardio, a heart rate. So the percentage is converted into a target heart rate, THR, which the client follows on a device. That's part five. Pause and think. Why do we need the client's age at all? Because without age there's no maximum heart rate, and without that there's no intensity. Exactly. Here are the five things to remember. One, workload is the amount of work, intensity is the level of effort. Two, cardio intensity is heart rate during activity as a percentage of own maximum. Three, low fifty to sixty, moderate sixty to seventy, high seventy to eighty five, very high above eighty five. Four, promotion depends on fitness test results, not the calendar. Five, six equal factors, training experience, lifestyle, medical background, age, resting heart rate and goal. Next, calculating the target heart rate. See you in part five.

p: Part 5: Target Heart Rate, the Karvonen Method and Heart Rate Monitors
x: Welcome to part five. Last time we met Sumit, twenty years old, maximum heart rate two hundred, resting heart rate eighty, a beginner at fifty to sixty percent. Today we turn that percentage into a target heart rate, we see why a lower resting heart rate is better, and we look at the devices that monitor heart rate.

t: Target heart rate with the age predicted method
p: Part 5: Target Heart Rate, the Karvonen Method and Heart Rate Monitors
x: A target heart rate, THR, can be a single number, like one fifty five, or a range, like one fifty to one sixty. Which makes more sense, Dev? A range, I'd guess. Heart rate isn't fixed. Right. It fluctuates by a few beats, like room temperature. Over twenty minutes you can reach one fifty five, but maintaining exactly that is impossible. A range says, don't go below this, don't exceed that. Think of buying a shirt. Walk into a high end store and ask for a shirt of exactly four thousand eight hundred and thirty two rupees, and you'll be shown the door. You say, between four and five thousand. So we calculate twice. Yes, in both methods, once for the lower limit and once for the upper limit. Method one is the age predicted method, also called the MHR method, because it uses maximum heart rate. The formula is THR equals maximum heart rate times intensity, so two hundred and twenty minus age, times intensity. Same method, two names, so don't be confused if an exam uses either. Sumit's numbers? Lower limit, two twenty minus twenty is two hundred, times fifty over a hundred, which is one hundred beats per minute. Upper limit, two hundred times sixty over a hundred, which is one hundred and twenty. So the range is one hundred to one hundred and twenty. His resting heart rate of eighty isn't used at all. Does that make sense for a guy at eighty resting? That's the loophole. Follow Sumit's day. He wakes at eighty. After his morning routine, a ten minute walk to the gym and three floors by stairs, he's about ninety. After the gym tour, mobility drills and waiting at the treadmill, about ninety five. So cardio starts at ninety five. If he just walks casually and chats with a friend, within two minutes he's in the one hundred to one hundred and twenty zone. Does that look like fifty percent intensity? No, that's barely effort. Exactly. The method only considers age. It never considers current fitness level, which the resting heart rate shows. All twenty year old beginners would get the same range, but one may be near sixty, one at seventy, one at eighty. Like three friends, all thirty years old, and a salesman who gives all three a thirty six waist jeans. Body composition isn't the same for all thirty year olds. We need a customised target.

t: The Karvonen method and the reserve
p: Part 5: Target Heart Rate, the Karvonen Method and Heart Rate Monitors
x: That's why Karvonen, an exercise physiologist, came up with the heart rate reserve method, also called Karvonen's formula. THR equals heart rate reserve times intensity, plus resting heart rate. So before we multiplied the maximum, now we multiply the reserve and add resting rate back. Yes. To make it ready to use, open it up in steps. Heart rate reserve is maximum minus resting. And maximum is two twenty minus age. So THR equals, two twenty minus age minus resting rate, times intensity, plus resting rate. Sumit again. Lower limit. Two twenty minus twenty minus eighty. Brackets first. Two twenty minus twenty is two hundred, minus eighty is one hundred and twenty. Then multiplication before addition. One twenty times fifty percent is half of one twenty, which is sixty. Then add eighty. One hundred and forty. Upper limit, one twenty times sixty percent is seventy two, plus eighty is one hundred and fifty two. So the range is one forty to one fifty two. Why does the order matter? Think of the letters BODMAS. Brackets, order, division, multiplication, addition, subtraction. If you jumped to one twenty plus eighty first, your answer changes entirely. So the same client went from one hundred to one twenty, to one forty to one fifty two. Yes, and the new lower limit is above the old upper limit. The age predicted method uses age only, and gives a generalised range. The Karvonen method uses age and resting heart rate, and gives a customised one. This is the method accepted worldwide. One thing, if you convert one forty to one fifty two back into percent of maximum, that's about seventy to seventy six percent, which looks like the high band. The notes flag that, and the lecture doesn't discuss it. In this method the fifty to sixty percent is applied to the reserve, not to the maximum. The E-book also uses forty to sixty percent of reserve for initial conditioning, so check your course material. Now why is a lower resting heart rate better. Heart rate reserve is a range for the heart to go up, from resting, eighty for Sumit, to maximum, two hundred. Like a reserve fuel tank in a vehicle. The bigger the reserve, the better. If three litres can't reach a petrol pump, five litres helps. Or extra cash for a metro traveller. With a hundred rupees you can take a cab home. With five hundred you can also have a meal and a coffee. And in the heart? If the heart rate gets very close to maximum during work, you feel exhausted. If Sumit's resting rate were seventy instead of eighty, the same work leaves him further from exhaustion, because he has a bigger tank. Mathematically, reserve is maximum minus resting, so a lower resting rate widens the reserve. Maximum can't be changed, it depends on age. But resting heart rate can be worked on, because cardio reduces it. Is there a story? The guitar class. Sumit finishes college at four, and his guitar class is at four fifteen, up some stairs. With resting rate eighty, he reaches the building at four twenty five, exhausted, sits on the stairs gasping, arrives in class at four thirty five, recovers by four forty, and a track has already been taught. After three months of cardio, resting rate seventy, he reaches the building around four twenty, climbs without a break, waits briefly on the third floor at four twenty five, and arrives at four twenty eight. After three more months, resting rate sixty, he arrives at four ten, needs no break, and is seated at four fifteen sharp. So cardio shows up in daily life. Exactly. Now for three clients with resting rates eighty, seventy and sixty, call them A, B and C, all with maximum two hundred. If all got one forty to one fifty two, that would be unfair. The notes computed them with the same formula, not in the lecture. Client B, reserve one thirty, range one thirty five to one forty eight. Client C, reserve one forty, range one thirty to one forty four. Customised, valid and accurate. Recap? Range, not a single number. Age predicted, two twenty minus age times intens

t: Monitoring heart rate with electronic devices
p: Part 5: Target Heart Rate, the Karvonen Method and Heart Rate Monitors
x: Once Sumit has his range, how does he check it? There are three types of electronic devices. First? The chest strap, known for high accuracy. The main unit sits just above the sternum, closest to the heart, with electrodes behind it. The electrodes receive the heart's electric signals, and the heart rate shows on a phone or watch connected by Bluetooth. Athletes need this almost real time accuracy. Brands, Wahoo, Garmin, Polar. And the smartwatch? Known for convenience. Rings use the same technology. Accuracy varies with price. Basic models give calories, steps and heart rate. Expensive ones add VO₂ max, sleep quality, GPS and more. Mostly used by gym goers. Brands, Apple, Samsung, Fitbit, Garmin, and cheaper ones like Xiaomi. How does it measure heart rate? Photoplethysmography, PPG. On the back of the watch, some circles are LED lights and some are light sensors. The LED lights send light into the body. When the heart beats, blood flow is higher, so more light is absorbed. Between two beats, flow drops, so less is absorbed and more is reflected back. The sensors capture the reflected light, and the watch analyses it and shows the heart rate. And the third? Grip sensors, the built in monitors on gym machines. You put your fingers in holes on the handles. They're not recommended, for three reasons. Weak signals, because each beat creates only weak electric signals on the skin. Motion interference, because contact can't be maintained when jogging or running. And salt accumulation, because sweat salt and sanitiser leave an invisible barrier on the sensor. What do I say to a client who refuses to buy a watch? That even a basic smartwatch is not an overhead expense, it's an investment in themselves.

p: Part 5: Target Heart Rate, the Karvonen Method and Heart Rate Monitors
x: Pause and think. Sumit's resting rate is eighty and age twenty. What is the Karvonen upper limit at sixty percent? Reserve is one twenty, times point six is seventy two, plus eighty is one fifty two. Correct. Here are the five things to remember. One, give a target range, calculated twice, lower and upper. Two, age predicted, two twenty minus age times intensity, ignores resting heart rate. Three, Karvonen, two twenty minus age minus resting, times intensity, plus resting, brackets first. Four, lower resting heart rate means bigger reserve, and cardio lowers it. Five, chest strap most accurate, smartwatch convenient, grip sensors not recommended. Next, estimating intensity without devices, and training methods. See you in part six.

p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity, Training Methods and the Final Quiz
x: Welcome to the final part. We have intensity as a percentage of maximum, the six factors, two ways to calculate a target heart rate, and the devices. Now three things remain. How to estimate intensity without devices, the types of cardio training, and how to progress. We end with a twelve question quiz.

p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity, Training Methods and the Final Quiz
x: Some clients should not be given a target heart rate number. Patients with heart, joint or neurological conditions. Pregnant women. People on special medication such as beta blockers. The slides add cardiac and diabetic patients, and clients without access to monitors. Give a heart patient a target of one sixty, and they may end up somewhere else. So these clients self regulate, because only they can say, this is still fine, beyond this is risky. What's a beta blocker? A medicine from cardiologists that artificially holds the heart rate down and never lets it pass a certain level. If it caps at one hundred and the target is one forty, the heart rate will never get there. So an experience based method is needed. First method? RPE, rating of perceived exertion, from the exercise physiologist Gunnar Borg. Rating, a score. Perceived, the client's experience. Exertion, the difficulty. Think of a restaurant feedback form, zero to five. The Borg scale runs zero to ten. Zero is rest. One and two, easy. Three, moderate. Four, sort of hard. Five and six, hard. Seven and eight, really hard. Nine and ten, maximal effort. The slide names nine really really hard and ten maximal, so check your course material. How is it used? The trainer says, do this at three, moderate. The client rates it. Ideally the client says three. If at a higher speed it feels more than three, that speed isn't right. What if the client says five when the trainer expects three? A mismatch, from two factors. State of mind, like a birthday dinner that started badly and ended with a good rating. In cardio, a client who just got a telling off message from the boss will find everything harder. And environment, a broken air conditioner or poor ventilation makes a moderate activity feel like a five. So it's subjective. Isn't that a weakness? It's the point. Like rating a movie, one person finds six kilometres per hour moderate, another finds it really easy, a person with a medical condition may say eight. That's why it's an estimation. The client has the authority to self regulate. Second method? The talk test, an observation method. The trainer watches breathing and talking. Low intensity, breathing normally, talking yes. Moderate, breathing deep and often, still able to talk. High, breathing deep and quick, talking only briefly, half air, half word. Where does it help? When the trainer is busy with another client. A heart patient is on treadmill three at low intensity, and the trainer asks the general trainer on duty to chat about yesterday's cricket match and watch. If replies are clear and breathing normal, fine. If not, tell the personal trainer. The E-book says it is meant for beginners and used with RPE and a monitor, so check your course material. Recap? Without devices, for patients, pregnant women and beta blocker users. RPE is experience based, zero to ten. The talk test is observation based, breathing and talking.

t: The phases and the first training methods
p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity, Training Methods and the Final Quiz
x: How should cardio be done, non stop, or in phases? Continuous, also called steady state, is non stop. Interval is in phases. Like driving, a highway is non stop, city traffic is in phases. Interval has subtypes, low or moderate intensity interval training, high intensity interval training, and Fartlek. Is there a common structure? Every graph has three phases, with intensity on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal. The re warm up, rising. The main or work phase, different for each method. The cool down, falling. Example, five minutes re warm up, twenty minutes main phase, five minutes cool down, thirty in total. Twenty is only an example. Why re warm up, if we've done mobility drills? Mobility drills are the general warm up. The re warm up is cardio specific, to reach the heart rate zone. Sumit starts at ninety five, so he goes speed two, four, six, eight, and at eight his watch shows he's in his zone, after about five minutes. And the cool down? At the end of the main phase his heart rate is still in the zone, so he can't hit the emergency stop. It's to avoid syncope, dizziness or blackout when activity stops abruptly. There's a saying, calves are the second heart of the body. They pump blood back up from the lower body. Stop abruptly, and for a fraction of a second that return halts, and the heart and brain miss that blood. Now the methods. Continuous. Main phase is a flat line. The target range, one forty to one fifty two for Sumit, is held throughout. Speed and intensity stay fixed. Aerobic pathway, slow twitch fibres, RPE about three to four. And the second? LIIT and MIIT, low and moderate intensity interval training. The graph looks like buildings. The top is moderate, the gap between is low. For a beginner, jogging is moderate and walking is low. Jog two to three minutes, then walk, jog, walk, jog, walk, jog. Four jog bouts and three walk bouts. For an intermediate, running is moderate and jogging is low. Same pattern, different activities. Speed varies, aerobic, slow twitch, RPE five to seven. The notes say the seven bouts add up to fourteen to twenty one minutes, so treat twenty as schematic.

t: HIIT, Fartlek, progression and class questions
p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity, Training Methods and the Final Quiz
x: HIIT, high intensity interval training, looks like mountains. Peaks are sprints. Gaps are active rest. Four sprints, three active rests in the example. In the sprint, intensity goes above eighty five percent. It's anaerobic, because it can't last more than three minutes. A sprint is usually ten to thirty seconds. It uses fast twitch fibres, brings an adrenaline rush, and RPE nine to ten. What's active rest? Don't rest completely. Do something at moderate intensity. You can't drop to walking, because the heart rate falls too low to get back above eighty five percent. You can't keep running, because intensity only drops to seventy to eighty percent, which limits your sprints. So jog. The sprint to rest ratio is one to two or one to three. For a thirty second sprint, one minute of rest is one to two, one and a half minutes is one to three. In active rest the body goes aerobic, slow twitch. So aerobic, anaerobic, aerobic, anaerobic. Who can do HIIT? Not beginners, because they're limited to fifty to sixty percent. And even intermediate or advanced clients, not more than twice a week, to protect against fatigue. The notes flag that sprints above eighty five percent belong to super advanced in the classification, which the lecture doesn't reconcile. Gym group classes called HIIT are often branding, and many are really MIIT. And Fartlek? Swedish for speed play. It's interval, but randomly up and down like a mountain range, with speed and direction varying as per need. Think of fielding in cricket, where you don't know the direction or speed of the ball. On the slide's track, green is jogging pace, blue running, red sprints. The athlete wears a chest strap, heart rate goes to the trainer's phone, and the trainer calls, jog, run, sprint. The E-book lists it separately from interval training. And progression? Six ways. The first three are workload factors, speed, distance and duration. Then angle, flat to incline on a treadmill. Resistance level, the knob on a bike or cross trainer. And gradient, running uphill outdoors. How long should cardio be? It depends on the goal. Marathon training needs longer sessions. For strength or size, cardio is fitted in on non weight training days. And a lower resting rate with cardio isn't only about stroke volume. Cardio lowers resting heart rate and raises stroke volume, and that improves overall cardiac output, mainly at high effort.

p: Part 6: Estimating Intensity, Training Methods and the Final Quiz
x: Here are the five things to remember. One, without devices, use RPE, zero to ten, or the talk test, for patients, pregnant women and beta blocker users. Two, every session has a re warm up, main phase and cool down, and the cool down prevents syncope. Three, continuous is flat, MIIT is buildings, HIIT is mountains. Four, HIIT is anaerobic sprints above eighty five percent, not for beginners, not more than twice a week. Five, progress by speed, distance, duration, angle, resistance and gradient. Now the quiz. Twelve questions, answers straight after. One. What does cardio mean? Heart, from the Greek cardium. Two. Maximum heart rate formula? Two twenty minus age. Three. Which category is the elliptical trainer? Weight bearing, non impact based. Four. Which arteries carry blue blood? The pulmonary arteries. Five. VO₂ rest? Three point five millilitres per kilogram per minute, one MET. Six. Cardiac output formula and rest value? Stroke volume times heart rate, about five litres per minute. Seven. Speed for two kilometres in twelve minutes? Ten kilometres per hour. Eight. Moderate intensity as percent of maximum? Sixty to seventy. Nine. Karvonen formula? Two twenty minus age minus resting, times intensity, plus resting. Ten. Sumit's Karvonen range? One forty to one fifty two. Eleven. Which device is most accurate, and which is not recommended? Chest strap, and grip sensors. Twelve. Why cool down? To avoid syncope. That's the whole topic. Well done for sticking with it. Go and apply it with real clients.

Course: Personal Training Certification Topic: Fitness testing, part 1 of 2 About these notes: Detailed notes from the Fitness Testing 1 lecture, written so the whole lecture can be studied without watching the recording. Every concept, example, analogy and class question is covered. For a short revision version see the Study Notes.

Short form | Meaning | PAR-Q | Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire | NOC | No objection certificate (a doctor's written clearance) | BP | Blood pressure | SYS / DIA | Systolic / diastolic blood pressure (as shown on a BP monitor) | mmHg | Millimetres of mercury (Hg is the symbol for mercury), the unit of blood pressure | BW | Body weight | LBM | Lean body mass | BF | Body fat | VF / SF | Visceral fat / subcutaneous fat | EF | Essential fat | WC | Waist circumference | HC | Hip circumference | WHR | Waist to hip ratio | BMI | Body mass index | BIA | Bioelectrical impedance analysis | IMTG | Intramuscular triglyceride | TG | Triglyceride | RM | Repetition maximum (1 RM is the heaviest weight that can be lifted for one repetition) | FT | Fitness testing |

This lecture uses ideas from earlier topics. You should already be familiar with: the five components of fitness and their interdependence (cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition), the definition of body composition and the make-up of body weight, the definitions of muscular strength and muscular endurance, flexibility versus mobility and the factors affecting mobility (tissue temperature), the cardio lectures (heart rate as the key measure in cardio) and 1 RM from weight training.

Part | Topic | 1 | Introduction: standardised tests, test norms, why test at all | 2 | Objectives of fitness testing (global and client) | 3 | Health screening before testing: PAR-Q and informed consent | 4 | The correct order of fitness testing, and why | 5 | Test 1: blood pressure | 6 | Body composition tests: overview and classification | 7 | 2.1 Anthropometric data: waist circumference, waist to hip ratio, body mass index | 8 | 2.2 Skinfold measurement (caliper) | 9 | 2.3.1 BIA test | 10 | 2.3.2 Bod Pod test | 11 | Wrap-up and preview of Fitness Testing 2 |

p: Part 1: Introduction
x: Fitness testing is taught in two parts, Fitness Testing 1 and Fitness Testing 2. Together they cover the standardised fitness tests that are conducted worldwide in the same way, with the same guidelines, procedures, methods and test norms. A test norm is a reference sheet. After a test is conducted, any outcome (for example a number or score) is checked against the test norm sheet, which shows where that person stands for the fitness component being tested. Fitness is made of five components, so a person's fitness level cannot be assessed or declared "fit" from one or two components. Tests related to all the components must be conducted. These tests were not drafted by the course. They were developed through research by international bodies working in fitness science and fitness research, and they are accepted and conducted worldwide.

p: Part 1: Introduction
x: Testing in general means evaluating something to check its performance, quality or efficacy. It exists in many fields: Medicine: doctors conduct tests to diagnose disease. Manufacturing: brands test a product before launch to see whether it will succeed. IT: software is tested heavily. Education: knowledge is tested in exams (the final exams of this course are an example). Fitness: a person's fitness is evaluated, with defined objectives.
The objectives are grouped into two perspectives: the global perspective and the client perspective. Objectives of fitness testing

p: Part 2: Objectives of Fitness Testing
x: Standardisation. Because the tests use the same procedure and method everywhere, a given component is tested the same way all over the world. For example, muscular strength is not tested with a lat pull down in Mumbai, a shoulder press in Tokyo and a bench press in France. One of the worldwide tests of muscular strength is the bench press, and nobody may invent a different method. (The strength tests themselves are covered in Fitness Testing 2.) Standardisation allows comparison: athletes or bodybuilders of one country can be compared with those of another on the same parameter. Performance benchmarking. Suppose a country's athletes will take part in a global tournament. Unless it is known where the competition stands (for example South African athletes here, New Zealand there, the USA elsewhere), there is no milestone or benchmark to aim for. Benchmarking shows how far a team lags, or how far ahead it is. Being ahead is also useful information, because then the standard has to be maintained. From a global point of view, fitness testing is all about performance benchmarking made possible by standardised methods.

p: Part 2: Objectives of Fitness Testing
x: If fitness testing helps the client, it also helps the trainer. A client who enjoys the benefits stays, renews training and becomes a brand advocate (tells others about the trainer). 1. Baseline results (the first test). The trainer knows nothing about a new client. Testing all five components gives the baseline that shows where the client stands today. 2. Progress tracking (the re-test). Only with baseline numbers can progress be tracked. After, say, 3 months of training a re-test shows how far the client has come. The trainer can show the client: "this is where you started and this is where we have brought you". This builds confidence and motivation, because numbers speak louder than words. It also shows that the trainer is number-driven and goal-oriented, not someone making vague promises such as "give me one year, I will do magic". 3. Goal setting. Baseline results (first test) and re-test results together support goal setting. Without baseline results goals would be set randomly. After a re-test the goals can be tweaked depending on whether the plan is working. Instead of vaguely saying "one year, two years", the trainer sets short-term, mid-term and long-term goals (actual milestones, for example at 3 months and 6 months). This keeps the client consistent and driven. When clients meet these goals they look up to the trainer and may ask for the bar to be set higher. 4. Strengths and areas to work on. The baseline shows what the client is good at and what needs work, which lets the trainer design a customised and suitable workout plan. Wording matters. Fitness is a service industry, so the word "weakness" is avoided. Use strengths and areas to work on. A client meeting the trainer for the first time may react badly to a list of "weaknesses". "Strength" here does not mean only muscular strength. It is the ordinary English word and can come from any of the five components. Analogy: the debate competition. A school girl takes part in a debate and her teacher gives feedback afterwards. The weaknesses mentioned are pronunciation of certain words and grammar. The strength is good voice modulation (the line "what are the objectives of fitness testing" did not sound like a robot, which made it impactful). Strengths can lie in any field. Using strengths. A client with very good cardiorespiratory endurance can be helped to maximise that potential and even build a career from it. A client with very good upper body muscular strength can be given more advanced upper body exercises and helped to nail those lifts. Using areas to work on. A client with poor flexibility (flexibility has its own tests) gets a balanced plan in which not a single day passes without stretching: mobility drills as well as static stretching. A client with a contraindication can be protected. A contraindication is any movement that causes discomfort or pain (the word is often used by physiotherapists). It may be in the upper limb, lower limb or back, for example raising the hand with the elbow bent. If a particular machine or exercise bothers the client, it can hinder performance, so an alternative is chosen. This avoids the risk of injury. Fitness testing is therefore a powerful tool for designing the most suitable workout plan.

t: Part 3: Health Screening Before Fitness Testing

p: Part 3: Health Screening Before Fitness Testing
x: Before the correct order of tests is discussed, there is a pre-step that takes place even before fitness testing: health screening. The class was asked what "screening" means. Answers included checking records, a health check and filtering. The simplest way to understand it is baggage screening at airports, metro stations and hotels, or X-ray screening. Screening means scanning something. Security personnel scan everybody's luggage so that people in a public area are safe and nothing dangerous is found. In the same way, health screening makes sure that the person whose fitness test is about to be conducted is safe and sound and that no problem will occur during the test. The course slides define it as: a procedure performed on asymptomatic populations to assess the likelihood of a particular disease. Health screening does not require inviting a doctor to the gym. It uses two simple forms. The trainer reads the form to the client (or the client reads it), the client fills it in and signs it. The two forms are the PAR-Q and the informed consent form. Sample copies of both are in the course slides and can be printed and used later, for example if a gym has no such process (introducing one is usually welcomed). The forms are also a requirement of the international registration body, so trainers must be aware of them.

p: Part 3: Health Screening Before Fitness Testing
x: PAR-Q stands for Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire. It is a set of about 10 questions (the sample in the slides has 10) about the client's medical background: for example heart-related conditions, joint-related conditions and neurological disorders such as epilepsy. The questions are close-ended: next to each there are only two options, Yes or No, and the client selects one. There are no lines for writing an essay about a past problem. Clearance rule. The PAR-Q is considered cleared, and the fitness test can be conducted, only when all answers are No. A single Yes is a signal to stop and ask the client about it. To be sure the client is still eligible for fitness testing, the client must bring a NOC (no objection certificate) from their doctor. Why documentation matters. Today a client may blame the trainer and threaten legal action very quickly. Getting everything documented and signed before the journey starts means nobody can hold the trainer responsible later. The more detailed the form, the better. The sample PAR-Q in the slides (ages 15 to 69) contains these questions, each answered Yes or No: No. | Question (summary) | 1 | Has your doctor ever said you have a heart condition and that you should only do physical activity recommended by a doctor? | 2 | Is there any history of heart disease in your family? | 3 | Do you feel pain in your chest when you do physical activity or exercise? | 4 | In the past month, have you had chest pain when you were not doing physical activity? | 5 | Do you lose your balance because of dizziness, or do you ever lose consciousness? | 6 | Do you have a bone or joint problem (for example back, knee or hip) that could be made worse by a change in your physical activity? (If yes, give details.) | 7 | Do you suffer from asthma, diabetes, epilepsy or high blood pressure? (If yes, give details.) | 8 | Do you have any other medical or physical condition (such as diabetes, cancer, osteoporosis)? | 9 | Do you have any current injuries or conditions, and if so, are they being treated by a doctor or other health professional such as a physiotherapist? | 10 | Do you know of any other reason why you should not do physical activity or exercise? | The form ends with a note: if you answered YES to any question, check with a member of staff before taking part, because you may need to be referred to your doctor first.

p: Part 3: Health Screening Before Fitness Testing
x: The word informed means there is a script that the client reads, or that the trainer reads aloud. It informs the client about: the kind of machines that will be used, the exercises and activities (strength training, cardio, stretching and so on), the possible risks involved. This form is not only for fitness testing. It covers the overall fitness journey, because a client who has signed up is tested first and then the journey begins. Consent is the closing statement in which the client says they are fully aware of everything and willingly agree to take part in the fitness journey or fitness test, followed by the signature. It is a win-win: the client is aware and the trainer is protected. The sample consent form in the slides includes statements that the programme includes exercises to build the cardiorespiratory system (heart and lungs) and the musculoskeletal system (muscles, joints and bones) and to improve body composition. Exercise may include treadmill, running, walking, bike, rowing, group aerobic exercises, weight training and exercises for mobility and flexibility. The client confirms that it is their responsibility to inform the trainer of any health problems, injuries or pregnancy, to obtain written medical clearance if required, to monitor their own condition and stop and inform the trainer if unusual symptoms occur, and that they have read the form and their questions have been answered. Student question: "In every gym, consent forms are mandatory, aren't they?" A: If a gym already has its own format, follow it. Some gyms do not like changes to their standard process, and there is no need to go against the system. Where nothing exists, a trainer can introduce one. It will be seen as a positive step, working for the organisation and not only for oneself. Once these two formalities are done, fitness testing can begin.

t: Part 4: The Correct Order of Fitness Testing

p: Part 4: The Correct Order of Fitness Testing
x: There are five components and several tests for each. The question is which component's tests come first and which last, so that the results are valid and reliable. Order of fitness testing Step | Test | Why it sits here | Pre-step | Health screening (PAR-Q and informed consent) | Safety and legal protection before anything else | 1 | Blood pressure test | Health marker for the day of testing | 2 | Body composition tests | Needs a neutral, unchanged body state | 3 | Cardiorespiratory endurance tests | Heart rate must rise only because of the cardio task | 4 | Muscular strength tests | Maximal force needs fresh muscles | 5 | Muscular endurance tests | Easier after the strength test (priming effect) | 6 | Flexibility tests | Warm tissues lengthen better | Steps 2 to 6 are the five components of fitness. Step 1 is an additional health marker test. The numbers 1 to 6 are an order, not a rank: blood pressure is not "most important" and flexibility is not "least important". All components are equally important (see the interdependence of components in the Intro to Fitness lecture). The order simply gives the most accurate results for all tests.

p: Part 4: The Correct Order of Fitness Testing
x: The PAR-Q and consent form describe the client's medical background over the last 3 or 6 months. The client's condition on the day of testing (especially the very first time) also has to be checked, because nothing is known about the client. A blood pressure test shows whether the client is ready to be taken through the tests today. If BP is already elevated or high and the client has not mentioned any such history, physical activity during the tests could push it up further, and things could go out of control. It must therefore be normal at the start. If BP is elevated or high on the day: Make the client sit down in a calm, relaxed environment and offer water. Check again after some time. If it is back to normal, begin. If it stays high, avoid the fitness test that day. Try on the second day and the third day. If BP is high on all three days, it can indicate a high blood pressure condition, and the client should be told to see a doctor if they have not already. Three days are used because one high reading may be due to a stressful day, physical activity before coming to the gym, or some other factor. The aim is to be certain that the day on which testing is done is a normal day.

p: Part 4: The Correct Order of Fitness Testing
x: Body composition is defined as the ratio of body fat and lean body mass (answered by the class). Body weight can be divided into two main parts: Body weight, lean body mass and body fat Lean body mass (LBM): Muscles, Organs, Bones, Fluids and Essential Fat (memory aid M, O, B, F, EF). Body fat (BF): visceral fat (VF) and subcutaneous fat (SF). Why first? Body weight changes before and after a workout, because physical activity causes metabolic changes: sweating causes fluid loss and salt depletion. To test body composition in the most accurate and reliable way, the test must be done when everything is neutral and nothing in the body has changed. That is why, for the popular BIA machine, people are told to do the test first thing in the morning before eating or drinking anything. Body composition tests are therefore conducted before any other test.

p: Part 4: The Correct Order of Fitness Testing
x: In the cardio lectures the key factor was the heart rate (just as RM is the key factor in weight training). In both cardiorespiratory endurance tests, heart rate is monitored. Reasoning. Suppose a client does 10 body weight squats, 10 push-ups and then 10 minutes of jogging, and the heart rate is then found to be 132 (a hypothetical number). There is no way to say how much of that heart rate comes from the jogging, because squats and push-ups also raise it. The increase should be solely the contribution of the cardio task. Muscular strength and muscular endurance tests would raise heart rate, and so would flexibility (stretching). So the cardiorespiratory endurance test is done before all of them, to get the most accurate result.

t: 4.5 Steps 4 and 5: strength before endurance (class vote)
p: Part 4: The Correct Order of Fitness Testing
x: The class was asked to vote on whether muscular strength or muscular endurance comes first. The majority said strength first, which is correct. (When this vote is held, many people say endurance first.) Definitions recalled. Muscular strength: the ability of the working skeletal muscles to contract and generate maximum force in one single effort. Muscular endurance: the ability of the working skeletal muscles to contract submaximally for a long period of time without getting fatigued. Reason 1: fatigue. Take the pectoralis major. A bench press (a 1 RM style test) tests strength and push-ups test endurance. If push-ups are done first, the muscle is fatigued, and it would then be expected to generate maximum force, which is unfair. The muscle must be fresh so that it can contract and generate maximal force. Reason 2: the priming or relativity effect (it helps endurance too). Imagine sitting in a car at 100 km/h, which feels very fast on Indian roads. Later you sit in a car (say a Lamborghini) at 200 km/h, double the speed. When that car comes back down to 100 km/h, 100 km/h no longer feels as fast, because you are coming down from 200. In the same way, a muscle that has gone through a 1 RM test (maximum force in a single effort, the "200 km/h" test) finds the endurance test (the "100 km/h" push-ups) less challenging. A client who could do X push-ups when push-ups come first might do more than X when push-ups follow the strength test. So both tests benefit from this order.

p: Part 4: The Correct Order of Fitness Testing
x: Flexibility and mobility go hand in hand, and the factors that affect mobility affect flexibility too. One of those factors is tissue temperature (from the stretching lecture): warmer tissues extend better, and colder tissues are stiffer. Flexibility is the ability of the soft tissues to lengthen passively, so flexibility tests involve stretching the muscles. If flexibility were tested at position 1, 2 or 3, no physical activity would have been done yet and the tissues would be cold. After steps 3, 4 and 5 the tissues are warm and lengthen better. So flexibility is tested last, to expect the best possible results. Analogy: making tea. If a host puts ginger and cardamom in the utensil first, roasts them, then adds tea, and only at the end adds water and milk, the tea will not turn out right (guests would end up ordering tea from outside). Even a simple routine activity needs the correct order for a successful result, and so does fitness testing. Student question: Do we have to test mobility too? A: Flexibility and mobility go hand in hand. Mobility is the ability of joints to move freely and actively through a full range of motion without discomfort. Some flexibility tests check the range of motion at a joint, so mobility is tested side by side. It is not listed separately only because there is no component named mobility; the tests are named after flexibility.

p: Part 5: Test 1, Blood Pressure
x: A BP reading looks like 115/75 mmHg. In everyday language these are called the "upper one" and the "lower one". The professional terms are: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure Systolic BP (the upper, larger number): when the heart beats and the left ventricle pumps blood into the vessels, the pressure in the vessels is highest. This is the systolic pressure. Diastolic BP (the lower, smaller number): in the gap between two heartbeats the pressure falls. The lowest pressure in the vessels is the diastolic pressure. Normal ranges: systolic 90 to 120 mmHg and diastolic 60 to 80 mmHg. mmHg is the unit: millimetres of mercury (Hg is the symbol for mercury). A reading of 115/75 lies in both normal ranges, so it is normal BP. (Many animation videos show systolic and diastolic clearly.)

p: Part 5: Test 1, Blood Pressure
x: Older manual equipment, still used by some nurses and doctors, has a balloon that is pumped, a tube connected to a cuff that inflates, and a rectangular meter containing mercury that rises and falls (a sphygmomanometer). The person testing also uses a stethoscope to hear the pulse sounds. No such skill is needed here. A simple automatic digital machine is used (for example the Omron brand, which is quite reliable). The tube from the cuff is plugged into the monitor, the cuff is wrapped on the upper arm, and the start button is pressed. The machine does everything. The display shows SYS (systolic), DIA (diastolic) and also the pulse rate per minute. After pressing start a mild sound and vibration indicate that the cuff has started inflating by itself.

p: Part 5: Test 1, Blood Pressure
x: Step | Instruction | 1 | Plug the tube end into the device | 2 | Tie the cuff on the upper arm with both the tube and the arm (palm) facing up | 3 | Position the cuff edge 2 to 3 cm above the elbow so that it does not cover the elbow joint | 4 | The cuff should be snug but not too tight: two fingers should fit under it | 5 | The tube should pass along the medial side of the arm (not anterior, not lateral) | 6 | The cuff should be at the same height as the heart (use a table or armrest) | 7 | Correct posture: legs not crossed, feet flat on the floor, back supported; no talking and no stress, by the client and by the tester |

p: Part 5: Test 1, Blood Pressure
x: After the numbers are ready they are checked against a chart, like the test norm sheets for most upcoming tests. Blood pressure category | Systolic mmHg (upper number) | | Diastolic mmHg (lower number) | Low blood pressure (hypotension) | Less than 90 | Or | Less than 60 | Normal | 90 to 120 | And | 60 to 80 | Elevated | 120 to 129 | And | Less than 80 | High blood pressure (hypertension stage 1) | 130 to 139 | Or | 80 to 89 | High blood pressure (hypertension stage 2) | 140 or higher | Or | 90 or higher | Hypertensive crisis (consult a doctor immediately) | 180 or higher | And/or | Higher than 120 | Language. "Hypo" means less (hypotension is low BP), "hyper" means excessive (hypertension is high BP). Applying the chart. 115/75 falls in both normal ranges, so it is normal. If either the systolic is below 90 or the diastolic is below 60, it is low BP. At 140 or higher (systolic) or 90 or higher (diastolic) it is high blood pressure stage 2. Safety link. If the client already had hypertension stage 1 and a physical activity pushed BP further to stage 2 or a hypertensive crisis, it could be very risky. This is why BP is a health marker checked first.

Body composition has eight tests that are grouped into three categories. This makes it the longest component of fitness testing (it may be started in one lecture and finished in the next). Classification of body composition tests Category | Tests | Machine needed? | 2.1 Anthropometric data | Waist circumference (WC), waist to hip ratio (WHR), body mass index (BMI) | No | 2.2 Skinfold measurement | Skinfold caliper test (3 sites) | No (a small hand device) | 2.3 Use of machines | BIA, hydrostatic (underwater) weighing, Bod Pod (air displacement), DEXA (dual energy X-ray absorptiometry) | Yes | The goal is to be aware of all eight tests, not to conduct all of them. After the pros and cons of each have been discussed (finishing in Fitness Testing 2), the most suitable test will be chosen. Numbering system. The number 2 stands for the second type of fitness test (body composition). Under it, 2.1 is the first category (anthropometric data), 2.1.1 to 2.1.3 are its tests, 2.2 is skinfold measurement and 2.3 is use of machines (2.3.1 BIA, 2.3.2 Bod Pod). This makes it easy to remember which test belongs to which category. Pattern followed for each test: objective, procedure (site or steps), norms or results, then advantages and disadvantages.

p: Part 7: 2.1 Anthropometric Data
x: Anthropo means the human body and metric refers to measurements and proportions. Anthropometry is the scientific study of the measurements and proportions of the human body, and anthropometric data are the numbers collected in this study. Three key measurements are taken: Height, measured with a stadiometer. The person stands bare feet on a small platform connected to a pole, with the hips, shoulder blades and head aligned to the pole. A headboard is lowered to touch the crown of the head. The pole carries a scale in feet, inches and centimetres, from which the reading is taken. Weight, measured with a weighing scale. Circumference, the length of the boundary of something, measured with a tape (the same kind a tailor uses for chest, shoulder and lengths). Slide guidelines (height and weight). Height: explain the procedure, remove shoes, stand tall and straight with shoulders relaxed, hands at the sides, thighs together and feet flat and slightly apart. Heels, buttocks and shoulder blades should touch the surface of the measuring board. Lower the headboard until it firmly touches the crown of the head. Record height to the nearest quarter inch or cm, rounding up or down. Weight: explain the procedure, remove shoes, stand in the centre of the scale, stand still with even weight on both feet and arms hanging freely at the sides, and record the weight shown. Some tests use only circumference, others use height and weight. The three tests of this category are WC, WHR and BMI.

p: Part 7: 2.1 Anthropometric Data
x: Test | Objective | 2.1.1 Waist circumference (WC) | Tells whether there is a health risk due to visceral fat (central obesity) | 2.1.2 Waist to hip ratio (WHR) | Tells whether there is an overall health risk | 2.1.3 Body mass index (BMI) | Places the person in a category: underweight, normal weight, overweight or obese | Visceral fat is the deep fat towards the centre, away from the surface, which is why it is also called central obesity. Subcutaneous fat lies towards the skin surface. Important: WC only says whether the risk is high or low. It does not give a visceral fat percentage. WHR is not specific to visceral fat; it gives the general overall health risk.

p: Part 7: 2.1 Anthropometric Data
x: Site. Place the measuring tape across the iliac crest (the highest point of the ilium, which can be felt by standing and touching it). Across the iliac crest the tape also passes through the belly button, and this is the widest part of the waist. Touch and consent. A test with physical touch needs permission, whatever the gender. If the client is comfortable, the trainer takes the measurement. If not, the trainer shows the position on their own body and the client places the tape on themselves, and the trainer notes the reading on the tape. Language with clients. Avoid jargon. A client told "put it across your iliac crest" will ask "where?". Say instead "the widest part of your waist", which automatically falls across the iliac crest. Normal values (for Indians, and applicable to Asians overall). These differ for males and females, and are defined as low health risk. | Low health risk (normal) | Males | WC less than 35.5 inches (90 cm) | Females | WC less than 31.5 inches (80 cm) | The tape has inches on one side and centimetres on the other. These values were not set by the course. They were tried, tested and suggested by research bodies and international bodies. The slides summarise it as: measures risk due to central obesity or visceral fat (risk for lifestyle disorders), with the same Asian values, and a diagram of the iliac crest, visceral fat, abdominal muscles and subcutaneous fat. Their guidelines say to demonstrate to the subject, have them stand upright and relaxed, wind the tape around the greatest anterior extension of the abdomen (usually at the level of the umbilicus and directly above the iliac crest), ask whether the subject wants to be measured or measure themselves, and record the measurement.

p: Part 7: 2.1 Anthropometric Data
x: Formula. The ratio of waist circumference to hip circumference: WHR = WC / HC Both measurements must be in the same unit (inches with inches, or cm with cm; never mix them). Sites. The waist site here is different from the WC test above, even though the same letters "WC" are used. Measurement | Site | Plain wording for clients | Waist (WC) for WHR | The narrowest part of the waist: the midpoint between the last rib and the iliac crest | "Narrow part of the waist" | Hip (HC) | The widest hip area (the slides: maximum circumference of the buttocks) | "Widest part of the hips" | There is no narrow or wide choice for the hips and no special medical term, just the widest hip area. Normal values (low health risk). | WHR | Males | Less than 0.95 | Females | Less than 0.86 | Worked case study. A male client's narrowest waist is 36 inches and his hip is 40 inches (inches for both). WHR = 36 / 40 = 0.90 For a male the limit is 0.95, so 0.90 is below it: low overall health risk. Using the same numbers for a female (the slides use a female for this case): the limit is 0.86 and 0.90 is bigger than 0.86, so the result is high overall health risk. The same number gives different results for the two sexes. Measuring sites and norms for WC and WHR

p: Part 7: 2.1 Anthropometric Data
x: The first two tests use only circumference. BMI uses the other two anthropometric measurements, weight and height, through a formula. Formula. BMI = body weight (kg) / [height (m)]² The unit of BMI is kg/m². Squaring means multiplying a number by itself once (2² = 2 x 2, 3² = 3 x 3 = 9), so the height in metres is multiplied by itself. Online BMI calculators exist, but a trainer should know the formula and calculation (for example when asked in an interview). Converting height to metres. Heights usually come in a mixed form such as 5 ft 8 in. Make it a single unit (inches): 1 ft = 12 in, so 5 ft = 5 x 12 = 60 in. Then 60 + 8 = 68 in. Multiply the inches by the constant 0.0254 to get metres: 68 x 0.0254 = 1.7272 m. Worked example (as done on the board). Body weight 90 kg, height 5 ft 8 in. The height was taken as 1.7 m, then 1.7 x 1.7 = 2.89, written as 2.9: BMI = 90 / 2.9 = 31.03 kg/m² (written 31.02 and 31.03 on the board) (Using the exact 1.7272 m gives about 30.17. See the points to confirm; the category is the same either way.) Worked BMI example and classification BMI classification (proposed Asian criteria, as in the slides). The slide chart is adapted from The Lancet 2004;363:157-63. Category | BMI (kg/m²) | Underweight | Less than 18.5 | Normal range | 18.5 to 22.9 | Overweight | 23 to 24.9 | Obese | 25 and above (the slide prints "> 25") | At 31, the example client is placed in obese.

p: Part 7: 2.1 Anthropometric Data
x: The lecture stressed that BMI should not be relied on as accurate, because of loopholes: BMI limitations 1. It does not differentiate body fat from lean body mass. Suppose a client's details (90 kg and 5 ft 8 in) arrive on WhatsApp or from the gym manager before the first meeting, and the trainer calculates BMI as homework and concludes that he is obese. At the first meeting the client turns out to be a muscular person. The trainer would feel awkward saying "I thought you were obese as per your BMI". Two people of the same height and weight (the slide shows a bodybuilder and an obese person on the same scale, both 90 kg) can have very different compositions, because weight comprises both lean body mass and body fat. People with the same weight cannot be assumed to have the same body composition. 2. "Skinny fat". Suppose the data gave a BMI of 21, which is normal. The client may actually be skinny fat: the upper and lower limbs are lean (no visible fat) but there is adiposity in the belly region. Calling this person normal is also incorrect, because BMI does not count body fat; it only looks at weight and height.

t: What the three anthropometric tests cannot do
p: Part 7: 2.1 Anthropometric Data
x: None of the three tests gives an actual body fat percentage. The ideal body fat levels (from the body composition lecture and the slides) are less than 15% for males and less than 20% for females, so a percentage number is needed to judge ideal body composition. The slides illustrate these levels with figures from 45% down to 15% for females and 35% down to 8% for males. The three tests are not discarded or degraded. They are used, but only as short-term or mid-term goals for the client (for example: "as per the WC test you are 2 inches above the normal value, so your short-term goal is to get below it so there is no health risk"). They cannot be relied on for body composition. The search for a percentage continues with the next tests.

p: Part 8: 2.2 Skinfold Measurement
x: There is only one test in this category: the skinfold test, using a skinfold caliper. The caliper looks like the compass used to draw circles: it has two arms with a pointed surface at the end of each. The trainer pinches and holds the skin to make a skin fold and uses the caliper to measure the thickness of that fold. The slides show the steps: pinch the skinfold between the fingers, then place the caliper on the skinfold to measure the fat percentage. Calipers come in several designs (four types are shown), but the process is the same. What it measures and the principle. A pinch of skin and fat measures the subcutaneous fat (not the deep, internal fat). The principle: the higher the subcutaneous fat, the higher the body fat percentage.

t: 8.2 Sites (3 sites each for women and men)
p: Part 8: 2.2 Skinfold Measurement
x: | Women | Men | Site 1 | Triceps fold | Chest: midpoint between the top of the armpit and the nipple | Site 2 | Suprailiac fold: supra means superior, iliac refers to the iliac crest, so the fold just above the iliac crest on the waistline | Abdomen: 1 inch from the belly button (left or right, anywhere) | Site 3 | Mid thigh | Mid thigh | The mid thigh is the one site common to both sexes.

p: Part 8: 2.2 Skinfold Measurement
