x: Advantages | Disadvantages | Portable: small and handy, fits in a bag or a deep jacket pocket | Measures only subcutaneous fat (no visceral fat), so it does not tell how much is subcutaneous and how much is visceral; it cannot be relied on alone | Easy to use: once the three sites for each sex are known, there is no rocket science | High standard error of plus or minus 3% | Time saving: it takes only a few seconds | Not suitable for the very obese or the very lean | | Pinching discomfort: not everyone is comfortable being pinched | Standard error explained. Calipers range in price from about Rs 300 to Rs 5,000, and more spending may give better accuracy, but the method itself is still not considered fully accurate, even for an expensive one, because accuracy comes from the type of test and the steps taken, not from the price. Accuracy of any test is compared with the gold standard. If the gold standard says a person has 20% body fat, the caliper result can fall anywhere from 17% to 23% (plus or minus 3 of that number). Caliper standard error Why not suitable for extremes. A very lean person may have so little fat that no fold can be pinched, so nothing can be measured. A very obese person may have more subcutaneous fat than the maximum opening of the caliper arms. The slides list the same points: easy to use once the skill is mastered, does not require much time, easy portability; error of plus or minus 3% (compared with underwater weighing), does not differentiate subcutaneous from visceral fat, not ideal for the obese and very lean, and individual preference about being pinched. From this test onwards, the advantages and disadvantages of each test are noted so that a final choice can be made.

t: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)

p: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)
x: The BIA machine is the machine seen in most gyms that looks like a weighing scale: people stand on it and hold a handle connected by a chain or rope at chest level. It is often wrongly called the "BMI machine". It is called that because one of its results is BMI, which it calculates automatically. But the correct name is the BIA machine. BIA = Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis. Part | Meaning | Bio | Life, a living organism | Electric | Electric current | Impedance | Resistance | Analysis | Study | The slides describe it as a test that measures the difficulty level of an electric current moving through the body (resistance to the passage of current in the body).

p: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)
x: A person stands barefoot. The platform has metal plates (in some machines the whole platform is metallic, in others a plastic platform has a metal footstep). These are electrodes through which a very mild current enters the body. It is not felt as anything more than a mild vibration. The machine analyses how much difficulty the current faces moving through the body: is it resisted and restricted, or does it move smoothly? From this it works out who has more fat and who has more muscle. Key scientific principle: water is a good conductor of electricity. Water can amplify an electric current (the reason one is told to stay away from open wires near water). Comparing muscle and fat. From the body composition lecture: | Muscle cell | Fat cell | Water | 75% | 10% | Other content | 20% muscle protein (actin, myosin), 4% intramuscular triglyceride (IMTG), 1% glycogen (total 100%) | 90% triglyceride (TG) | Effect on the current | Plenty of water, so the current passes smoothly | Little water, so the current is restricted | A person with more fat mass has more fat cells, hence a smaller proportion of water per cell, so the current faces restriction. A person with more muscle mass has more water in the body, so the current passes smoothly. The machine reads the resistance level and then reports fat mass and muscle mass percentages. BIA principle: water content of muscle and fat The slides present the same idea: lean body mass has higher water and salts and lesser fat (it conducts, allowing the current to pass faster), while adipose tissue has low water and higher fat content (it insulates, so the current passes slowly). Compared with earlier tests. The anthropometric tests gave no percentage. Skinfold gave a percentage that was not fully reliable because it ignores visceral fat. BIA considers both visceral and subcutaneous fat and gives a percentage.

p: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)
x: Types of BIA machines Foot to foot: looks like a weighing scale. Current enters through the feet only, the machine analyses the lower body and estimates for the full body. Hand to hand: looks like a video game controller. Electrodes are only in the hands, so current enters only through the hands, the machine analyses the upper body and estimates for the full body. Hand to foot (latest machines): electrodes in the hands and the feet, so there is no estimation and the entire body is analysed. Price and features. BIA machines come in a wide price range, from about Rs 10,000 up to Rs 45 lakh per machine. High-end machines give segmental analysis: fat mass and muscle mass for the arms, chest, abdomen, thighs and pelvis separately. They also consider extracellular and intracellular water. A popular brand has 3 series, 6 series and 9 series models, with better features in the higher models.

p: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)
x: The video showed the steps: The person steps on the scale barefoot. The footprints are the metal electrodes, and the platform is also a weighing scale, so the machine measures weight first. The height is entered manually on the screen. The trainer has already measured it with the stadiometer. The person holds the hand electrodes, pressing the thumbs against the metal part, and raises the handle slightly to chest level, keeping the arms raised and still. The machine runs the test and gives the analysis. Below the weight and height, three results appear: body fat percentage, muscle mass and BMI.

p: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)
x: The conditions must be met before taking the test. The goal is to stand on the machine with neutral hydration: nothing extra added from outside and nothing lost. Prerequisites for a BIA test Prerequisite | Reason | Well rested | Basic requirement | Empty stomach: no water, no food (food contains water) | Water or fluid taken before the test hydrates the person, which is like cheating. The machine does not ignore it: it counts that water and amplifies the current | No coffee | A student asked about black coffee (because getting out of bed is hard). Coffee cannot be had without water, so the answer is no | No alcohol, with a gap of 48 hours | The effect needs to be neutralised before the test | No exercise before the test, with a gap of 12 hours | Sweating loses fluid, so the person is dehydrated and the machine reads the lower hydration level, which is a loss for the person | No metallic objects (ornaments, jewellery, bracelets, watches, gadgets, phones, belts) | Metal conducts electricity, just like water, and can influence the reading | Not during periods (women) | Fluid loss during periods influences the results | Student question: What is the time interval for food (for example 12 hours before)? A: The preferred condition is an empty stomach along with being well rested. That is why the test is said to be done first thing in the morning: there is then automatically a gap of at least about 6 hours since dinner.

p: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)
x: Advantages | Disadvantages | Time saving: hardly a minute | Some models might show standard error. Not every model is meant, but they cannot be as accurate as the gold standard (so not 100% reliable), though still better than the earlier tests | Easy to use: even front desk staff at a gym can conduct it if the correct method is followed; no certified trainer, physician or exercise physiologist is needed | Hydration level can impact results: if the person is dehydrated or over-hydrated, the numbers cannot be relied upon, because the whole principle is that water conducts electricity | Needs only an electric switch and socket: it is not portable like the caliper, but it is small, easy to move, takes little space and needs no heavy equipment | |

p: Part 9: 2.3 Use of Machines: the BIA Test (2.3.1)
x: Q: Does the machine show the percentage of muscle and fat, or the actual weight in kilograms? A: It depends on the model. The screen next to the machine is only a display screen connected to a system on which the entire report appears. A very expensive, high-end model shows a body chart with the body divided into segments, with percentages and kilograms for each segment. Q: If someone is more hydrated, will the muscle mass show higher? A: Yes, and that is why the number cannot be relied on in that case. Be careful about hydration. Q: The price varies from Rs 10,000 to Rs 45 lakh. Does a low-cost machine give more errors, or does a costly one just give more details? A: Accuracy does not always come with spending. Entry-level or mid-level models may not give features such as in-depth analysis, but the number they give cannot be called totally untrustworthy or completely unreliable. Using the best test to check a gym's machine. One of the later tests (the final choice, to be revealed in the next lecture) is not conducted in gyms, but it gives very accurate, reliable and worldwide accepted numbers. A client can get that test done once, and then compare the gym's BIA machine (entry level or mid level) against it, to get an idea of how close the machine is and how much standard error it has. A student guessed which test this is (DEXA), and the answer was left for the next lecture.

p: Part 10: The Bod Pod Test (2.3.2)
x: Bod Pod: Bod refers to the body, Pod refers to a sealed chamber. The machine is a big egg-shaped chamber. (Similar sleeping pods exist at some airports, where people lie down, a panel closes, and there is soothing music. The Bod Pod has no such music: the person sits in the machine, the door closes, and the test is run.) It is also called the air displacement method.

p: Part 10: The Bod Pod Test (2.3.2)
x: The Bod Pod belongs to the densitometry methods of body composition. There are two tests in this group: the Bod Pod, and another test that comes next lecture. Densitometry uses body density to measure body fat percentage. Body density = body mass (body weight) / body volume Once the machine calculates body density, it applies the Siri equation to calculate body fat percentage: Body fat % = (4.95 / body density - 4.50) x 100 These formulas need not be memorised. The computer does everything, and the technician does not have to do anything. They are explained to show the science behind the machine. How the Bod Pod calculates body fat percentage

p: Part 10: The Bod Pod Test (2.3.2)
x: The slide shows the machine and a cut-away view. The part where the person sits is the test chamber. Behind the seat is the reference chamber. In the reference chamber there is the grey box, which is the weighing scale that measures body weight. A diaphragm behind the backrest measures the volume of air inside the test chamber. How body volume is found by air displacement. Before anyone sits inside, the diaphragm measures the volume of air in the empty chamber and stores it. The person sits in the chamber. The person takes up some space, so some air is displaced. The diaphragm measures the volume of air again, and it is different. The difference between the two volumes (empty chamber minus chamber with the person) gives the volume of the person. Body mass is already known from the scale, so body density is calculated, and then the Siri equation gives body fat percentage. Student question: When the door opens, the air volume and pressure change. How is that handled? A: The machine has already stored the volume of the empty chamber. It analyses both air volume and air pressure, and after the door opens, the person sits and the door closes, it compares what the chamber measured earlier with what it measures now. The video also showed a tube into which the person breathes out (a small breathing manoeuvre). It measures the air in the lungs, so the machine can remove that air as well and consider only the person's body volume. Lung volume measurement improves the accuracy of the test. Clothing. The person wears a swimming costume (spandex or swim shorts for men, a swimsuit for women, body-hugging material) and a tight swimming cap. No extra air must go inside with the person. Ordinary clothes carry air in the shirt and the trouser pockets, and hair has gaps that hold air, so a tight cap is worn.

p: Part 10: The Bod Pod Test (2.3.2)
x: In the video the result screen shows body fat percentage and also the masses of fat and fat-free mass. In the example shown, a person's total weight of 97 kg was made up of 82 kg of fat-free mass and 15 kg of fat mass, which can also be expressed as percentages. Fat-free mass is the same as lean body mass (confirmed by a student's question). From these figures the fat percentage is 15 / 97, about 15.5% (calculated for these notes; the recording did not state it).

p: Part 10: The Bod Pod Test (2.3.2)
x: Advantages | Disadvantages | Accurate: comparable to the gold standard. Note that it is not the gold standard itself, but accuracy is always compared with the gold standard, so it is almost at par | Expensive: not every facility can afford it | Time saving | Not available in India (as written on the board); availability is limited | No technical expertise needed: the machine does everything | | Suitable for all ages and special cases: all ages, patients (heart related, joint related, neurological), obese people, children, very elderly people and hydrophobic people (people afraid of water). It is safe and easy to use | | Why "hydrophobic" is mentioned. The next test, the water displacement method (hydrostatic or underwater weighing), measures body volume with the person submerged in a tub of water. A person afraid of water, a patient, an obese person, a child or a senior citizen may not manage to go underwater and stay there during the test. The Bod Pod, in which the person only sits in a chamber, is safe for them. The slides add: pretty accurate compared with hydrostatic weighing, easy to operate, short measurement time, well suited to all populations (children, obese, elderly, disabled); disadvantages: expensive and not easily available. Two key parameters for the final choice. When all tests are compared to pick the best one, affordability and availability will also be considered, along with accuracy. There is no point in a very accurate test that is not available in the country, or that is too expensive for the facility or the client.

t: Part 11: Wrap-up and Preview of Fitness Testing 2

p: Part 11: Wrap-up and Preview of Fitness Testing 2
x: Topic | Key points | Objectives | Global: standardisation, performance benchmarking. Client: baseline, progress tracking, goal setting, strengths and areas to work on | Pre-step | Health screening with PAR-Q (all No, otherwise NOC) and informed consent | Order | BP, body composition, cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility | BP | Systolic (upper, 90 to 120) and diastolic (lower, 60 to 80); seven-step procedure; classification chart | Anthropometric | WC (visceral fat risk), WHR (overall risk), BMI (category); no body fat percentage | Skinfold | Caliper, subcutaneous fat, plus or minus 3% | BIA | Water conducts current; muscle 75% water, fat 10%; prerequisites | Bod Pod | Air displacement, body density, Siri equation |

t: 11.2 Comparison of the body composition tests so far
p: Part 11: Wrap-up and Preview of Fitness Testing 2
x: Test | Gives % body fat? | Measures | Accuracy | Main advantages | Main disadvantages | WC | No | Circumference (risk from visceral fat) | Risk only | Simple, no machine | No percentage | WHR | No | Circumference ratio (overall risk) | Risk only | Simple, no machine | No percentage | BMI | No | Weight and height (category) | Low reliability | Easy formula | Cannot tell fat from muscle, misses skinny fat | Skinfold caliper | Yes | Subcutaneous fat | Plus or minus 3% | Portable, easy, quick | No visceral fat, not for very obese or very lean, pinching | BIA | Yes | Resistance to current (visceral and subcutaneous) | Some models have standard error | Quick, easy, needs only a socket | Hydration sensitive | Bod Pod | Yes | Body volume by air displacement | Comparable to gold standard | Accurate, quick, suits all populations | Expensive, availability |

p: Part 11: Wrap-up and Preview of Fitness Testing 2
x: Two machines remain for body composition: the hydrostatic (water displacement) test and the second remaining machine (the lecture used the numbers 2.3.3 and 2.3.4). Once those are covered in Fitness Testing 2, the best test for body composition will be disclosed (after comparing pros and cons, including cost and availability), and the lectures will move on to the other components.

These are places where the recording was unclear or inconsistent, or where it differs from the slides or E-book. The lecture's version is used in the notes. BMI worked example numbers. The recording converts 5 ft 8 in to 68 in correctly (the speaker briefly said "5 ft 6" but the board shows 5 ft = 60 in and 68 in). It then multiplies 68 by 0.0254 and says the result is 1.7526, but 68 x 0.0254 = 1.7272 m (1.7526 is the value for 69 in). The board rounds to 1.7 m, squares it to 2.9 (1.7 x 1.7 = 2.89) and gets BMI 31.03 (board 31.02 and 31.03). The slides use 1.72 m, 2.95 and 30.50. With the exact 1.7272 m the BMI is about 30.17. All versions fall in the obese category. These notes show the lecture's calculation and note the exact value. BMI categories. The lecture and slides use the proposed Asian criteria (underweight below 18.5, normal 18.5 to 22.9, overweight 23 to 24.9, obese 25 and above). The lecture said "anything more than 25 is obese", and the slide prints "> 25". The E-book (Chapter VII) uses overweight 25 to 29.9 and obese 30 and above. The recording did not give the overweight band, which is taken from the slide. Waist circumference thresholds. The lecture and slides give 90 cm (35.5 in) for men and 80 cm (31.5 in) for women for Indians and Asians. The E-book's obesity risk factor table uses waist above 102 cm for men and 88 cm for women (and BMI above 30, WHR above 0.95 for men and 0.86 for women). 35.5 in is 90.2 cm, so 90 cm is an approximation. WC measuring site wording. The lecture says across the iliac crest, passing through the belly button (the widest part). The slides say the greatest anterior extension of the abdomen, usually at the level of the umbilicus and directly above the iliac crest. The E-book abdomen site is at the greatest anterior extension, usually at the level of the umbilicus. For WHR the lecture and slides agree (midpoint of the last rib and the iliac crest), and the E-book describes the waist as the narrowest part of the torso. WHR case study. The lecture used a male (low risk) and then a female (high risk) with the same numbers; the slide shows only the female case (high risk). Both are consistent. The E-book says WHR risk limits vary with age and sex (for example 0.95 for young men and 0.86 for young women, with higher limits at 60 to 69). Skinfold sites. The lecture and slides agree: chest (midpoint between nipple and top of the armpit), abdomen 1 inch from the belly button and mid thigh for men; triceps, suprailiac and mid thigh for women. The E-book describes an abdomen site 2 cm to the right of the umbilicus, a chest fold at one-half the distance between the anterior axillary line and the nipple, and says measurements are taken on the right side of the body. What the caliper error is compared with. The lecture says plus or minus 3% compared with the gold standard (without naming it); the slide says compared with underwater weighing; the E-book also gives plus or minus 3%. Which test is the "gold standard". The lecture did not name it (a student guessed DEXA and the answer was left for the next lecture). The slides and E-book describe hydrostatic (underwater) weighing as the gold standard in percent body fat measurement. Confirm in Fitness Testing 2. PAR-Q length. The lecture said 10 or 12 questions; the slide sample has 10 questions. Blood pressure classification boundaries. The slide table has overlapping boundaries (for example 120 appears in both normal and elevated, and 80 as the top of normal diastolic and the start of stage 1). The lecture only stated the normal range (90 to 120, 60 to 80), the low BP rule (systolic below 90 or diastolic below 60) and the stage 2 rule (140 or higher, or 90 or higher). Elevated, stage 1 and crisis values are taken from the slide. Three-day blood pressure rule. Repeating the check over three days when BP is high is the lecture's practice and is not in the slides. Course: Personal Training Certification Topic: Fitness testing, part 1 of 2 About these notes: A short revision version of the Fitness Testing 1 lecture: key tables, key terms and 20 revision questions with an answer key. For the full explanation see the Detailed Notes. Sources: the lecture, the course slides ("Fitness Testing 1 & 2"), board photos from the lecture and E-book Chapter VII (Health Screening and Fitness Testing). Big idea: Fitness is tested with standardised, worldwide tests. Before any test, screen the client's health. Then test in an order that protects the accuracy of every result: blood pressure, body composition, cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility. Body composition has eight tests, and six of them (waist circumference, waist to hip ratio, BMI, skinfold, BIA and Bod Pod) are covered today.

t: 1. Why test? Objectives of fitness testing
x: Objectives of fitness testing Perspective | Objective | Meaning | Global | Standardisation | Same test, procedure, method and norms everywhere (for example bench press is the worldwide muscular strength test), so results can be compared | Global | Performance benchmarking | Shows how far a country's athletes lag or lead, so the standard can be chased or maintained | Client | Baseline results | First test: where the client stands today | Client | Progress tracking | Re-test (for example after 3 months): numbers show progress, build confidence and motivation | Client | Goal setting | From baseline and re-test: short-term, mid-term and long-term milestones, tweaked after the re-test | Client | Strengths and areas to work on | Customised plan (say "areas to work on", not "weaknesses"); strength can come from any of the five components | A test norm is a sheet that shows where a score stands for a component. All five components must be tested before calling someone fit. A contraindication is any movement that causes discomfort or pain: choose an alternative exercise to avoid injury. Poor flexibility result: stretch every day (mobility drills and static stretching).

Health screening is a procedure done on people without symptoms to assess the likelihood of a disease. Think of baggage screening at an airport: make sure the client is safe before testing. It uses two forms, filled and signed by the client. Form | Key points | PAR-Q (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire) | About 10 close-ended Yes or No questions on medical background (heart, joints, neurological). All No means cleared. Any Yes means stop, ask, and get a NOC (no objection certificate) from the doctor | Informed consent | A script that informs the client about machines, exercises (strength, cardio, stretching) and risks, for the whole fitness journey, ending with a statement of willing agreement and a signature | Document everything and get it signed: it protects the trainer. If a gym already has its own forms, follow them. If it has none, introduce them.

Order of fitness testing Step | Test | Why here | 1 | Blood pressure | Health marker for the day; high BP could shoot up during testing | 2 | Body composition | Needs a neutral body (exercise, sweat, food and water change body weight and composition) | 3 | Cardiorespiratory endurance | Heart rate must rise only from the cardio task | 4 | Muscular strength | Maximum force in one effort needs fresh muscles | 5 | Muscular endurance | After strength: priming or relativity effect (the 100 km/h feels slower after 200 km/h) | 6 | Flexibility | Tissues are warm after steps 3 to 5, so they lengthen better | The order is not a ranking of importance. Muscular strength: maximum force in one single effort. Muscular endurance: submaximal contraction for a long time without fatigue. Mobility (joints moving freely and actively through full range of motion without discomfort) is tested side by side with flexibility.

Systolic and diastolic blood pressure Systolic (upper): highest pressure, when the left ventricle pumps. Normal 90 to 120 mmHg. Diastolic (lower): lowest pressure, between heartbeats. Normal 60 to 80 mmHg. mmHg is millimetres of mercury. Category | Systolic | | Diastolic | Low (hypotension) | Less than 90 | Or | Less than 60 | Normal | 90 to 120 | And | 60 to 80 | Elevated | 120 to 129 | And | Less than 80 | Hypertension stage 1 | 130 to 139 | Or | 80 to 89 | Hypertension stage 2 | 140 or higher | Or | 90 or higher | Hypertensive crisis | 180 or higher | And/or | Higher than 120 | Seven steps with a digital monitor: 1 plug the tube into the device; 2 cuff on the upper arm, tube and palm facing up; 3 cuff edge 2 to 3 cm above the elbow; 4 snug (two fingers fit); 5 tube along the medial side of the arm; 6 cuff at heart height (table or armrest); 7 legs uncrossed, feet flat, back supported, no talking. If BP is high: rest, offer water, re-check. If still high, skip the test and try the next day, up to three days. High on all three days: refer to a doctor.

Body weight, lean body mass and body fat Classification of body composition tests Category | Tests | 2.1 Anthropometric data | WC, WHR, BMI | 2.2 Skinfold measurement | Skinfold caliper | 2.3 Use of machines | BIA, Bod Pod (today); hydrostatic weighing and DEXA (Fitness Testing 2) | LBM = muscles, organs, bones, fluids, essential fat (M, O, B, F, EF). BF = visceral fat and subcutaneous fat. Anthropometry = study of measurements and proportions of the human body (height with a stadiometer, weight with a scale, circumference with a tape). Body composition is tested first (after BP) because weight and fluid change after activity. BIA is best done first thing in the morning.

Test | Objective | Site / formula | Norm (low risk) | WC | Health risk from visceral fat (central obesity) | Across the iliac crest, through the belly button (widest part of the waist) | Men below 35.5 in (90 cm), women below 31.5 in (80 cm) | WHR | Overall health risk | WHR = WC / HC. Waist: narrowest part (midpoint between last rib and iliac crest). Hip: widest part | Men below 0.95, women below 0.86 | BMI | Category: underweight, normal, overweight, obese | BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)². Unit kg/m² | See table below | Measuring sites and norms Ask permission before measuring (or let the client place the tape). Say "widest part of your waist", not "iliac crest". WHR case: waist 36 in, hip 40 in gives 0.90. For a man that is low risk (below 0.95). For a woman it is high risk (above 0.86). Use the same unit for waist and hip. WC and WHR give risk only, not a body fat percentage. BMI classification (Asian criteria, slides): Category | BMI (kg/m²) | Underweight | Below 18.5 | Normal | 18.5 to 22.9 | Overweight | 23 to 24.9 | Obese | 25 and above | BMI calculation: 5 ft 8 in = 5 x 12 + 8 = 68 in. Multiply by 0.0254 to get metres (68 x 0.0254 = 1.7272 m; the board used 1.7 m). Lecture example: 90 / (1.7 x 1.7) = 90 / 2.9 = 31.03 kg/m², obese. Worked BMI example Shortcomings of BMI: it does not separate body fat from lean body mass (a muscular person and a fat person of the same height and weight get the same BMI), and it misses "skinny fat" people (BMI normal, for example 21, but fat in the belly). BMI limitations Ideal body fat: men below 15%, women below 20%. None of the three tests gives this percentage. Use them only as short-term or mid-term goals, not to judge body composition.

A compass-like caliper measures the thickness of a pinched skin fold, which is subcutaneous fat. More subcutaneous fat means a higher body fat percentage. | Women | Men | Sites | Triceps, suprailiac (just above the iliac crest), mid thigh | Chest (midpoint of armpit top and nipple), abdomen (1 inch from the belly button), mid thigh | Advantages | Disadvantages | Portable, easy to use, time saving | Only subcutaneous fat (no visceral), standard error of plus or minus 3%, not for the very obese or very lean, pinching discomfort | Caliper standard error Price (about Rs 300 to Rs 5,000) does not remove the error. A reference of 20% can read 17% to 23%.

Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis: bio (living organism), electric (current), impedance (resistance), analysis (study). Often wrongly called the "BMI machine" (it also reports BMI). Principle: water is a good conductor of electricity. A mild current enters through electrodes (metal plates); the machine measures resistance. BIA principle | Muscle | Fat | Water | 75% | 10% | Current | Passes smoothly | Restricted | Types of BIA machines Types: hand to hand (upper body, then estimated), foot to foot (lower body, then estimated), hand to foot (latest, whole body). Price about Rs 10,000 to Rs 45 lakh; high-end models give segmental analysis and intracellular and extracellular water. Results: body fat %, muscle mass, BMI. Prerequisites for a BIA test Advantages | Disadvantages | Time saving (about a minute), easy to use (even front desk staff), needs only a switch and socket | Some models show standard error (not as accurate as the gold standard), hydration level changes results |

Bod = body, Pod = sealed chamber (egg-shaped). Air displacement method, a densitometry method. Body density = body mass / body volume. Volume = air in the empty chamber minus air with the person. A diaphragm measures air volume; a scale in the reference chamber measures weight. Siri equation: body fat % = (4.95 / body density minus 4.50) x 100 (no need to memorise). Wear spandex or a swimsuit and a tight swim cap so no extra air enters. A breathing tube helps account for lung air. Bod Pod calculation Advantages | Disadvantages | Accurate (comparable to, but not, the gold standard), time saving, no technical expertise, suits all ages, patients, obese, children, elderly and hydrophobic people | Expensive, limited availability (not available in India, as on the board) | Example in the video: 97 kg total = 82 kg fat-free mass + 15 kg fat mass (about 15.5% fat, calculated for these notes). Affordability and availability are also criteria when the best test is chosen in Fitness Testing 2.

Global: standardisation and performance benchmarking. Client: baseline results, progress tracking, goal setting, strengths and areas to work on. A reference sheet used to check a test score and see where the person stands for that fitness component. A client meeting the trainer for the first time may react badly to being told they have "weaknesses", and the service industry needs polished wording. Strength here can come from any of the five components. All answers must be No. With a Yes the trainer stops and asks, and the client must bring a NOC from their doctor. The PAR-Q is a set of Yes or No medical questions that screens readiness. The informed consent form is a script that informs the client about machines, exercises and risks, ending with willing agreement and a signature. Blood pressure, body composition, cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility. It is a health marker: if BP is elevated or high, activity during testing could push it up dangerously. If high, the client rests, drinks water and is re-checked. If it stays high the test is skipped and tried again on the next days; high on three days means referral to a doctor. A fatigued muscle cannot produce maximum force. Strength first also makes the endurance test feel easier (priming or relativity effect), so more repetitions may be done. Warm tissues lengthen better. After the other tests the tissues are warm, so flexibility results are best. Heart rate is the measure, and strength, endurance and stretching tests would also raise it, so the rise must come only from the cardio task. Systolic 90 to 120 mmHg, diastolic 60 to 80 mmHg. 115/75 is within both, so it is normal BP. On the upper arm, with the edge 2 to 3 cm above the elbow, snug but not tight (two fingers fit under it), tube on the medial side, cuff at heart height. It tells whether there is a health risk from visceral fat (central obesity). The tape goes across the iliac crest and belly button (widest part of the waist). Low risk: men below 35.5 in (90 cm), women below 31.5 in (80 cm). WHR = 30 / 36 = 0.83. For a woman the limit is below 0.86, so it is low overall health risk. 63 / (1.75 x 1.75) = 63 / 3.0625 = 20.6 kg/m², which is normal (18.5 to 22.9). It does not separate body fat from lean body mass (a muscular person can be called obese), and it misses skinny fat people (normal BMI but fat in the belly). It measures the thickness of a skin fold, which is subcutaneous fat (no visceral fat). A true 20% may read anywhere from 17% to 23%. Bioelectrical impedance analysis. Water is a good conductor of electricity, so current passes smoothly through muscle (75% water) and is restricted by fat (10% water). Rested and empty stomach (no water, food or coffee), no exercise for 12 hours, no alcohol for 48 hours, no metal objects, and women not during periods. It subtracts the air volume of the chamber with the person from the air volume of the empty chamber (air displacement). A tight cap and swimwear stop air trapped in hair and clothes from entering the chamber.

p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: The lecture continues from Fitness Testing 1 using the same numbering system. Test type 2 is body composition, category 2.3 is the use of machines, and the test now being studied is the third machine, 2.3.3. The two machines already covered were: BIA: bioelectrical impedance analysis. Bod Pod: also called air displacement. It is one of the densitometry methods. There is another densitometry method that uses water displacement instead of air displacement. This is the hydrostatic method. Its details involve a lot of physics, so only the essential principles are studied.

p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: The same test has several names, and decoding the names explains the procedure and principle. Name | What the name tells you | Hydrostatic test | Hydro = water, static = still. The water is not moving | Underwater weighing test | The person is sent underwater and their weight is measured underwater. The person goes into a tub of still water, not a river | Water displacement method | Water is displaced when the person goes in, and the displaced water gives the volume | All three names refer to the same test.

p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: Densitometry methods are based on body density: Body density = weight (mass) / volume In this test the weight is checked underwater, using a special apparatus (seen in the demonstration video), and the volume is found from the water displaced. Once weight and volume are known, body density is calculated. Body density is then fed into the Siri equation (the same equation used for the Bod Pod) to calculate the body fat percentage. Hydrostatic weighing procedure

p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: The method rests on the principle given by the scientist Archimedes. It is explained in the simplest way, for students without a science background. Setup. Imagine a tub filled to the brim with water, and a box (an object) that is lowered into it. As the object goes underwater, some water obviously spills out. Part 1 (AP 1). The volume of the object that goes underwater is equal to the volume (amount) of water displaced. This is why the test can find a person's volume: the displaced water is collected through a proper drainage system (some set-ups use a tank, a tub or a small swimming-pool-like system). Nobody stands outside with a bucket. The displaced water equals the volume of the person's body. This is the same idea as the Bod Pod, where the person takes up space in the chamber and displaces air; here the person takes up space in the tub and displaces water. Part 2 (AP 2). When an object goes underwater, an upward force acts on it. This is the buoyant force. Buoyancy is the ability of an object to float. Anyone who has been in a swimming pool has felt this upward push from the bottom of the pool. Archimedes also discovered that the water displaced is equivalent to the buoyant force applied on the object. Putting the two parts together: more volume means more water displaced, and more water displaced means a higher buoyant force. Less volume means less water displaced and a lower buoyant force.

t: 1.5 Fat versus muscle: why the test is so detailed
p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: Exercise physicists compare fat and muscle to a very deep level to reach the most accurate body fat percentage. The comparison written on the board has four points. Q (to the class): Which takes more space, 1 kg of fat or 1 kg of muscle? A: Fat. The weight is the same, but fat has more volume and muscle has less volume. # | Fat | Muscle | Where it comes from | 1 | More volume | Less volume | Property of the tissues | 2 | More water displaced | Less water displaced | Archimedes part 1 | 3 | Higher buoyant force | Lower buoyant force | Archimedes part 2 | 4 | Lighter than water | Heavier (denser) than water | A unique property of fat and muscle, not Archimedes | Result | Tendency to float | Tendency to sink | | Archimedes principle applied to fat and muscle Reading the whole story for fat. More volume gives more water displacement, so a higher buoyant force pushes the piece up. On top of that, the fat is lighter than water. That is why fat floats. Reading the whole story for muscle. Less volume gives less water displacement, so the buoyant force that could push the piece up is low. On top of that, muscle is heavier than water, so it is even harder for the force to lift it. That is why muscle sinks. Important points about this comparison: It compares fat and muscle as separate tissues. A real body contains both, so a person does not completely float or completely sink. It is a visual indicator: a person who floats more can be read as having lower muscle mass (more fat), and a person with a greater tendency to go down has more muscle mass. The slides show the same idea for two people. With low body fat percentage: less volume (space), displaces less water, less buoyant (heavy), weighs more in water. With high body fat percentage: more volume, displaces more water, more buoyant (light), weighs less in water. | Low body fat % | High body fat % | Volume (space) | Less | More | Water displaced | Less | More | Buoyancy | Less buoyant (heavy) | More buoyant (light) | Weight in water | Weighs more | Weighs less |

p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: Because of this level of analysis, hydrostatic weighing is given the title gold standard of body composition tests. It is known for the highest accuracy, and other machines and tests have their accuracy compared against it. For comparison, skinfold testing was mentioned in Fitness Testing 1 as having a high standard error of about plus or minus 3 percentage points. For example, if skinfold says 20 percent, the true value may lie anywhere from about 17 to 23 percent. A result from the gold standard method can be relied on far more.

p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: A video from a university exercise physiology laboratory shows how the test is conducted. The details explain why the test is so accurate and why it is demanding. Two measurements are needed: body mass, measured easily on a scale, and body volume, which is the whole point of putting the person in the tank. The weighing scale is connected by a rod to a seat. The client sits on the seat and goes underwater, and that is how the weight underwater is measured. The principle is Archimedes' principle: the amount of water displaced equals the volume of whatever is put into the tank. The client sits on the chair with the water level at the neck, so she does not have to bend far. Two things make a person float: fat and air. Fat floats because of the properties above. Air floats too: this is why life-savers at pools and beaches keep air-filled tubes, and why beginners learning to swim use air-filled floats. The air already in the lungs would influence and distort the reading. So the client is told to blow out all the air from the lungs under water. She is told to push out a little more even when she thinks all the air is out, and to be as still as possible (movement makes the needle on the scale hard to read). She comes up when she needs air, nobody signals her. The tester watches the bubbles. While bubbles still appear, the client is still exhaling. When the bubbles stop, all the air has gone from the lungs and the reading is taken. Several trials are done, so that the reading is the same each time. A single trial may be wrong if the client did not exhale properly or moved a lot. Why this is difficult. Staying under water without breathing is hard for someone who is not used to water. Exhaling under water is even harder: it is an unnatural manoeuvre, because naturally a person going under water holds the breath. A person who is afraid of water cannot be expected to do it. This is why the Bod Pod, which suits all ages and patients, has benefits that this test lacks.

p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: Advantages | Disadvantages | Accuracy: the reason it is called the gold standard | Needs technical expertise: the person conducting the test must be qualified (in the Bod Pod the machine does most of the work) | | Expensive: the cost of a skilled operator plus the entire set-up | | Not available to the general public, and not available in India (the board says "not available in India") | Affordability and availability matter when choosing the best test out of the eight body composition tests. A test cannot be called "the best" if the client has to travel abroad (for example to Australia or New Zealand) to get it done.

t: 1.9 Class question: accuracy of the Siri equation
p: Part 1: Hydrostatic (Underwater) Weighing
x: Q: Body fat percentage is found with the Siri equation. How accurate is the Siri equation itself? A: The equation is not where accuracy is judged. What matters is how accurately the body density that goes into the equation is measured, and the gold standard method measures body density very accurately. The Siri equation is well proven and well tested, and the gold standard method itself uses it, so there is a lot of research showing that it gives the closest, most ideal figures for body fat percentage. Some small error is always present, because no method is 100 percent accurate. But what is fed into the equation decides whether the answer is accurate. The Siri equation does not need to be memorised for this course. It is good to know that it exists and what it does.

t: 2.1 The full form and its spelling
p: Part 2: DEXA Scan (Test 2.3.4)
x: DEXA = Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry. Dual means two. Energy: two energies of radiation are used, a low energy beam and a high energy beam. Hence "dual energy". X-ray: the radiations. Absorptiometry: measuring the ability of the body's tissues to absorb the radiation. Note the spelling: the word is absorptiometry, not "absorption". The final "n" of "absorption" is missing. This is not a spelling mistake, and it is a detail that tests can use as a trap in answer options.

p: Part 2: DEXA Scan (Test 2.3.4)
x: The tissues of the body are drawn as three blocks with different densities (the block that looks the most dense takes the least volume; the least dense takes the most volume): Block | Density category | Example tissue | First (smallest volume) | High density | Bone | Second | Moderate density | Muscle | Third (largest volume) | Low density | Fat | Principle: the higher the density of a tissue, the more radiation it absorbs. The lower the density, the poorer the absorption. Two beams (one high energy, one low energy, drawn in two marker colours on the board) are sent into the body. Bone (high density): absorption is very good. Only a little radiation passes through, because most is absorbed. Fat (low density): absorption is poor. Most radiation passes through and very little is absorbed. Muscle (moderate density): absorption is slightly less than bone and slightly more than fat. Some radiation is absorbed and some passes through. DEXA principle The machine analyses how much of the radiation was absorbed and how much passed through, and from that works out how many tissues of each kind there are. This is also how the colouring is done. A DEXA report shows an image of the body with colour coding (three colours for bone, muscle and fat), in the same way that a weather alert highlights a region on a country's map in a different colour. It then gives proper numerical data.

t: 2.3 What DEXA reports: three categories instead of two
p: Part 2: DEXA Scan (Test 2.3.4)
x: Body weight, as studied in the body composition lecture, can be split into two divisions: Lean body mass: muscle (M), organs (O), bone (B), fluid (F) and essential fat (EF). Body fat: subcutaneous fat (SF) and visceral fat (VF). The Bod Pod and the water displacement method also gave only two categories: fat mass and fat-free mass. DEXA goes one level further and gives an in-depth analysis in three categories: DEXA category | Contains | Fat-free mass | Muscle, organs and fluid | Fat mass (purely fat) | Subcutaneous fat, visceral fat and essential fat (the fat in myelin sheaths around motor neurons, hormones and so on) | Bone and mineral mass | Bone, which now has a category of its own | Body composition models: two categories and DEXA's three Student question: Is fat-free mass the same as lean body mass? Answer: Not exactly. In the two-category view, lean body mass includes bone and essential fat. In DEXA, bone is separated into its own category and essential fat is counted in the fat mass, so "fat-free mass" in a DEXA report is a narrower group (muscle, organs, fluid). Why this matters. The radiations tell about all types of tissue, not just fat and muscle. For this reason DEXA was originally used only in orthopaedics: orthopaedic doctors gave it to patients to check bone density. As often happens in medicine, something invented for one purpose later serves several purposes. DEXA was meant for bone density but is now commonly used for overall body composition analysis, because it separates fat, fat-free mass and bone mineral so neatly. The slides state it briefly: DEXA measures bone mineral mass, fat mass and lean mass.

p: Part 2: DEXA Scan (Test 2.3.4)
x: The board list (with a point added at the end) is: Advantages | Disadvantages | Low risk of radiation: people worry that radiation might be cancerous or cause problems in the long run, but both the low energy and the high energy radiations used are of low risk | Might be expensive for some (subjective, depends on the person and on where the test is done) | No special preparation or prerequisite: no fasting as in BIA, no special clothing as in the Bod Pod (one can lie down on the machine even in a loose Indian outfit) | | Good accuracy (compared to the gold standard), like the Bod Pod | | Time saving (short test) | | No technical expertise needed: lab technicians conduct it easily | | Suitable for all cases listed for the Bod Pod (all ages, patients and so on) | | Available in India: it is commonly available (the board shows "Available in India") | | In-depth, well segregated analysis (the three categories above) | | About the cost. The disadvantage depends on the person and the place. It does not mean the cost of the machine (gyms do not keep this machine; laboratories and health centres do, not fitness centres). It means the cost of one test to the user, like paying a laboratory for an MRI or an X-ray. Place | Approximate cost per test | Public facility (for example a government hospital) | About 3,000 to 4,000 | Premium private hospital | About 12,000 to 15,000 | The currency was not stated in the recording (taken as rupees). It is described as "might be expensive for some" because it varies with where the test is done. How to talk to a client about the cost. The cost can be explained as an investment, not an overhead expense: the client gets a detailed, accurate and in-depth analysis of their body composition. It is not a recurring monthly cost, because a fitness test is not done every other month. It can be repeated after about six months.

t: 2.5 Class question: entry-level BIA machines and the gym
p: Part 2: DEXA Scan (Test 2.3.4)
x: Student question: What about the entry-level BIA machines that gyms have? Answer (the practical plan): Get a DEXA done, then compare it with the BIA reading in the gym. If the BIA reading for fat-free mass or fat mass differs from the DEXA by about plus or minus 5 percent, the client at least knows how far off the gym machine is and can keep that margin in mind when using it between tests. After about six months, when a proper and accurate analysis is needed again, get another DEXA.

t: 2.6 Class question: do the machines separate subcutaneous and visceral fat?
p: Part 2: DEXA Scan (Test 2.3.4)
x: Student question: These testers give a fat percentage, but do they differentiate subcutaneous and visceral fat? Answer (as far as it could be followed in the recording): In general the testers give a combined fat figure. Entry-level BIA machines give a combined figure: visceral fat is still taken into account inside that number, but it is not shown separately. High-end BIA machines (the class discussion mentioned a very expensive model) can show the subcutaneous versus visceral figures separately. This passage was unclear in the recording and is listed under Points to Confirm.

t: 2.7 The final choice among the eight body composition tests
p: Part 2: DEXA Scan (Test 2.3.4)
x: The eight tests are: waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), BMI, skinfold, BIA, Bod Pod, hydrostatic weighing and DEXA. The choice is made step by step, first on the basic factor of validity. Validity. A body composition test is valid only if it gives the body fat percentage. A test that only talks about health risk or weight category does not meet this. Step | Group | Verdict | 1 | Anthropometry (2.1): waist circumference (health risk from central obesity), WHR (overall health risk), BMI (underweight, normal, overweight, obese) | Not valid: none gives a body fat percentage. Reliability, accuracy and expertise do not even need to be discussed | 2 | Skinfold (2.2) | Gives a percentage, so valid, but not reliable: it covers only subcutaneous fat and does not factor in visceral fat | 3 | Machines (2.3): four options left | Hydrostatic weighing and Bod Pod are not available in India. Their good accuracy is of no practical use, so they are out of the picture | 4 | BIA versus DEXA | DEXA has the edge: in-depth analysis, its accuracy is still compared with the gold standard, while BIA's accuracy was never compared directly with the gold standard. All its other benefits apply too | Choosing among the eight body composition tests Conclusion: DEXA is the most recommended body composition test, considering all factors. This was described as the longest component of fitness testing; each remaining component has only two or at most three tests.

Test type 3 in the order of testing. It is also called the cardiorespiratory endurance tests. There are two types: VO2 max test Heart rate recovery test Overview of the cardiorespiratory fitness tests The slides define them as follows: Test | Definition on the slides | VO2 max | Measures an individual's aerobic capacity: the maximal oxygen uptake or consumption during incremental exercise or physical activity | Heart rate recovery | The ability of the heart to return towards normal heart rate after an activity within a specific amount of time |

p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: Recall from the cardio lecture. The VO2 max graph was discussed there, with the promise that how VO2 max is measured would be covered in this lecture. When someone does an incremental activity (a brisk walk, then a jog, then a run, then a sprint), heart rate rises as the intensity rises, and VO2 (the volume of oxygen consumed to produce energy) rises as well. At the level beyond which the heart rate cannot go up any more, near the maximum heart rate (MHR), the volume of oxygen consumed is the maximum aerobic capacity, the VO2 max. The board shows this as a small graph with HR on one axis and VO2 on the other, with points for brisk walk, jog, run and sprint, and the sprint point circled as VO2 max near the MHR line. HR and VO2 during incremental activity (schematic) Better VO2 max, better cardio. A higher VO2 max means higher cardiorespiratory fitness.

p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: The VO2 max test has two sub-categories. Category | For whom | Why | Maximal | Athletes | The person is taken all the way to their peak, above 85 percent (the sprinting zone, as in HIT) | Sub-maximal | General lifestyle clients | Not every client can or should be taken to maximum effort. Most clients are non-athletes (business people, homemakers, students, corporate employees), and they also deserve to know their VO2 max |

p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: In a laboratory, the athlete does an incremental activity (a treadmill with the incline increased every minute, aiming to reach the maximum in about ten minutes) while connected by tubes to a system that measures breathing. The system monitors in real time, per second, the volume of oxygen consumed (and CO2 produced). It displays the VO2 max at the end. The demonstration video (a sports medicine institute) explained that the test finds the body's maximal oxygen consumption and muscle efficiency, the heart rate max, and an estimated lactate threshold, so that heart rate training zones can be set. It is best used as a change-over-time measure to see how a training plan is going. The screen output shows a split graph: one panel for HR rising over time and one for VO2 (in ml per kg) rising over time, with tables of per-second and per-minute data changing continuously. That is how the machine arrives at the final number. The graph drawn on the board earlier combined both on one set of axes.

t: Sub-maximal test: Rockport 1 mile walking fitness test
p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: For the sub-maximal category, an organisation in Rockport (United States) created a method. Both the name of the organisation and the task are hidden in the test name: Rockport one mile walking fitness test. Task: walk 1 mile (1.6 km) as fast as possible, non-stop. A distance of 1.6 km can be marked by setting a vehicle's trip meter to zero at the start and noting the end point at 1.6 km. The start and end points are noted and the client walks that distance. The condition: walk as fast as possible. Even though this is a sub-maximal test, it still estimates VO2 max, so the client must be taken to their level best. The walk must not be like a relaxed post-dinner walk. The norms chart. Many tests use a test norms chart. The score or calculation from the test is looked up in a table for that gender and that age, and the table shows the fitness level (good, bad, average, excellent and so on). In this test, the result to look up is the VO2 max value calculated from a formula. The formula needs four things (one formula for males, one for females): Time taken to complete the mile (in minutes). The trainer notes it. Pulse, noted immediately at the end of the mile (not after the client relaxes or has lemon juice). Immediately after the activity the pulse is at its peak, and this test is about VO2 max. Age. Weight in pounds (lbs), not kilograms. Multiply the kg weight by 2.2 to get pounds. Example: 60 kg = 60 x 2.2 = 132 lbs. Q (to the class): Should the pulse be counted for a full 60 seconds, or counted for 10 seconds and multiplied by 6? A: Count for 10 seconds and multiply by 6 (an aggregate of 60 seconds). The formula asks for the pulse over one minute. If the pulse were counted for a full minute, the heart rate would come back down and recover during that minute, so the figure would not be the peak figure that this test needs. The first 10 seconds are when the heart rate is at its highest. The 10-second count is therefore multiplied by 6. Student question: But VO2 max is always a 1-minute volume of oxygen. Why is an aggregate acceptable? Answer: In the maximal test the machine measures the oxygen consumption live, throughout the activity, on a real-time basis, which is why it can give a per-minute figure. In the sub-maximal test the activity is finished first and the pulse is noted afterwards, so there is no live measurement. The 10-second count multiplied by 6 stands in for the one-minute figure.

p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: Weight is in pounds, time in minutes, pulse in beats per minute (10-second count x 6). | Formula | Women | VO2 max = 132.85 - (0.388 x age) - (0.077 x weight in lbs) - (3.265 x time) - (0.156 x pulse) | Men | VO2 max = 139.168 - (0.388 x age) - (0.077 x weight in lbs) - (3.265 x time) - (0.156 x pulse) | The formulas do not need to be memorised. Many online calculators ("Rockport walking fitness test calculator") ask for the same four inputs: age, weight, time taken and pulse, and use these formulas. In both formulas all the variables are multiplied by exactly the same numbers (0.388 for age, 0.077 for weight, 3.265 for time, 0.156 for pulse). Only the first number differs: 132.85 for women and 139.168 for men. The result is in ml of oxygen consumed per kg of body weight per minute.

t: 3.2 The heart rate recovery test: YMCA sub-maximal 3 minute step test
p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: Heart rate recovery (HRR): the client does an activity, the heart rate goes up, and the test checks how well and how soon it recovers. Q (to the class): Whose cardiorespiratory fitness is better: the person whose heart takes more time to recover, or less time? A: Less time. A faster heart rate recovery means a healthy and fit heart (as stated on the slide). The post-activity heart rate is looked up in a table for the client's gender and age. The test name again contains the body and the task: YMCA (the Young Men's Christian Association, a well-known international body that also does fitness testing) and 3 minute step test. For 3 minutes, non-stop, the client steps up and steps down on a step board. This is not the "step-up" exercise from the legs lecture: this is stepping up and down. Step test and curl-up metronome beats

p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: Fitness tests worldwide are standardised: every basic procedure, guideline and step is done in exactly the same way, under the same conditions. Only then are results comparable and only then can a result be looked up in the chart. A modified test, for example one changed because something was not available ("it works if you do this much modification"), gives a number that is not worth looking up, because the table assumes everyone worldwide followed the instructions word by word. The YMCA presets these conditions: Condition | Why it is fixed | Setting | Step board height | If one client gets a higher board and another a lower board, the task differs and the results are not comparable | 12 inches (1 foot). Custom-made boards of this height are kept for the test | Speed | If one client steps fast and another slowly, again not comparable | 96 beats per minute, set with a metronome | The metronome. A metronome (beat counter) is a small device, used by drummers of music bands, that ticks at a set number of beats per minute. At 30 beats per minute the pace would be slow, at 200 both clients would fall down; after much testing the most suitable speed was set at 96. How the beat is used. One step is up, up, down, down. A single tick is used for a single move: tick 1 up, tick 2 up, tick 3 down, tick 4 down. No beat may be missed. The client does not count the beats and just follows the beat.

p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: Set the step board (12 inches) and the metronome (96 bpm). The client steps up, up, down, down to the beat for 3 minutes non-stop. When the 3 minutes are over, the client sits down immediately (for example on the same board). Count the pulse for one complete minute. This 1-minute count is the recovery heart rate. Look up the post-exercise heart rate in the chart for the client's gender and age. The trainer's role. The trainer gives commands and cues in rhythm ("up, up, down, down") and motivates the client, because 3 minutes sounds short but feels long. Examples: "good going", "follow the beats", correcting the foot placement (the whole foot on the board), and time cues such as "only 30 seconds remaining" and a countdown from 10. After the 3 minutes the trainer notes the pulse while watching the clock for a full minute. This takes a lot of presence of mind and alertness. Why one full minute here, and not 10 seconds x 6? The purpose of this test is recovery. The heart needs time to recover, so the pulse is counted for one complete minute. Student question: How is the heart rate "after 1 minute" calculated? Answer: The pulse is counted over the whole minute (60 seconds) immediately after the exercise. The number of beats counted in those 60 seconds, at the end of the 60th second, is the result that is looked up. Summary of the difference between the two pulse methods: Test | Pulse method | Reason | Rockport walk | 10 seconds x 6, immediately at the end | Needs the peak heart rate (VO2 max) | YMCA step test | One complete minute, starting at the end of the test | Needs the heart to recover |

p: Part 3: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Tests
x: Post-exercise heart rate 85 bpm. Female, 26-35 years column. In the women's chart anything less than 88 is Excellent, so her heart recovered well within 1 minute: Excellent. In this test the charts are separate for men and women (not combined). The slides add: a fast heart rate recovery means a healthy and fit heart.

x: Test type 4. Muscular strength is the ability of the working skeletal muscles to contract and generate force in one maximum effort. The weight used must therefore be the weight with which the person can do only one repetition, the 1 RM. Two tests are conducted: one for upper body strength and one for lower body strength. The test measures relative strength, not absolute strength.

p: Part 4: Muscular Strength Tests
x: Q: What is the difference between relative and absolute strength? A: Absolute strength is just the total weight somebody has lifted. Relative strength is the weight lifted in relation to the person's own body weight, as a ratio: Relative strength = weight lifted / body weight It is also called the strength ratio, because it is a ratio of the weight lifted and the body weight of that person. The same logic is used for the upper body test and the lower body test; only the exercise differs. Strength tests Body region | Test (1 RM) | Upper body | Bench press | Lower body | Leg press | The strength ratio comes out as a decimal. Using the ratio, the client's gender and age, the chart shows the category (good, bad, average, excellent and so on). The charts are percentile based, and there is a separate table for the leg press.

t: 4.2 Why leg press and not squat
p: Part 4: Muscular Strength Tests
x: Q: Why is the leg press used for the lower body and not the squat? A: The squat is unsupported and also engages the core. Imagine two people tested with a squat, one with a strong core and one with a weak core. The person with a weak core may have good leg strength but cannot show it because the weak core compromises the squat. The leg press is supported by default (just as the bench press is supported for the upper body), so everyone gets a fair, supported version in which they do not depend on the core. Whatever the total weight lifted in one single repetition maximum with correct form, technique and full range of motion, divided by body weight, gives the ratio.

p: Part 4: Muscular Strength Tests
x: The slide uses a shortcut: it states the strength ratio directly. To understand it, suppose (hypothetically) that the weight lifted is 124 kg and the person's body weight is 100 kg. Then 124 / 100 = 1.24. Only the gender, age and strength ratio are needed to use the chart. t: 4.4 Beginners are not tested for strength at the first test
p: Part 4: Muscular Strength Tests
x: Q (to the class): Will this test be conducted for beginners? A: No. For beginners no neural pathways have been formed yet, no form and technique are in place, and there is no kinetic chain, no Valsalva manoeuvre and no proprioception: everything is still in the learning phase. What to do with a beginner: In the first test, skip this test. All the other components are done. In the retest (test number two), when everything is in place, that test is treated as the first time muscular strength is tested. From the third test, progress in muscular strength can be tracked. (The recording says "muscular endurance" at the start of this question, but the explanation and the retest rule are about muscular strength. See Points to Confirm.)

Test type 5. Two tests: Push-up test (upper body endurance). Curl-up test (endurance of the abdominal region). Muscular endurance is the ability of the working skeletal muscles to contract maximally (as stated in the recording, "to contract some maximum") for a long period of time without getting fatigued.

t: 5.1 What is common to both tests
p: Part 5: Muscular Endurance Tests
x: Q (to the class): For an endurance test, do you give a number of repetitions (such as 10 push-ups) or tell the client to do as many as possible until failure? A: Until failure. Endurance is tested by counting how many repetitions the client can do, so no target number is given. The client is told the correct form and technique and the complete range of motion, and the final count for that gender and age is checked in the chart. Both tests are conducted till failure. Muscular endurance board

p: Part 5: Muscular Endurance Tests
x: The form and the range of motion that count as full are demonstrated in a video. The client must be told before the test that repetitions without full range of motion will not be counted. Full range of motion (as per the test makers): In the eccentric phase, at the bottom, the chin touches the floor. On the way up, the arms are fully extended. No half repetitions are counted. Even when the test is done on the knees, the range of motion must be fully met (chin to the floor). Males and females do the test differently: | Position | Males | On the toes (palms and toes) | Females | On the knees (palms and knees) | This is not gender bias: the reference values in the chart were built keeping in mind the genetic differences between the genders. A female who can do it the male way is at the top tier, but for the test the standard way must be followed. The comparison must be like with like ("apples with apples"), otherwise the count cannot be validated against the table. The standard variation must be followed even though a client could do more repetitions the other way. Case studies (slides): a 30-year-old male doing 30 push-ups is Excellent (30 or more is excellent for ages 30-39). A 30-year-old female doing 27 push-ups is Excellent (27 or more). The charts take the gender difference into account, so the female number is lower for the same category. p: Part 5: Muscular Endurance Tests
x: The curl-up is a forward crunch: spine flexion, the function of the rectus abdominis. In the crunch exercise from the earlier lecture the hands were interlocked behind the head with the elbows facing the ceiling. In the test the hands are not behind the head. The body is in a supine position and the palms are flat on the mat (palms facing the mat). Why the palms are on the mat. In spine flexion the palms travel to and fro on the mat (they move forward in the concentric phase and back in the eccentric phase). The distance the palm travels sets the range of motion for everyone, so the results can be compared. Otherwise one client might go much deeper into spine flexion than another.

t: Setting the range of motion: the tape
p: Part 5: Muscular Endurance Tests
x: Two pieces of tape are placed on the mat. Tape A marks the starting position, and a second tape marks how far the fingertips must travel. The fingertip of the hand must go and touch the far tape and come back to tape A. Therefore the range of motion is automatically the same for everyone. The distance between the tapes depends on age, not on gender: Client's age | Distance between the tapes | Younger than 45 | 12 cm | Older than 45 | 8 cm | Younger clients get the longer distance. The distance is measured from the inside edge of one tape to the inside edge of the other. The tape itself is 2 cm wide. For example, for a client over 45 (say 57 years) the inside edge of the second tape is at 8 cm (the tape itself covers 8 to 10 cm), and the distance between the tapes is still 8 cm. For a younger client, a third tape is placed 4 cm further (4 more cm, making 12). Curl-up tape set up (The board marks the tapes A, B and C, with A to B = 8 cm and a further 4 cm from B to C.) No cheating. Some people lift the palm off the mat just to make the fingertip reach the tape. That repetition does not count. The whole hand must stay grounded while going forward and coming back.

t: Setting the speed: the metronome again
p: Part 5: Muscular Endurance Tests
x: Within the same age bracket, speed has to be the same too (someone moving fast and someone slowly would not be comparable). The speed is set with a metronome at 40 beats per minute. The 96 beats of the step test would be too fast for this. How the beat is used (different from the step test). In the step test one beat is one move. Here a single beat is used for the concentric phase and a single beat for the eccentric phase, so two beats complete one repetition: tick 1 from tape A to tape B (or C), tick 2 back to tape A.

Test type 6, the last. There are three categories (just as body composition had three categories): Use of a goniometer. Visual assessment. Sit and reach tests. Flexibility tests overview

p: Part 6: Flexibility Tests
x: A goniometer measures the range of motion at the joints (the angle at the joint). It looks like the protractor from a school geometry kit, which measured the angle between two lines. It has a stationary (fixed) arm, a moving arm, and a central point around which the moving arm moves; as it moves, the angle number changes. Why trainers do not use it. It needs technical expertise. Only a physiotherapist or an orthopaedic doctor can use it correctly. The central point must be placed exactly over the joint, and the fixed and moving arms must be placed correctly along the bones. In the slide photo of the knee, the fixed arm is on the femur and the moving arm is on the fibula, because it is placed on the lateral side. Without the skill to find the exact positions in the body, the angle reading is not accurate. So trainers rely on visual assessment. (The class asked whether mobility is also measured; the goniometer is the tool that checks range of motion at joints.)

p: Part 6: Flexibility Tests
x: No device is used. The flexibility of four regions is assessed visually: Quadriceps Hamstrings Hip flexors (the iliacus and the psoas, together the iliopsoas) Shoulder For the first three regions there is a passing criterion and the client is simply pass or fail (not good, average or below). The shoulder is graded good, average or poor. Each side (right and left) is checked separately. Definition used: flexibility is the ability of the muscles to lengthen passively, meaning with the help of external support or force. The trainer is the external force, so the trainer helps the client in these tests. If the client still has a lot of discomfort or a huge gap despite the help, the client fails. A client who passes on the right side cannot be assumed to pass on the left, so both sides must be tested. The common logic. In each test the movement is the opposite of the muscle's own action, because flexibility is lengthening: quadriceps do knee extension, so the test is knee flexion; hip flexors do hip flexion, so the test is hip extension; hamstrings are tested with hip flexion with a locked knee. Region | Position | Test | Pass criterion | Quadriceps | Lying prone on the mat (not standing) | The trainer assists the heel toward the buttock (knee flexion), each side | Heel touches the buttock, right heel to right buttock and left heel to left buttock. A huge gap despite help is a fail | Hamstrings | Lying supine (facing up), one leg at a time, the other leg stays on the floor | Hip flexion with a locked knee, like a leg raise. The trainer helps lift the leg | The leg goes above 70 degrees (if 90 degrees is vertical). The angle can differ between legs (for example 70 on one and 90 or 80 on the other: both pass). If one leg is 80 degrees and the other stays at 60 degrees despite help, the client shows a stiffer hamstring on that leg, needs stretching and fails the test for that leg. There is no upper limit: going beyond 80 degrees is simply better | Hip flexors | Lying on a board or table of decent height (like the 3 ft step board), hips at the edge, one knee hugged, the other leg suspended over the edge | Check the suspended leg | The knee of the hanging leg goes below the hip level (at hip level or below). If the knee stays higher above the hip, the hip flexor is stiff or tight | Shoulder | Standing or sitting | One hand goes up and behind the head, the other hand comes from behind and under the opposite shoulder; try to touch fingers | Good: fingertips touch (or hands can clasp). Average: a small gap. Poor: the distance is too great. Check both sides by changing hands, because they can differ | Student question: In the hip flexor test, which leg is being tested, the leg being hugged or the suspended leg? Answer: the suspended leg. The hugged leg already has the hip in flexion (hip flexors contracted). The test needs to see how much the muscle can lengthen, so the suspended leg is tested: the more it goes toward hip extension (or hyperextension), the better the flexibility. The slides show the criteria with photos, and give the hamstring angle as 70-80 degrees. The board and lecture use above 70 degrees, and the lecture explains why no upper limit is needed (a larger angle is only better). The board also shows a small leg diagram marked "above 70".

p: Part 6: Flexibility Tests
x: As the name says, the client sits in a particular posture and reaches forward; the muscles lengthen, and the farther the reach, the better the flexibility. The test measures hamstring and lumbar flexibility (the posterior chain: everything in the posterior chain, including hamstrings and lumbar region, is stretched and lengthened). There are two methods.

p: Part 6: Flexibility Tests
x: A special custom-made box is used (available in some gyms, not in others). Place the soles of the feet against the inside wall of the box. Sit with the knees locked (extended, no bending). Bend forward with the hands one above the other and push the marker on the top surface as far forward as possible. The marker is on a scale with numbers (inches). The reading is the distance reached. Look up the distance in the table for that age and gender (very similar to the other charts: good, poor, average, excellent and so on).

t: Method 2: YMCA sit and reach test (no box)
p: Part 6: Flexibility Tests
x: The YMCA gives a way for gyms without the box. All that is needed is a mat, brown tape and a measuring tape. The client sits like in the box test, knees straight, without bending the knees. A brown tape, 1 foot in length, is placed heel to heel, which fixes the heel-to-heel distance. A measuring tape is laid out so that it starts somewhere between the knees, placed so that the tape reads 15 inches where it crosses the brown tape. This 15 in point is the zero point. The client brings the arms forward, one hand on the other, and reaches as far as possible. YMCA sit and reach layout Why the zero point is set at 15 inches. It is assumed that a person by default should be able to reach at least 15 inches, so the real test of flexibility is how far the client goes beyond 15. A second reason: a client with poor flexibility who reaches only about 7 inches can still be given a number (7 inches), because the measuring tape starts between the knees. If the tape had started at the brown tape, there would be no number to give. With a number, the trainer can set a mid-term goal (for example, to at least reach the brown tape next time) and focus on stretching. Case study. A male client aged 35 reaches 2 inches beyond: 15 + 2 = 17 inches. In the table, for a 35-year-old male (26-35 years column), 17 shows Good flexibility. YMCA sit and reach performance table (inches) Each category lists the higher value first and then the lower one (the pair of percentile values shown in the E-book table: for example Excellent covers the 90th and 80th percentile). Well below average has a single value (the 10th percentile). p: Part 7: Summary and Closing Questions
x: Step | Test | Key points | 1 | Health screening and blood pressure (Fitness Testing 1) | Seven-step blood pressure procedure; systolic (upper) and diastolic (lower) value; chart from normal, elevated, hypertension stage 1 and 2 to hypertensive crisis | 2 | Body composition (three categories) | Anthropometry (waist circumference, WHR, BMI), skinfold, machines (BIA, Bod Pod, hydrostatic weighing, DEXA). BMI does not distinguish body fat from lean body mass: two people of the same height and weight fall in the same category. Skinfold measures only subcutaneous fat. BIA works because water is a good conductor of electricity, and hydration affects the result. Bod Pod works on air displacement. Hydrostatic weighing is the gold standard and works on Archimedes' principle. DEXA is the most recommended | 3 | Cardiorespiratory fitness | VO2 max (maximal, with the lab set-up; sub-maximal, the Rockport 1 mile walk) and heart rate recovery (YMCA 3 minute step test) | 4 | Muscular strength | Bench press (upper) and leg press (lower), 1 RM, relative strength | 5 | Muscular endurance | Push-up test and curl-up test, both till failure | 6 | Flexibility | Goniometer, visual assessment, sit and reach |
