t: Part 1: The goal and the master table
x: Using everything from the earlier lectures, the aim is to learn how to analyse or design a workout split. The board was divided in two. The left side holds the master table. The right side is for the research studies, which supply the factors to consider while selecting or prescribing a workout split. This mirrors the cardio lecture, which had "factors to consider while prescribing cardio intensity". The discussion is about weight training. A day with no weight training (a non-WT day) is free room that can be used for cardio. It is not a rest day. Exactly one day a week, Sunday, is the mandatory rest day. The master table has these columns, filled in this order: No. of sets (main sets per muscle) Recovery period Weekly outlook Training frequency Split types (which splits line up with each scenario) Training level (beginner, or intermediate and advanced) Ideal set range The last two columns are conclusions, so they are filled in at the end.

The three scenarios come straight from Scheduling 1. In the weekly outlook, a star marks a training day for that muscle. Main sets per muscle | Recovery period | Weekly outlook (Mon to Sun) | Training frequency | 1 to 3 | 48 hours | Train Mon, gap Tue, train Wed, gap Thu, train Fri, gap Sat, rest Sun | Thrice a week | 4 to 5 | 72 hours | Train Mon, gap, gap, train Thu, gap, gap, rest Sun | Twice a week | More than 5 | 1 week | Train Mon, gap for the whole week, rest Sun, train again next Mon | Once a week | The repeated reminder: the number of sets is main sets per muscle, not the total for every exercise in the session. The same muscle can be trained by one exercise or by several (for example, two sets of lat pulldown, or one of lat pulldown and one of bent-over row). It is the muscle's total that counts.

t: Part 3: What is a workout split?
x: A workout split is how your weight training sessions (your exercises) are arranged across the week, following some logic. Different splits follow different logic. Full body workout (FBW). Every session trains the whole body. Upper/lower split. Upper days train only upper body muscles (back, chest, shoulders, arms). Lower days train only lower body muscles. (Training anterior thigh muscles on one leg day and posterior on another is a variation, but upper body muscles are not trained on a lower day.) Push, pull, legs (PPL). Muscles are grouped by movement pattern. A pull day contains the pulling movements: rows, lat pulldowns, and also biceps curls (which is why back and biceps are trained together). A push day contains the pushing movements: bench press (chest), vertical push (anterior deltoid), and triceps (which is why chest, shoulders and triceps are trained together). The remaining day is legs. Bro split (body part split). One body part per day, for example back on Monday, chest on Tuesday, then a gap, then legs, shoulders, arms, and a cardio day. Shoulders and arms are kept away from back and chest days so the same joint is not used on back-to-back days.

t: How each split lines up with the table
p: Part 3: What is a workout split?
x: Scenario | Split that fits | Weekly outlook | Why it fits | 1 to 3 sets, 48 h, thrice a week | Full body | Mon F, Tue non-WT, Wed F, Thu non-WT, Fri F, Sat non-WT, Sun R | Each muscle is trained every other day | 4 to 5 sets, 72 h, twice a week | Upper/lower | Mon U, Tue L, Wed non-WT, Thu U, Fri L, Sat non-WT (cardio), Sun R | Upper trained Mon and Thu, lower trained Tue and Fri, each with 72 hours between | More than 5 sets, 1 week, once a week | PPL and bro split | PPL: Mon P, Tue gap, Wed P(ull), Thu gap, Fri L, Sat cardio, Sun R. Bro: Mon back, Tue chest, gap, legs, shoulders, arms, a dedicated cardiorespiratory endurance day, R | Each muscle gets one session a week |

t: Frequency is per muscle, not per WT day
p: Part 3: What is a workout split?
x: In the upper/lower split there are four WT days, but ask how often the legs are trained: twice. Someone might answer "four" by counting WT days, which is exactly why the frequency pillar was taught first. The frequency of a muscle is still two. Upper muscles are trained on Monday and Thursday and lower muscles on Tuesday and Friday, and each gets its 72 hours. In PPL, the latissimus dorsi is trained once (on pull day). In the bro split, the latissimus dorsi (on back day) and the pectoralis major (on chest day) are each trained once, and the shoulders once. Because the frequency is the same, everything learned from the studies applies the same way to both PPL and the bro split.

t: A question about PPL done twice
p: Part 3: What is a workout split?
x: Q: "We do PPL, then PPL again, six WT days. Is that not the usual way?" A: In that version you do six WT sessions. You may be overtraining, and the overall hypertrophy stimulus may not be high enough to justify the risk of six days. A similar weekly stimulus can come from training three times a week with adequate recovery in between. The studies below explain why. The numbers in the set-range column are not just "what scientists say". There is a logic behind them: why more than five sets once a week, and why fewer sets are enough when the muscle is trained thrice a week. That logic is the main content of this lecture.

p: Part 3: What is a workout split?
x: The goal is not to criticise or demonise any split. The aim is to break the mindset that "full body is only for beginners, so why are you doing full body if you are advanced?" The point to prove: any training level (intermediate or advanced too) can pick a split from any of the three scenarios, as long as they do the ideal number of sets: not under, not over.

t: Part 4: Training level and the F and I relationship
x: For beginners the options are limited, because there is a logical best choice. Two pillars of the FITT principle are linked: F is proportional to 1/I (frequency is inversely proportional to intensity). When intensity goes up, frequency goes down; when intensity goes down, frequency can go up. Reasoning: Beginners use low intensity. From the intensity lecture, beginners train at 15 to 20 RM (light weight, high reps, learning sets). Because intensity is low, the muscles do not reach major fatigue. High frequency is therefore not a problem for them. (If intensity were high, high frequency would pile on fatigue.) Why frequency should be high for beginners: beginners have a lot to learn.Neural pathways. The gap between two motor neurons is a synapse. A new movement has a weak pathway. It becomes stronger the more often it is repeated. The lecture compared this with a person crossing a gap between two mountains on a bridge: the first crossing is the hardest, and each later crossing is more confident. The kinetic chain, for example the arch of the body in the bench press while pressing into the floor. Proprioception, with proprioceptors working efficiently for each exercise. Grip and tightness. The Valsalva manoeuvre and breathing: when to inhale and exhale in each movement. If a muscle (say the chest) is trained only once a week, bench press is practised only once a week. Neural pathways, the kinetic chain and technique take much longer to form. With full body training, three days a week (Monday, Wednesday, Friday), a beginner practises each movement often with light weights and low intensity. The usual 2 to 3 months beginner phase is then used productively. With low frequency they would take months and months to finish the learning phase. So the best choice for beginners is full body. Because beginners were taught this way, the industry created a stereotype that full body is only for beginners. The data in the next parts show that intermediate and advanced trainees can also make the most of full body, if the set range is followed.

t: Part 5: Factor 1, stimulus per set (the law of diminishing returns)
x: Each study gives a takeaway, and the lecture names each takeaway so it can serve as a "factor". The first factor is stimulus per set (SPS). Question: if you do one set for a muscle, how much growth stimulus does that muscle get? This applies to every muscle (lats, pectoralis major, biceps, triceps, shoulders and so on). The stimulus here is the hypertrophy stimulus: "stimulus" comes from stimulation, meaning a change. The researchers measured it in arbitrary units (AU), not kg or grams. To make it easier to relate to, the lecture replaced the unit with a currency: 1 AU is shown as one rupee. (The board uses the rupee sign. The idea is only an analogy.)

p: Part 5: Factor 1, stimulus per set (the law of diminishing returns)
x: Sets in a session | Net stimulus (total) | Stimulus per set (what this set added) | 1 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 2 | 1.39 | 0.39 | 3 | 1.61 | 0.22 | 4 | 1.77 | 0.16 | 5 | 1.90 | 0.13 | 6 | 2.00 | 0.10 | How to read it: One set gives 1.00. If two sets doubled it, you would expect 2.00, but two sets give only 1.39. Three sets give 1.61, not 3.00. It takes six sets to double what the first set alone gave. That is five more sets to earn one more unit. The "stimulus per set" column is the difference between consecutive totals. For set 2: 1.39 minus 1.00 = 0.39. For set 3: 1.61 minus 1.39 (not minus 1) = 0.22. A common mistake is to subtract from 1.00 every time. Total net stimulus keeps rising, but each set contributes less and less. This is the law of diminishing returns (an idea from economics). "The more the merrier" is not always true. Sets 2 to 6 added together contribute about 1.00, the same as the first set alone (0.39 + 0.22 + 0.16 + 0.13 + 0.10 = 1.00; 2.00 minus 1.00 = 1.00). The published data goes beyond six sets: 7 sets about 2.09, 8 sets 2.16, 9 sets 2.23. The contributions keep shrinking (the 7th set about 0.09, the 8th about 0.07).

p: Part 5: Factor 1, stimulus per set (the law of diminishing returns)
x: Put the number of sets on the x-axis and stimulus on the y-axis. Plotted points: 1 set at 1.00, 2 sets at 1.39, 3 at 1.61, 4 at 1.77, 5 at 1.90, 6 at 2.00. If doubling held, the line would shoot up steeply (2 sets at 2.00). Instead the curve rises quickly at first and then flattens. The curve will eventually take a U-turn. The more sets you do, the more muscle damage occurs, and damage is plotted as a second curve that stays near zero for the first few sets and then rises. When damage begins to matter, it pulls the net stimulus curve down. The two curves approach each other, giving an inverted U shape for net stimulus. Diminishing returns Notes on damage: Some muscles are more easily damaged and others less easily damaged. This varies by muscle and by person. In the published graph, a more easily damaged muscle (yellow net curve) gets about 1.77 at 4 sets, goes a little higher at 5 and 6 sets (1.9 to about 2.0), then turns back down to about 1.77 by 9 sets. The extra five sets add nothing, so the first four were enough for that muscle. A less easily damaged muscle (green net curve) rises to about 2.0 at 6 sets and returns to about 2.0 at 9 sets. The extra three sets are unnecessary, so stopping at six would have been enough. This is why the upper limits (max 3, max 5, max 10) in the set-range column exist. In the third scenario ("more than five sets") the set range was left blank because "more than five" can be 20 or 25 sets. Five is the minimum, and an upper cap is needed.

t: Part 6: Factor 2, stimulus retention per set
x: Question: once you earn a stimulus (1.00, 1.39, 1.61...), how long does the muscle keep it? The stimulus is not a fixed deposit that stays forever like money in a bank locker. If the muscle is not trained again in time, atrophy sets in and the stimulus falls to zero. This factor is called stimulus retention per set. Take the training day as day 1, then count the following days. The studies found: Sets | Net stimulus | Stimulus reaches zero on | 1 | 1.00 | Day 5 | 2 | 1.39 | Day 6 | 3 | 1.61 | Day 7 | 4 | 1.77 | Day 8 | 5 | 1.90 | Day 9 | 6 | 2.00 | Day 10 | Pattern: add 4 to the number of sets, and that is the day on which the stimulus reaches zero if the muscle is not trained again. One set lasts until about day 5, and each extra set buys about one more day. The 0.39 from the second set bought one more day, and so did the 0.22 from the third set. Stimulus retention These are not fixed numbers. Some studies say four days and others five for one set. The lecture picked the middle of the range. Q: Does this change with intensity (beginner, intermediate, advanced)? A: No. It applies to every level, whatever weight is lifted. Reps are already set around stimulating reps. A 4 to 6 RM weight differs from person to person, but the stimulus each person earns at their own level stays for the same number of days.

The sets from the master table can now be linked to the weekly outlook. Take the latissimus dorsi as the example muscle. Everything applies to every muscle. FBW (1 to 3 sets): the lats are trained on all three full body days, so frequency is three. Upper/lower (4 to 5 sets): the lats are trained on Monday and Thursday, then next Monday. PPL (more than 5 sets): the lats are trained once, on Monday, and again next Monday.

t: What goes wrong at low sets and low frequency
p: Part 7: Combining the two factors
x: Suppose someone on a once a week split (PPL) does only one or two sets per muscle. One set (1.00) reaches zero on day 5, and two sets (1.39) on day 6. By the next Monday (day 8), everything earned has gone to zero. The muscle starts from scratch every week, with nothing carried forward. Then there is no point in weight training: gaining and losing, and starting again. You do not have to carry all of the 1.77 (for example) into the next week, but you should carry something forward. That is how muscle size builds up.

t: Why a thrice a week lifter can do fewer sets
p: Part 7: Combining the two factors
x: Someone doing FBW with two sets per muscle: the 1.39 would take until day 6 to reach zero. But the muscle is trained again on Wednesday, and again on Friday, long before it reaches zero. They push it up again before it falls. So two sets per session is enough, as long as they train three times a week. That person cannot do two sets once a week.

t: Why a once a week lifter must do more sets
p: Part 7: Combining the two factors
x: Someone training once a week should do at least about six sets. Six sets (2.00) last until day 10, and the next session on day 8 happens before it reaches zero. In the lecture's example, about 0.4 of the stimulus was still left (an illustrative figure from the board). That balance is carried into the new session, on top of the new 2.00. Key takeaway: lower frequency means more sets per session; higher frequency can be managed with fewer sets per session. Do not follow the crowd that says "only two sets, how will you get hypertrophy?" Two sets are enough when the muscle gets three chances a week. Do not choose the higher number of sets at high frequency either: the person would only be getting tired.

p: Part 7: Combining the two factors
x: For the same total of six sets in a week, how much stimulus does each split earn? Add up each session's net stimulus: Split (frequency) | Sets per session | Calculation | Net weekly stimulus | FBW, three times a week | 2 | 1.39 + 1.39 + 1.39 | 4.17 | Upper/lower, twice a week | 3 | 1.61 + 1.61 | 3.22 | PPL / bro, once a week | 6 | 2.00 | 2.00 | Net weekly stimulus The weekly stimulus is highest when a muscle is trained three times a week. Full body workout is therefore not "underrated for no reason". Fewer sets per session is not a loss; at the end of the week the full body lifter has earned more than someone who trained the muscle once. This does not mean PPL or the bro split is bad. There is an advantage too. People who want to become professional bodybuilders and win competitions must focus on every individual muscle. They need a training day with room to add many specific exercises for each muscle. In a full body session of about 10 to 12 exercises, you do not have room for niche exercises such as reverse shrugs for the lower fibres of trapezius for every muscle. When a whole day is dedicated to back, or to the upper body, there is more room. PPL and bro splits can also be used by intermediate and advanced trainees. Many factors decide the choice, including goals and training level. The lecture ranks nothing; it only shows how the three categories (thrice, twice, once a week) should be understood.

t: Part 8: Factor 3, determinants of frequency (hypertrophy and atrophy)
x: After the break, the drop in stimulus was made more precise. There are two determinants of frequency: Hypertrophy is growth in the cell size of the muscle. Atrophy is reduction in the cell size of the muscle.

p: Part 8: Factor 3, determinants of frequency (hypertrophy and atrophy)
x: GAS stands for general adaptation syndrome: how the body adapts in general. MyoPS stands for myofibrillar protein synthesis. "Myo" refers to muscle, and here specifically to the myofibril, an element inside the muscle. Inside a myofibril are sarcomeres with the proteins myosin and actin (thick and thin filaments, also called myofilaments). Hypertrophy here is the building of these contractile proteins. After training a muscle (whether one set or six), hypertrophy (MyoPS elevation) continues for the first 48 hours. After 48 hours atrophy begins.

p: Part 8: Factor 3, determinants of frequency (hypertrophy and atrophy)
x: Imagine a big rubber (Swiss) ball shot upwards by a gun. It rises, curves (a parabola) and starts to come back down. The goal is not to let the ball (the hypertrophy curve) touch the ground. Before it falls to the ground, shoot it up again. The 48 hours says the ball keeps going up for 48 hours and then begins to fall. The question for any program: do you shoot it again at the last minute, a little earlier, or at the exact moment the fall starts?

t: Comparing three scenarios over two weeks
p: Part 8: Factor 3, determinants of frequency (hypertrophy and atrophy)
x: Three people are compared, each with six sets a week for the muscle: 6 sets once a week (PPL type), 3 + 3 sets twice a week (upper/lower type), and 2 sets three times a week (FBW type). Day 1 is a Monday training day. Hypertrophy and atrophy cycles How to read the figure: the coloured line is hypertrophy (it rises for 48 hours after every session) and the orange line is atrophy (it starts when the 48 hour window ends and continues until the next session). Each session starts from whatever balance the previous one left, which is the "bank balance". Each panel has its own vertical scale, so compare the shapes: how many days each person spends on the orange (atrophy) line in a week. That is 5 days for once a week, 3 days for twice a week, and only 1 day (the weekend) for three times a week. Once a week (6 sets, 2.00). The 2.00 is not in the pocket straight after the gym. It builds up over the first 48 hours, then the ball starts to fall. If he does nothing, it reaches zero on day 10 (6 + 4). He trains again on day 8 (next Monday). He avoided part of the atrophy, but still had to face a lot of it. The curve then goes higher than 2.00, because he is carrying a bank balance from the previous week. That is how muscle is built, and the logic behind designing a split. A limitation of the board: only two weeks fit. The following Monday would be day 15. Twice a week (3 + 3 sets, 1.61 each). Peak at 48 hours (Wednesday). Zero would be on day 7 (3 + 4) with no more training. He trains again on Thursday (day 4), so he avoids more atrophy and faces less than the once a week lifter. The new session starts from the carried balance and rises again for 48 hours (to Saturday), then drops over the weekend. The drop here is slightly larger because of the extra rest day. Overall the curve stays higher than the black (once a week) curve. Three times a week (2 sets, 1.39 each). 48 hours after Monday is Wednesday, which is the next training day. Atrophy was supposed to start, but he shoots the ball up again at exactly that moment. The 48 hour window after Wednesday ends on Friday, which is again a training day, and after Friday the window ends on Sunday. The "blessing in disguise" of full body: the day atrophy would begin is the day of the next session, so almost no atrophy occurs during the week. Only the weekend (rest day) brings some drop, and then a new cycle begins on Monday. This is why the full body lifter, even with only two sets, always stays near the top of the curve.

Putting the studies together, the ideal ranges per muscle per session, with an upper limit to avoid damage and fatigue, are: Frequency | Ideal main sets | Upper limit | Three times a week (FBW) | 1 to 2 | max 3 | Twice a week (U/L) | 2 to 3 | max 5 | Once a week (PPL, bro) | 6 to 8 | do not cross 10 | If frequency is high, the number of sets can stay at the lower end. The upper limits come from the muscle damage curve (Part 5).

t: Part 10: The published studies behind the factors
x: The lecture showed published graphs for each factor. They are redrawn here at high resolution from the numbers on the charts, so that every study has a clear figure next to its explanation. The original charts come from a members-only research review (Strength & Conditioning Research) and are copyrighted, so they are not copied into these notes. The chart titles and the study references printed on them are given below so you can find the original papers.

t: Recovery against number of sets (supports the master table)
p: Part 10: The published studies behind the factors
x: The chart shows, for each study, the day on which strength had fully returned to baseline after a workout of moderate loads (6 to 15 RM) taken to failure at least once, in strength-trained lifters. The relationship between sets and recovery time is approximately linear: more sets, more time. Study (as labelled on the chart) | Sets | Days to recover (approximate) | Farrow et al. 2020 | 2 | 1 | Moran-Navarro et al. 2017 | 3 | 3 | Haun et al. 2017 | 4 | 3 | Belcher et al. 2019 | 4 | 4 | Gonzalez-Hernandez et al. 2020 | 6 | 3 | Davies et al. 2018 | 6 | 4 | Ferreira et al. 2017 and Bartolomei et al. 2017 | 8 | 5 | Fernandes et al. 2019 | 10 | 4 | Recovery time against number of sets The chart's own conclusions are the three rows of the master table: "We can probably recover from 3 sets within 48 hours to do full body workouts." "We can probably recover from 4 to 5 sets within 72 hours to do upper/lower splits." "We can probably do 10 to 12 sets and recover within a week for body part splits."

t: Stimulus per set (the diminishing returns graph)
p: Part 10: The published studies behind the factors
x: Based on a meta-analysis of resistance training volume and muscle growth (Schoenfeld, Ogborn and Krieger, 2017). The original meta-analysis found that to double the hypertrophy of one set per workout you need about six sets. The diminishing returns graph in Part 5 is the redrawn version of this chart (see the figure there). The graph expresses the first set as 1.0 AU and adds each later set with diminishing returns: 1.00, 1.39, 1.61, 1.77, 1.90, 2.00, 2.09, 2.16, 2.23 (at 9 sets). The inverted U shapes may be caused by muscle damage, which is deducted for more easily damaged and less easily damaged muscles.

t: Recovery rates differ between muscles (why damage differs)
p: Part 10: The published studies behind the factors
x: A study (Chen and colleagues, 2019) had young untrained males do the same workout of nine eccentric exercises (5 sets of 10 reps at 80% of maximum voluntary isometric contraction, with a 5 second lowering). Strength was measured by isometric contractions as a percentage of baseline over five days. Strength dropped the most for the pectoralis major, biceps and triceps, and these recovered slowest. At the end of five days the pectoralis major was still well short of full recovery. The drop was smallest for the quadriceps (and calves), which were closest to full recovery by day five. Since recovery of strength is an indicator of muscle damage (and associated central fatigue), the best frequency may differ between muscle groups. Recovery of strength by muscle This is the "more easily damaged" (pectoralis major, biceps, triceps) and "less easily damaged" (quadriceps and others) distinction used in Part 5. The values in the figure are approximate, read from the published chart.

p: Part 10: The published studies behind the factors
x: The graph shows stimulus for 1, 2, 3 and 4 sets from day 1 to day 7, with a shaded stimulus period (the first 48 hours, supported by studies that correlate 48 hour MyoPS elevations with long-term hypertrophy) followed by the atrophy period. Maintenance research shows 3 sets once a week produces no gains and no losses in muscle mass. The hypertrophy stimulus from the workout cancels the atrophy that follows. A stimulus of 1.61 (the value for 3 sets) disappears over the five days after the 48 hour stimulus period, so roughly 0.32 AU is lost per day (1.61 divided by 5). One set once a week is expected to be insufficient for week-on-week hypertrophy. Conclusion: frequency matters. The retention graph in Part 6 is the redrawn version of this chart: a stimulus period of 48 hours, then the atrophy period, with the zero day moving one day later for each extra set. Sources named on the chart: Schoenfeld et al. (2017); Bickel et al. (2011), exercise dosing to retain adaptations; Damas et al. (2016), MyoPS and hypertrophy after attenuation of muscle damage.

All the programs are samples only, made to follow the studies of this lecture. Do not copy them. The statement shown with them: in the real world, effective programs are designed only after personally interacting with the client: their goals, strengths and weaknesses, likes and dislikes, available training time, preferred frequency, medical concerns and many other individual factors. No program can be called "best" unless it is created with the specific client in mind. This is where scheduling began: what, when and how to train, keeping in mind the body's natural rhythm of fatigue, progress and recovery. One or two warm-up sets are to be done before the main sets to prepare the body. The samples show only main sets.

t: Sample A: full body (three days a week, main sets per exercise)
p: Part 11: Sample programs

Friday repeats Monday and the next Monday repeats Wednesday. (The sets for those columns are taken as the same.) Points explained about this sample: Legs: squats work the hip extensors and knee extensors. The knee extensors get an isolation exercise (leg extension) on Wednesday and the knee flexors get leg curl on Monday. On Wednesday the hamstrings get the SLDL (also a kind of isolation, with hip extension). Calves are trained on both days. There are many ways to build a sample. Other muscles: latissimus dorsi (row, pulldown), pectoralis major (presses), middle deltoid (lateral raise), and elbow flexors. Count the synergists. Triceps do not have a direct exercise on Monday, but they work in the presses. On Wednesday, triceps get an extension as the prime mover; the biceps work as synergists in the pulldown. So elbow flexors are not trained only once and the triceps are not forgotten. Frequency of a muscle is counted over all the exercises where it works, not only the exercise named after it. The Monday, Wednesday and Friday pattern repeats, with the exercises alternating.

On Monday, Wednesday and Friday of a full body week you might target the pectoralis major with flat, incline and decline presses on different days (the flat press targets the sternocostal and abdominal heads, the incline the clavicular head). Now all heads can be trained on the same day, and isolation exercises (pec deck fly) can be added. Deltoid. Shoulder press for the anterior deltoid, the high row (a prone high row) for the posterior deltoid, and lateral raise for the middle deltoid. Counted together: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 sets for the deltoid overall. Latissimus dorsi. Supported row and wide grip lat pulldown (items 5 and 6) cover the diagonal and horizontal fibres (shoulder extension and shoulder adduction based exercises). Shrugs train the upper fibres of the trapezius. Biceps and triceps. A non-technical trainer sees one exercise for biceps (number 10) and one for triceps (number 11). A trainer who understands frequency knows that biceps also work in the high row (elbow flexion) and in the rows and pulldowns, and triceps work in the shoulder press and the two chest presses. Do not go overboard and do not ignore the other places where the muscle works. Lower day. There is room for tibialis anterior work (toe raises, ankle dorsiflexion) and many isolation exercises. Isolation exercises matter for some muscles when the goal is hypertrophy. The choice depends on the goal.

Course: Personal Training Certification Topic: Scheduling, part 2 of 2 (analysing and designing a workout split) About these notes: Short revision version of the Scheduling 2 lecture. For the full explanation of every concept, example and class question, see the Detailed Notes. Sources: the lecture recording, the course slides ("Scheduling"), the board photos and the published graphs shown in class. Big idea: The number of main sets per muscle, the recovery needed, and how often the muscle is trained all fit together. Fewer sets work if you train the muscle more often, because each set adds less (diminishing returns) and the stimulus fades unless the muscle is trained again. Full body, upper/lower and PPL/bro splits are three frequency categories, and any training level can use any of them if the set range is respected.

Master table Main sets per muscle | Recovery | Weekly outlook | Frequency | Splits | Ideal sets | Upper limit | 1 to 3 | 48 h | Mon, Wed, Fri, rest Sun | 3x a week | Full body (FBW) | 1 to 2 | 3 | 4 to 5 | 72 h | Mon, Thu, rest Sun | 2x a week | Upper/lower (U/L) | 2 to 3 | 5 | More than 5 | 1 week | Mon, rest Sun, next Mon | 1x a week | PPL, bro split | 6 to 8 | 10 | Sets are main sets per muscle (not warm-up sets, not all exercises together). Frequency is per muscle, not per WT day. Upper/lower has four WT days, but each muscle is trained twice. A non-WT day is not a rest day: it can be used for cardio. Sunday is the one mandatory rest day. A workout split is how your weight training sessions are arranged across the week, following some logic.

Split | Logic | Example week | Full body | Whole body every session | Mon F, Wed F, Fri F, Sun R | Upper/lower | Upper body muscles on upper days, lower body on lower days | Mon U, Tue L, Thu U, Fri L, Sun R | Push, pull, legs | Grouped by movement pattern. Pull: back and biceps. Push: chest, shoulders, triceps. Legs | Mon P, Wed Pull, Fri L, Sat cardio, Sun R | Bro (body part) split | One body part per day; avoid shoulder work on back-to-back days | Back, chest, gap, legs, shoulders, arms, cardio, rest |

t: 3. Training level and F and I
x: F is proportional to 1/I: when intensity is low, frequency can be high, and vice versa. Beginners train at low intensity (15 to 20 RM), so high frequency is fine. Beginners also need high frequency to build neural pathways, the kinetic chain, proprioception, grip and tightness, and the Valsalva breathing technique. Training a muscle once a week would stretch the 2 to 3 month beginner phase. Hence full body, three days a week, is best for beginners. The belief that full body is only for beginners is a myth: intermediate and advanced lifters can use it too, with the correct set range.

Diminishing returns Sets | Net stimulus | Added by this set | 1 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 2 | 1.39 | 0.39 | 3 | 1.61 | 0.22 | 4 | 1.77 | 0.16 | 5 | 1.90 | 0.13 | 6 | 2.00 | 0.10 | The unit is arbitrary (AU). The lecture shows it as rupees to make it easier to relate to. "Added by this set" is the difference between consecutive totals (for example 1.61 minus 1.39 = 0.22). Six sets are needed to double the stimulus of one set. Sets 2 to 6 together add about 1.00, the same as set 1. Beyond six sets: 7 sets about 2.09, 8 about 2.16, 9 about 2.23. Muscle damage rises with more sets and pulls the net stimulus into an inverted U. This is why there are upper limits (max 3, 5, 10). More easily damaged muscles turn down earlier.

Retention Stimulus is not stored forever. If the muscle is not trained again, it reaches zero on day (sets + 4), counting the training day as day 1. 1 set: day 5. 2 sets: day 6. 3 sets: day 7. 4 sets: day 8. 5 sets: day 9. 6 sets: day 10. Each extra set buys about one more day. This applies to every level; only the weight and the person differ.

Low frequency with few sets means the stimulus is at zero before the next session, so nothing is carried forward. High frequency lets you keep the ball in the air with few sets per session. Lower frequency, more sets. Higher frequency, fewer sets. Split (frequency) | Sets per session | Net weekly stimulus | FBW (3x) | 2 | 1.39 x 3 = 4.17 | Upper/lower (2x) | 3 | 1.61 x 2 = 3.22 | PPL / bro (1x) | 6 | 2.00 | Weekly net stimulus Training a muscle three times a week gives the highest weekly stimulus. PPL and bro splits are not bad: they give room for many specific exercises per muscle, which suits bodybuilders.

Hypertrophy is growth of muscle cell size. Atrophy is shrinkage. GAS is general adaptation syndrome. MyoPS is myofibrillar protein synthesis (building the contractile proteins myosin and actin inside the myofibril). Hypertrophy (MyoPS) continues for the first 48 hours after training. After that, atrophy begins. Ball analogy: shoot the ball up again before it hits the ground. Cycles Atrophy days per week in the figure: 5 (once a week), 3 (twice a week), 1 (three times a week). FBW (3x): the 48 hour window ends exactly on the next training day, so almost no atrophy occurs during the week. U/L (2x): the muscle is trained again on day 4, before zero (day 7). PPL/bro (1x): 6 sets last until day 10, and the next session (day 8) carries some balance forward.

Recovery vs sets Recovery by muscle Recovery time rises roughly in line with the number of sets: up to 3 sets about 48 h, 4 to 5 sets about 72 h, 10 to 12 sets about a week. Muscles differ: the pectoralis major, biceps and triceps recover slowest (more easily damaged). Quadriceps and calves recover fastest. Maintenance research: 3 sets once a week gives no gain and no loss; about 0.32 units are lost per day after the 48 h window. The figures are redrawn from the published charts (values approximate).

Samples are not to be copied. Real programs are built around the client's goals, strengths, weaknesses, likes, time, preferred frequency and medical concerns. No program is "best" unless made for the specific client. Do 1 or 2 warm-up sets before the main sets. Count synergists: biceps work in rows and pulldowns, triceps work in presses. Frequency counts every exercise where the muscle works. A dedicated upper day gives room to hit all heads of the pectoralis major (flat for sternocostal and abdominal, incline for clavicular) and to add isolation. Main sets per muscle per session (not warm-up sets, not all exercises together). 1 to 3 sets: 48 h, thrice a week. 4 to 5: 72 h, twice. More than 5: 1 week, once. Frequency is counted per muscle. Each muscle is trained twice even though there are four WT days. Full body, upper/lower, and PPL or bro split. By movement pattern: pull (back, biceps), push (chest, shoulders, triceps), and legs. One body part a day. Shoulders are kept apart so the joint is not used on back-to-back days. F is proportional to 1/I: high frequency goes with low intensity. Neural pathways, the kinetic chain, proprioception, grip and tightness, and the Valsalva technique (any three). Low intensity allows high frequency, which speeds the learning phase. Intermediate and advanced lifters also gain with full body if they follow the set range. 1.00 for one set; 1.39 for two. 1.61 minus 1.39 = 0.22. Six sets (2.00). Each extra set adds less stimulus than the previous one, even though the total rises. Muscle damage rises with sets and is deducted from the stimulus. Day (sets + 4), with the training day as day 1. Higher frequency retrains the muscle before the stimulus reaches zero, so fewer sets are enough; once a week must use more sets to carry some balance forward. 4.17, 3.22 and 2.00. General adaptation syndrome and myofibrillar protein synthesis; about 48 hours. The day atrophy would begin is the day of the next session, so almost none occurs. 3x a week: 1 to 2 (max 3). 2x: 2 to 3 (max 5). 1x: 6 to 8 (not above 10).
